Tabling of Documents—Description of Documents

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Yesterday you set out a very clear set of requirements for tab ling documents:
the source, the date, and a brief description. Yesterday the Minister of Health tabled a
document, with the approval of this House, that does not have the source identified and
has a different date from that claimed by the Minister in the H ouse. I am going to ask
you to look at this because we want consistent application of your requirements for the
tabling of documents. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I will look at the matter.
Economy—Employment
1. CHRIS BISHOP (Nation al) to the Minister of Finance : What reports has he
received on the outlook for the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: More positive reports on the outlook
for the New Zealand economy. Treasury released its Monthly Economic Indicators
report for April. It says that economic growth looks set to continue over the first half of
2015, supported by business and consumer confidence and elevated levels of investment
and hiring intentions, despite recent easing of those measures. The cost of living has
fallen in each of the last two quarters for the first time since 1999, and inflation
expectations and the expectation of businesses to increase their prices remain subdued.
With no sign of emerging inflation or interest rate pressure, which might normally be
expected when an economy is growing at 3 percent, the economy is exhibiting capacity
for further sustainable growth.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What are some of the current challenges and opportunities for New
Zealand businesses and households?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One of the challenges is, of course, the reality of lower
commodity prices. This includes the fall in dairy prices, which has continued in April.
Dairy prices are now back at levels last seen in December 2014. However, it is worth
putting this in an international context. Between mid -2011 and December 2014, New
Zealand terms of trade have actua lly increased by 3 percent. In the same period, the
Australian terms of trade fell by 23 percent, due to a large fall in the iron ore price. So,
although dairy prices are down, overall our terms of trade are roughly flat, and that
compares favourably with Australia, where the terms of trade have fallen by 23 percent.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of those answers, how does the Minister reconcile his
trumpeted 3 percent growth figure with the fact that in Northland unemployment is 9.9
percent, in Manawatū and Wanganui it is over 7 percent, and in Gisborne and Hawke’s
Bay it is over 7 percent, and that wage rises over the last period have been the lowest
that they have been in 2 years —where is the benefit in growth in the economy for
working New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: At any given time the growth rate is an average across the
country. The member, I presume, is not suggesting that someone is making up the
growth numbers. They come from Statistics New Zealand, which has stat utory
3216 Oral Questions  6 May 2015
independence. If the member wants to use anecdotes, unemployment in the South Island
is under 4 percent. I have to say, coming from the South Island, we would welcome
people from Wanganui, Gisborne, and Auckland turning up to fill the empty jobs in t he
South Island. One of the surprising things about this cycle is how sticky unemployment
appears to be in some areas where, clearly, there are not as many jobs as there are in the
South Island.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What reports has he received sho wing how growth in the economy is
helping to deliver more jobs and higher wages for New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Labour market statistics released today show that 16,000
more people were employed in the March quarter, meaning that in  the year to March
74,000 jobs were added to the economy. Labour force participation is now at an all-time
high of 69.6 percent and New Zealand has the fourth -highest employment rate in the
OECD—that is, the fourth-highest proportion of the working -age population actually in
work. Average wages increased by 2 percent over the same period, well ahead of
inflation of 0.1 percent.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What were the main drivers of employment growth over the last year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Employment growth has been reasonably broad -based.
Construction added 23,000 additional jobs. Retail, accommodation, and food services
added 14,000 jobs, and we know that Labour’s “manufacturing crisis” continues,
because the manufacturing sector added 1 6,000 jobs in the last year. Members in the
House may recall that in 2011 the Budget forecast 170,000 additional jobs by about
now, and the economy is over 20,000 ahead of that forecast.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I seek leave to table a document pre pared by the Parliamentary
Library, dated yesterday or today, which—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Yesterday, I am pretty sure. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is making a point of order. I wish to hear it. So
it is dated today, we have established.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Either yesterday or today. It came into my in-box overnight.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: All right. Just quickly describe the document and I will decide
whether to put the leave.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: The document is clear that a third of the economic growth is
attributable to the—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not need any more. The point of tabling that document
is to make a political point. It is not to inform members.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member attempting to relitigate a decision I have just made?
Because that will require the member to be leaving the Chamber immediately.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: It is a point of clarification.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not interested in a point of clarification. If it is a fresh point
of—[Interruption] Order! The level of complaints I had because of the noise coming
from this sector yesterday means that I intend to do something about it. I have ruled that
I am not interested in putting that piece of information to the House. It does not require
a point of clarification. My mind is absolutely clear. If the member has a fresh poin t of
order I will hear it, but I am not going to have arguments continuing on that particular
point of order. If the member wants to leave the Chamber, he is certainly welcome to do
so.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order. It had better be a fresh point of
order.
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3217

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Do you intend to rule on the length of answers we are getting
from the Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will also resume her seat. I will judge, as I have
said on many occasions, the length of answers. But when there are constant interjections
coming from my left -hand side to the Minister who is answering the question, clearly
that gives the opportunity for the Minister to then be responding to those interjections.
Whānau Ora—Auditor-General’s Report
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
have confidence in his Ministers’ implementation of the Whānau Ora programme in
light of the Auditor -General’s report finding $42 million of its $138 million budget in
its first 4 years was spent on administration?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: After the $42 million spent on administration and the untold millions
eaten up by service providers, how much Whānau Ora money is actually reaching
families in need?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have the exact number, but I can quote the Auditor -
General’s report where she talks about the success Whānau Ora has had for the many
families that they spoke to.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Wh y, when 2 years ago the Government announced Whānau Ora
was being overhauled because it was wasteful and ineffective, has nothing changed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Quite to the contrary, actually. I acknowledge that there were
some early teething  issues. When you try something new against a very complex and
complicated environment, and an environment that actually had not been delivering for
those families, I accept that there were some teething issues. But there are now joint
agencies, and what has happened is there are now three commissioning agencies. I think
the new structure that is in place is seeing a greater provision of services for those
families with those complex needs.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: When did senior Ministers on the Cro wn-iwi Whānau Ora
Partnership Group advise him that there were issues of wasteful spending in Whānau
Ora?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I simply do not have those dates, but I do know that over time
there have been reviews. As I said, the system was n ew and it was trying to tackle these
needs for complex families. I think it is actually building into a programme that has
been very successful for those families. In fact, if you go and have a look at the Ministry
of Health, for example, it has done a rev iew of Whānau Ora general practices and
compared them with mainstream general practices, and it has gone on to say that
Whānau Ora performs as well or better. This is a new way of doing things —putting
families at the heart of solving those issues, with a n avigator, with these commissioning
agencies, and I do think it is building into a programme that is delivering results.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has it taken the Auditor -General’s office and an expensive
audit report by her to identify the wastef ul spending and the $42 million spent on
administration, when he had Ministers such as Bill English and Steven Joyce sitting on
the Crown -iwi Whānau Ora Partnership Group who were there to advise him on the
progress of the implementation of Whānau Ora?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not think the member accurately categorises things. What
has happened is there were some one -off costs and there has been a new way of doing
things. I think that came with those costs and with some early teething issues. But the
changes that took pl ace took place because of the review work done by a variety of
Ministers, including the work done by Te Puni Kōkiri and by Tariana Turia, when she
was in Parliament. It actually led to these commissioning agencies, and I think they
3218 Oral Questions  6 May 2015
have done a much better job of tightening up the system and delivering the results we
want.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Having spent $137 million of taxpayers’ money on Whānau Ora,
does he agree with the Auditor -General that “It was not easy to describe what it is or
what it has achieved.”; if so, what consequences will his Ministers face?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, as I said, the Auditor -General’s report does not cover,
for the most part, the phase where now you have got the commissioning agencies. So
that is the first point I would make. Secondly, what I would say is that this is an area
where we have always spent a lot of money —successive Governments have, and
actually they have failed to deliver results. One of the reasons is that these families have
very, very complicated needs. So when you look at Whānau Ora, which nowadays has
commissioning agents, within that it has the providers that go out there and it has
navigators—the people who actually sit alongside the families and help them navigate a
range of different agencies and support measures. Actually, I think that is the right way
of tackling a very complicated and difficult area.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he accept that had he bothered to get value for money out of
Whānau Ora and other Government programmes he would now be in a position to keep
his promise to post a surplus in the Budget?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, quite the opposite, actually. This Government, over the
course of the last 6 ½ years, has challenged the siloed approach that was in place under
the previous Government. Actually, what it has delivered are far better results. That is
why the Government is actually quite happy to have Better Public Services targets, why
it actually measures those targets, and why, from everyt hing from health to education to
welfare, we are delivering better results for New Zealanders. We are doing things a
different way and, frankly, it is a more integrated and better way.
State and Social Housing—Sale of Housing Stock
3. TODD MULLER (Natio nal—Bay of Plenty)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: What recent announcements have been made about the next steps of the
Government’s Social Housing Reform Programme?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Bill English and I today
announced that Tauranga and Invercargill have been selected as the first regions for the
proposed transfer of Housing New Zealand houses into community ownership. This is
another important step in creating a more effective and efficient social housing sector,
and is a fantastic opportunity for community housing providers in these areas to deliver
housing services locally.  No decisions have been made on the number of houses that
will be transferred into community ownership.

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: Why have these areas been selected?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Tauranga and Invercargill have been chosen because they
have active community housing providers, as well as stable demand for social housing.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: And docile MPs.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: And I might add to that member that they have also got
fantastic members of Parliament in both places who actually understand their
communities and are able to do that. Actually, what is really important is there are very
good local people who understand local needs and are able to deliver services locally.
We want to back that, and that is part of this programme.

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: What does this announcement mean for tenants?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I think it is really important that tenants understand that
they will continue to be housed for the duration of their needs, that their rent will not go
up if houses are transferred, and that their eligibility for income -related rent will not
change unless their own circumstances do. These are tenants in these regions with long
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3219
and medium-term needs, which gives community providers the opportunity to integrate
housing with other services that they might provide, like mental health and disability
support and alcohol and drug counselling. The whole Social Housing Reform
Programme is about helping more l ow-income and vulnerable New Zealanders receive
the support that they need.
Budget 2015—Return to Surplus
4. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements in relation to the Budget?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, in the context they were given. I
particularly stand by my statement that Budget 2015 will be delivered in the context of a
strong and growing economy and improving Government finances.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Having failed to keep his promise to get the books into surplus this
year, will he guarantee New Zealanders that he will not be breaking any other promises?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think New Zealanders are smart enough to work out that this
is a Government that has picked up a hell of a mess from the previous Labour
Government. It was a disaster that it inherited —a pil e of unfunded programmes and,
frankly, economic leadership that would be welcomed in Greece but actually is not
welcomed in New Zealand—and it has tidied the shop up.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: In light of his backdown on getting to surplus this year, when will he
be honest with New Zealanders and give a real date on when he will finally post a
surplus?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is important to understand that the data that will be in the
Budget, like the data that is in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update and all the
others, is put together by Treasury based on the best estimates it has. As I said to the
House yesterday, interestingly enough, the revenue number for the Crown over the next
4 years is $15 billion lower than it would  have been, because of low inflation. It
happens to be great for businesses and for consumers—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Take some responsibility.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, actually, I will take responsibility for the fact that the
economy is growing, we have got the fifth -highest employment rate in the OECD, and
New Zealanders are flocking back to New Zealand having left in droves under the
previous Labour Government.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Can he confirm that he also has not kept his pr omise to lift exports
from 30 percent of GDP to 40 percent —in fact, exports have fallen back to just 29
percent of GDP?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am truly ambitious for New Zealand and for myself , but I
never realised that Andrew Little was so a mbitious for me, because that is our 2025
target. He is clearly expecting me to win quite a few elections between now and then.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: In light of the consistent slide in prices in recent global dairy
auctions, when can New Zealanders expect him to finally keep his export promise?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I thought we traversed this in the House yesterday, but the
Government is not responsible for dairy prices. I know that the Opposition might want
to blame us for them; it certainly did not want to give us any credit for them when they
were going up, but it does seem to want to criticise us when they are going down. But,
actually, here is a pretty simple test. We want to grow our exports. Let us sign up to the
Trans-Pacific Partnership. We are in. Are you in?

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Having failed to keep his promises, when will he stop making
excuses, front up, and admit he has let New Zealanders down yet again?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We are not making excu ses; we are actually presenting the
Government’s books. Actually, if the member wants to look at any indicators from
3220 Oral Questions  6 May 2015
consumer confidence, business confidence, right indicators, wrong indicators, the
election result, the exchange rate movements—all of those things are indicators that it is
not me who is telling New Zealanders that the country is going well; it is actually New
Zealanders who are indicating to pollsters and others that the country is going well.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Give them some credit.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, so give those New Zealanders credit; they know what
they are talking about.
Human Rights, Saudi Arabia—Trade Agreements
5. JAMES SHAW (Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by his statement
in relation to trade with Saudi Arabia that an “… FTA gives us yet another reason for
those relationships to grow and be closer together …”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My statement actually referred to the
potential free-trade agreement with the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the
Gulf, which covers six Gulf States. I stand by my statement: a free-trade agreement with
that group gives another reas on for relationships to grow and be closer together and
more focused for our businesses.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Why is he giving preferential treatment to a regime that has beheaded
72 people this year—three of whom were beheaded the day he flew out?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not think you can say we are giving preferential
treatment. What we are doing is trading with Saudi Arabia and with other countries that
make up the Gulf cooperation council. That is not actually new. The member probabl y
knows that our trade with the Gulf States is our fifth largest. In fact, we sell more
exports to the Gulf States than we do to the United Kingdom. Actually, we have been
doing trade for a long period of time. Eighteen senior business leaders came with me
because they actually see this as a market of opportunity. In the last question I just had
the Leader of the Opposition telling me he wanted us to do more in terms of exports.
Well, that is what we were doing last week: leading a trade delegation to grow our
exports.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Has he raised human rights with the Saudi regime, and will he make
any preferential trade agreement conditional on human rights being improved and
beheadings being stopped?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In terms o f the latter part of the question, no; in terms of the
former part of the question, yes. In fact, we had quite an extensive discussion with King
Salman, and we did raise human rights. And, actually, I might make the point that not
only did we raise it and have a reasonably extensive discussion  but we did more than
President Obama did, who did not actually raise human rights when he went to Saudi
Arabia. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Supplementary question, James
Shaw—[Interruption] Order! I am on my feet. I have called for order again, to allow Mr
Shaw to ask a supplementary question; the barrage continued. I will next be asking
somebody to leave the Chamber, to demonstrate that we have got to have a level of
decorum while questions are being asked.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Given that he has raised beheadings and human rights abuses with the
Saudi regime, what evidence does he have that the Saudi regime is improving its human
rights and stopping beheadings as a result of our trade agreement with them?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have with me the details of their record in this area
over time. But what I would say, though, is that there are two ways of approaching these
things, are there not? One is, ultimately, one of isolation, and one is engagement. And if
the member is suggesting that we should put Saudi Arabia into the camp of isolation,
then that is a legitimate argument you can make. But I would say that we also do not
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3221
agree with the death penalty in c ountries like the United States, and is he really arguing
that because Texas executes people we should actually have an isolationist policy when
it comes to the United States? My experience as Prime Minister is that when you have
good trading relationships , when you get to know people better, you can have more
fruitful discussions. And, actually, over time, I think you genuinely see change. I am not
saying Saudi Arabia has a record that we want in human rights, but the evidence that
people on the ground, at  least, suggested to me, is that over the last few decades it has
improved a bit.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: So does he stand by his statement to this House “I will not … stand by
… when people out there are being beheaded”, or does that apply only to non -trading
partners?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I absolutely stand by that statement. And there is a difference
between a country that has its own constitution, its own laws, and decides to follow
those laws, and the actions of a terrorist group. I might not agree, and I do not agree,
with the death penalty, but, as I said to the member, it is not solely unique to Saudi
Arabia. It is also true in the United States and other countries. It happens to be true, as
we know from last week, in Indonesia. In  the end, actually, there is quite a lot of
difference between a country and a terrorist group like the Islamic State of Iraq and the
Levant (ISIL).

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does he think it makes any difference to the people who are being
beheaded whether they are being beheaded by the Saudi regime or by ISIL?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the member is actually better than a sort of somewhat
flippant question. When people die it is a terrible thing, and I do not agree with
beheadings. But I am just saying that people live in that country and those are the rules
and laws of that country, just like we have rules and laws over here that people might
not agree with.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: How bad would human rights abuses have to be in another country for
New Zealand not to give preferential trade treatment to that country?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not think we are giving preferential treatment. What we
are trying to do is negotiate a free -trade agreement, which allows access on a  more
beneficial footing to both parties —and this happens to be the Gulf States, Saudi being
one of those six partners. If the member’s argument is that we should not actually
negotiate free-trade agreements with countries that have human rights records th at we
do not agree with, then you could apply that to quite a number of countries —and they
are countries that the previous Government also signed free-trade agreements with.
Whānau Ora—Auditor-General’s Report
6. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by his statement in regards to Whānau Ora, “They have to be ambitious
themselves—it’s a higher trust model and it has the potential to deliver better results not
only for families, but also for taxpayers who are not currently getting the value for
money they should be.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he agree with the Auditor -General in regard to
Whānau Ora that, using her words, “It was not easy to describe what it is or what it has
achieved.”, or that “We could not get a consistent explanation of the aims of the
initiatives in Whānau Ora”, or that “the situation has been unclear and confusing”; and
what, if anything, has he done about it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In terms of the latter part of the question, quite a bit, actually.
There has been a tightening up  of the system with the commissioning agents and
various other reviews that have taken place. In terms of the former part of the question,
3222 Oral Questions  6 May 2015
as I say, improvements have been made, but it is a new way of doing things in a highly
complex area. The member happe ns to be the MP for Northland. He probably knows
that in Northland there are some very complicated cases with families that need help
across a range of agencies. I am sure that when he is in his electorate office on
Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays , and Fridays, when he is not in
Parliament, seeing those constituents, he will have many of them coming to him talking
about those complicated needs. I look forward to seeing those constituents seeing him—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The answer is too long.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Talking about Northland, how come a third of all payments
made to Whānau Ora provider collectives went to just two of Te Puni Kōkiri’s 10
regions, and those two regions also happened , by sheer coincidence , to be where two
former Māori Party Ministers come from; and what did he do as Prime Minister to stop
this blatantly preferential treatment?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I reject the member’s proposition. Section 5 of the report  has
where all the money was spent and the different agencies that got them.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I asked him a very
serious question, and I am waiting for an answer. It is no use saying to me that section 5
has got where the money was spent.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Prime Minister rose to his feet and disputed the figures
that the member had given in his question. That is an answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If he wants to dispute that fact, which is easy to analyse—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just ask the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I am asking the question—all right?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. Now he will stand and
withdraw that remark immediately or leave the Chamber.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Which remark, Mr Speaker?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Stand and withdraw, without embellishment.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, I withdraw the remark if it was offending you, but I
had two remarks there.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just withdraw the remark, otherwise I will be—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I withdraw.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Now the member, when I ask him to take a supplementary question,
will stand and simply ask the supplementary question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he aware, if he wants to put that graph of expenditure
into contention, that nearly a quarter of all individuals accessing Whānau Ora funding
through the Whānau Integration, Innovation and Engagement Fund between 2010—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Is this English? Who wrote this?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, I wrote it myself, unlike that clown up there. I am
able to do my own homework.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! My patience will expire very quickly with this memb er. The
question should be concise. I will allow the member to start the question again, but
would he refrain from commenting, even if there is an interjection.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he aware that nearly a quarter of all individu als
accessing Whānau Ora funding through the Whānau Integration, Innovation and
Engagement Fund between 2010 and 2012 went to just one of Te Puni Kōkiri’s 10
regions, and that that region was where the former Minister for Whanāu Ora came from;
if so, what, if anything, did he do about that bias?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have two points. As I said in my earlier answer, the Office of
the Auditor-General report breaks down on a year-by-year basis the costs in regions and
the distribution of the mon ey in Part 5 of the report. I go on to say that the report says
that there is no suggestion of misspending or other unscrupulous activity. In relation to
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3223
the second point the member made about the Whānau Integration, Innovation and
Engagement Fund that was established, the point is that Whānau Ora was established in
about 2010. It had to start in one place. It did not roll out everywhere because there just
was not that capability all around the country from day one.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Pet ers
items.text: Which is a better use of Government resources: $20,000
spent on special needs education to support children with dyslexia and other conditions;
or the $20,000 his Government spent through Whānau Ora on Dunedin gang members,
who then used the money to buy cannabis; or $80,000 to Whānau Ora for the
Palmerston North women’s refuge, without one client, with the rest going, of course, to
the European women’s refuge; or $60,000 for Ōtaki’s Rahui rugby club for a 1 -day
hooley?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KE Y
items.text: I do not have the details of every individual one of those, but
what I can say is this: if you go back and look at the history of New Zealand and the
complications of these families and where that leads, you can see that if we have
somebody who goes to prison, it costs $105,000 a year to have that prisoner there.
When we have children growing up in very dysfunctional families—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was very
specific. I have been waiting, and I am waiting for—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat. The
question asked which one was the better use of taxpayers’ money, and then the member
gave quite a number of examples. The Prime Minister is attempting to explain the use of
taxpayers’ money, if you would allow the Prime Minister to finish his answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My main point is really that these are families that have high
needs. They have complicated needs, and ther e are a lot of costs incurred by the
Government and successive Governments as we try to support these families. Actually,
I think the way we have dealt with these issues in the past has not proven to be good
value for money for taxpayers.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston P eters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I set out one
alternative and three options. When will I get my answer? I am not hearing it yet.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member, if he had been listening, has had his answer. The
question has been addressed. If he wants to continue with a supplementary question, I
suggest he try.
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus
7. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by all his answers to Oral Question No. 12 yesterday?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, and I particularly stand by my
statement where I said that I stand by my statements.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has he received forecasts from Treasury that show a deficit for
the 2015-16 year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As I have indicated a number of times, the forecast s in the
Budget are likely to show, compared with the half -yearly update, a slightly increased
deficit for 2014-15 and lower surpluses for 2015-16.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek leave of the House to table an Official Information Act
document released by Treasury, dated 7 November 2014, which forecasts a deficit for
the 2015-16 year.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that particular Official Information Act
document. Is there any objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
3224 Oral Questions  6 May 2015

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that Treasury advised him that even if he made the
cuts to the Budget forward -spending allowance that he did, the surplus in 2015 -16
would happen only if the fall in dairy prices significantly rebounded?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Treasury may have given that advice at some stage; I do not
recall it. What I can tell the member is that the Budget is a fairly dynamic process —that
is, it is an interaction of Government decision -making and new information —and he
will just have to wait for the Budget later in May to see exactly where Treasury and the
Government ended up.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer, does the Minister recall paragraph (e) of
the paper dated 7 November 2014, which says that a Budget surplus in 2015 -16 could
happen only assuming dairy prices rebound as currently forecast?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not recall that particular paragraph, and in any case,
I would not say the advice is wrong; I would say it is partial. As we have discussed in
the House before, there are a lot of factors that lead to the operating balance of the
Government—the whole sweep of $73 billion of expenditure  and what is happening
with that—and, as we have discussed a lot over the last couple of weeks, other factors
that were not known in November, such as the inflation rate being a lot lower than
expected, and the impact of that on the total size of the economy.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is he aware of the Goldman Sachs report from July last year that
indicated that there was a 5 -year global milk glut, and that with the further fall in milk
prices last night, there is now a $7 billion hole in the New Zealand economy, and did he
take that into account when assessing whether a surplus was possible in 2015 -16, even
with a reduction in spending?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There have been any number of reports about where dairy
prices might or might not go, but I am a bit surprised at the Opposition attitude, because
those members are usually advocating that we have too much dairy, and so presumably
they are pleased when the prices are lower and the industry is not doing so well.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that not only has he failed to deliver his promised
surplus for 7 years but he is actually on track to fail for an eighth year in 2015 -16,
unless there is a major rebound in global dairy prices, which no one is predicting?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, but I can tell you that 8 years of political failure by the
Labour Party must be a lot more painful.
Broadband, Ultra-fast and Rural—Progress
8. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Communications
items.text: What progress can she report on the rollout of the Ultra -Fast
Broadband and Rural Broadband Initiatives?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Today I have released the
latest quarterly update on our ultra -fast broadband and Rural Broadband Initiative
programmes, showing that both continue to be ahead of schedule. With 46 percent of
the build complete, 618,000 homes, workplaces, and schools are now able to connect —
10 percent ahead of schedule. Eighty percent of the towers to be upgraded under the
Rural Broadband Initiative programme are complete, with an estimated 239,000 rural
households and businesses n ow able to connect. Uptake continues to be strong, with
85,000 end users connected to ultra -fast broadband, giving us an overall uptake rate of
13.8 percent.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What reports has she seen on the response of glo bal
industry experts to the ultra-fast broadband programme?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I have recently seen a report from international technology
company Alcatel -Lucent, which has evaluated the ultra-fast broadband and Rural
Broadband Initiative programmes in light of its international experience. The Alcatel
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3225
report is a glowing endorsement of the ultra-fast broadband and Rural B roadband
Initiative programmes, describing them as “uniquely well managed and cost effective”.
It sing les out the effect ive use of  public and private partnerships to deliver the
programmes, a flexible regulatory framework, and tender processes that create, in its
view, “a pioneering project designed to position New Zealand at the forefront of global
innovation and economic transformation”, and, I have to say, I agree.
Building and Construction Industry—High-alkali Cement
9. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Minister for Building
and Housing: Does he still accept assurances from officials that concrete used in New
Zealand is fit for purpose?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.role: Minister for Building and Hous ing
items.text: The member some
months ago sought assurance on whether imported high -alkali cement was fit for
purpose. The current issue is not about the standard of cement but concrete. One of
Firth’s batching plants in Auckland had a malfunction due to a faulty l oad sensor,
resulting in the incorrect mix and about 1,000 cubic metres of substandard concrete
being supplied to 35 customers. The cement used was not high-alkali, was not imported,
and was not at fault. The member seems confused about the difference betw een cement
and concrete. The former is costing—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It will be apparent to
you that this was a very simple question. How the member could be confused with
anything else, which is what he saying now, is surely nothing to do with the question. I
have asked him a simple question —is the concrete fit for purpose —and he is now
attacking me for no good reason at all. I have not started on him yet.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Speaking to the point of order—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not need any assistance. The issue of the question is, has
he accepted the assurances that everything is in order? If that could be addressed, I
would be happy.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, I will hear from the member.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The question is in respect of “does he still accept
assurances”. The assurances that I gave in the question in February, as you will clearly
see from Hansard, was in respect of cement, not concrete. I have given this member—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can the member simply answer the question today —has he
accepted the assurances? That is the question that is being asked. I will invite the Rt
Hon Winston Peters to re-ask his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker.  Does he still accept assurances
from officials that concrete used in New Zealand is fit for purpose?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I have not given the member any assurances in respect of
concrete. I did give him assurances in respect of cement. It is a pity the member does
not understand the difference. Perhaps I will take him to a building site.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: You sound like a concrete block right now. Is he—

items.speaker: Hon Maggie Barry
items.text: Says the member who’s named after one.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Oh, lighten up, honey. Is he aware that a batch of imported
cement in 2014 exceeded the 0.6 percent alkali safety level; if so, what did he do in
response to this issue at the time?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I sought advice from my officials. The member has not
produced a single qualified engineer who has concern about the high -alkali cement. The
concern is that if the cement is used correctly —as per the New Zealand standard —and
is mixed correctly, it produces perfectly safe and credible concrete.
3226 Oral Questions  6 May 2015

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If that is the case, if his officials were able to assure him
that imported cement is meeting the standard and does not pose a safety risk to the
public as he has stated again today, why, then, have officials in his office on 22 July
2014 stated that they were in a state of panic on getting questions on this issue?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Last year I asked for advice from officials about the
cement. They said that it complied with the standard. I made the point to ask whether
there were any engineers—people who are actually qualified in this subject —who were
concerned about it. The answer was there were not. My simple chall enge to the member
is if he has got a concern about high -alkali cement, rather than talking to those parties
who do not want to have imported cement competing with that in New Zealand, give us
an engineer’s report that has got concerns.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If it is good enough for Firth to do full plug inspections of
its concrete to ascertain the quality of it, why was he not prepared to do that on the
buildings that allegations of faulty cement were made about, rather than rely u pon
industry-conflicted assurances?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I relied on the advice of officials, who I do not believe are
conflicted. In respect of the difficulty that has occurred with Firth, it is not an issue with
the integrity of the ce ment. The issue is that a weighing device failed, the correct mix
did not occur, and the concrete is not up to strength. That has been picked up in the
testing, and the responsibility rests with Firth to work that issue through with the 35
customers who we re supplied with the understrength concrete. I stress that the cement
that was used in the Firth issue is perfectly up to standard.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: When will the Minister understand that this is not a
question about Firth but  about substandard concrete from imported cement that itself
was substandard, and why has he not conducted one test on any of the buildings in
which it is alleged this concrete cement was used?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I repeat the simple challenge I gave the member at the time
to table a single qualified engineer’s report of concern about the alkali cement, and I am
happy to then seek a review of that. Without that evidence the member is simply
playing a game of competition within the industry.
Health Services—Access
10. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Health:
Are patients receiving through New Zealand’s health care system the health care
recommended by their medical practitioner; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Yes, they are, and there
have been remarkable improvements over the last 6 years. This is reflected in the extra
50,000 first specialist assessments and 44,000 elective surgeries that are now being
delivered each year compared with 2008. Patients who are recommended for cancer
treatment are also receiving that faster and withou t being flown to Australia, as was the
practice prior to 2008.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If patients are receiving the care their medical practitioner
recommends, why did general practitioner Dr Tony Farrell from the Bay of Plenty come
out publicly on Saturday and say: “people whose X-rays showed bone on bone and were
in terrible pain were not being seen in a timely manner.”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: General practitioners do not direct treatment;
they seek a specialist opinion from a surgeon at the hospital. When they put that referral
in, there might be various reasons why there is not actually a specialist appointment or a
surgery. The information might be incomplete, there might be a need for further testing,
or it may actually be that that condition, like bone on bone arthritis, is better treated in
the community. So the situation is exactly not what she represents it as.
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3227

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Has he replied to Mrs Logan, who wrote to him on 17 April
asking why her husband has had to live with an internal catheter for the past 7 months,
which has blocked nine times, with severe effects on his health and daily life, and still
does not qualify for elective surgery?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN C OLEMAN
items.text: Obviously, I am not familiar with that
individual case, and, as Annette King said when she was the Minister: “It’s better to
help people than to use them.” But that notwithstanding, if Mrs King would like to send
me the details of the case, I can look into it to see what the real truth of it is.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What was his response to Mrs Leota, who wrote to him, the
Prime Minister, and her local member of Parliament 3 weeks ago highlighting the
number of people in Invercargill  living “with extenuating pain because they don’t have
enough points to qualify for a hip operation” and asking for urgent action?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: If the member just waits till 3.30, she might get
a very nice surprise as to what is happening in the community for people with
orthopaedic hip pain.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What reply did he give to Grey Power Hastings, which wrote to
him and the local member of Parliament, Craig Foss, on 4 March telling him how
concerned it was about the rejection letters older people in the Hawke’s Bay were
receiving and asking for “more honesty and fewer weasel words. Why pretend you can
offer a service that you can’t?”

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: In the Haw ke’s Bay, the percentage of first
specialist appointments has increased by 41 percent over the last 6 years, and there has
been a major uplift in elective surgery as well. There have been an extra 1,278
operations performed each year. So I am sure that if the former Minister goes and asks
her close relative the chief operations officer of Hawke’s Bay District Health Board, she
will be able to hear the truth, because I am sure this information is not being leaked by
him—surely not.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am wondering whom I
have to ask.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not a point of order. If the member wants to have a
supplementary question, use it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a po int of order, Mr Speaker. The member asks a
question of me. What is my response to that? He said to go and ask the chief executive
officer of Hawke’s Bay District Health Board.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No, the COO.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member resume his seat.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No question was asked; I made a statement.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I too was unaware of any question asked, either, but if the member
wants to ask a question, she has got the perfect opportunity.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I would like to make a point
of order and ask whether the Speaker heard my question. I asked what was the
Minister’s response to Grey Power—nothing to do with—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, the question, in my opinion, was addressed. I think that
when you put down a primary question like that and then you list a whole lot of
potential correspondence that has come out of the office of a Minister over the last 2
months, it is not unrealistic that he cannot recall the content of the letter.
National Certificate of Educational Achievement—Scholarships
11. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister of Educa tion: What is the
Government doing today to recognise the educational achievements of young New
Zealanders?
3228 Oral Questions  6 May 2015

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: This morning I was h onoured to
join the Prime Minister and many MPs in acknowledging the top National Certificate of
Educational Achievement  (NCEA) scholars, who came from schools all over New
Zealand. Westlake Boys High School student Joshua Hansen was this year’s recipient of
the Prime Minister’s Award for Academic Excellence. This scholarship is presented
annually to the student who has shown the highest overall level of academic excellence.
In addition, 35 top subject awards were given, as well as 10 premier awards to stud ents
who achieved scholarships in at least five subjects, and from those at least three
outstanding scholarships with one or more top 10 performances. To give the House an
idea of how accomplished these young people are, only around 3 percent of year 13
students studying each subject at NCEA level 3 are awarded a scholarship, and less than
0.5 percent will achieve outstanding scholarships. The premier scholars are truly the
best of New Zealand’s high academic achievers at secondary school level. Let us all
celebrate.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How are we achieving educational success for all young New
Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Across the country, every day, students are getting a better
education. The 2014 provisional results show that  86.8 percent of students achieved a
National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 qualification. This
means that in 2014 , 1,600 more students achieved NCEA level 2 than in 2013. The
2014 data shows that more than—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: What about UE? What about the reduction, the 10 percent
reduction, of Pacific getting UE?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, of course the Opposition is not interested in success,
because it went out as a Government when Māori achieveme nt was a shameful 44
percent. Under this Government in every year that achievement has gone up. And for
Pasifika, that party in Government was happy to settle at—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! [ Interruption] Order! When I call the
Minister to order she will resume her seat. There will be a general debate shortly.
Trade in Services Agreement—Education Franchises
12. CATHERINE DELAHUNTY (Green)  to the Minister of Education : Has she
been consulted on education being included in the Trade in Services Agreement (TiSA);
if so, have any concerns been expressed that this agreement could lead to foreign
corporations suing New Zealand in relation to education provision?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Otirā, ki a
koe e te mema. Yes, I have been consulted as part of the Cabinet decision to enter into
negotiations on the Trade in  Services Agreement and to establish parameters for which
officials should engage in that process. The approach we are taking to these negotiations
is consistent with New Zealand’s existing international trade commitments on private
education and reflects the priority we have always placed on advancing the export
interests of New Zealand private education providers. In regard to the alleged dispute
settlement provision referred to by the member, I am advised that no such provisions are
under discussion.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Has she been advised that if education is included in the
Trade in Services Agreement, large foreign profit -making educational franchises could
sue if New Zealand tried to stop them setting up schools here? Has she b een specifically
advised on that point?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I do not have primary responsibility for negotiating trade
agreements. This particular agreement has been in negotiation for 2 years. There have
been 11 rounds of negotiation. The  12th is due in July. But as to the specifics, I have
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3229
complete confidence in our Minister of Trade to seek any additional information should
he require it. So, no.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The questioner asked
whether the Minister was specifically consulted. She answered every other question but
that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No. Again, if the member would just wait for the answer to be
completed—her final word was no. The question has been addressed.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. If that is the case, and
she did get to it at the end, my point is: why was she allowed to go so long without
answering the question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Because I felt that the information she was giving was actually
helpful to the House, if members have a genuine interest in this matter.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Can she rule out any large foreign education franchises
demanding entry to New Zeala nd under the Trade in Services Agreement and running
schools that do not follow our curriculum, exclude kids on the basis of ability, and
charge huge fees?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Once again, I do not have responsibility for this trade
negotiation, but what I can tell the member is that we provide for private education in
this country and it makes up 3.7 percent of our schooling options. As to international
students, schools able to attract those students really value them. In terms of exportin g
our educational expertise to other countries, we are able to do that because they value
that expertise. So we will continue to seek those opportunities both here and abroad.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Why is she and the National Government so intent on signing
New Zealand up to trade agreements like the Trade in Services Agreement and the
Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement, which will open future Governments, wanting to
protect the public interest, to being sued?

items.speaker: Hon HE KIA PARATA
items.text: Because unlike that member we understand that income
allows us to purchase the things that we want, whether they are called education, roads,
or hospitals. All the things that that member and her party bang on about do not happen
by magic; they happen by earning income.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: I seek leave to table the Trade in Services Agreement’s
leaked annex of professional services—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am having trouble hearing. Can the member s tart her point
of order again.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: I seek leave to table the Trade in Services Agreement’s
leaked annex of professional services document released today, just this morning.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The date of the document?

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: It has been released today, and the original date was
September 2014.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If it is being released today, it is going to be available to all
members. There is no point in my tabling it.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: I do not think it is available.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!
New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill—Submissions
1. Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour —Hutt South) to the Chairperson of the

items.speaker: Justice and Electoral Committee
items.text: Further to her answer to Question to Members No.
1 yesterday, how many people has she requested appear before the committee who
submitted using the process she described as a form submission out of those who
submitted using the process she described as a form submission in total?
3230 Oral Questions  6 May 2015

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.role: Chairperson of the Justice and Electoral Committee
items.text: None of
them. The committee decided to treat 15,970 very similar emailed submissions as form
submissions. The committee also decided not to hear from those form submitters who
wished to be heard.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: In making her decision whom to request to appear, did she
regard people who made individual, unique submissions using links from their local
RSA Facebook pages as a form submission?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I did not make the decision about  who was to appear. The
committee decided not to hear from form submitters who wished to be heard.
New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill—Submissions
2. Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour —Hutt South) to the Chairperson of the

items.speaker: Justice and Electoral Committee
items.text: Further to her answer to Question to Members No.
1 yesterday, how many people has she requested appear before the committee who
submitted using the process she described as a form submission and how many people
who made such a request has she not requested appear?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.role: Chairperson of the Justice and Electoral Committee
items.text: None.
Eight hundr ed and one people making form submissions requested to be heard.
However, it was a decision of the committee not to hear from form submitters.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: In making her decision not to invite the 774 people who
asked to speak to their submissions, did she take into account the reputational damage to

6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3231

Whānau Ora—Auditor-General’s Report

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from the Hon Nanaia Mahuta seeking to
debate under Standing Order 389 some issues with Whānau Ora revealed in the report
by the Controller and Auditor -General, Whānau Ora: The first four years . The release
of the report is a particular case of recent occurrence. As it is an Auditor -General’s
report, there is no ministerial responsibility for the report, though I do accept that it
deals with matters involving ministerial responsibility.
The House has in place a procedure to consider reports from Officers of Parliament.
They stand referred to select committees for consideration and report. Any such select
committee report is set down for consideration as a members’ order of the day. But this
may ta ke some time. Ultimately, a debate on the committee’s report may provide an
opportunity to consider the quality of the Government’s response. However, serious
issues have been raised.
Although the release of an Auditor -General’s report will not always warr ant an
urgent debate, on this occasion I consider the need to maintain public confidence in
programmes such as Whānau Ora justifies the setting aside of the business of the House
today. I call on the Hon Nanaia Mahuta to move that the House take note of an  urgent
matter of public importance.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: I move, That the House
take note of a matter of urgent public importance . As you rightly note, Mr Speaker, this
is a serious issue. When the Auditor -General sought to look at issues around how
Whānau Ora  had been funded and the implementation of the policy over the first 4
years, there were a number of things that were raised that I think the House deserves a
response on. I am very pleased that we are able to have this debate today.
What is most concerning about the report is that the Auditor -General said of the
appropriations made in the first 4 years that a significant amoun t went into
administration—about $42 million —when it could have gone into front -line services.
After all, when this policy was promoted by the Māori Party as a part of the coalition
agreement with the National Government, Whānau Ora  was a flagship policy. It was
there to ensure that those most in need would have an opportunity to have a different
approach in the way in which services would be delivered to them. We heard numerous
debates in this House about a policy that would change the way in which Governm ent
departments responded to those in need. However, the Auditor -General’s report shows
that those other ministries involved in the implementation of Whānau Ora —the
Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Social Development —actually took a piecemeal
approach to the way in which they participated in Whānau Ora. In fact, they did not
change their funding strategies; they still funded individuals rather than what was
intended in the policy, which was a whānau -centred approach. The Auditor -General
highlighted that.
The other concern that we want to bring to the attention of the House is the role of Te
Puni Kōkiri. What we have found are numerous transfers and underspends over the first
4 years of funding for Whānau Ora. Except in 2010 and 2011, there were unders pends
in each and every year . The Auditor-General then highlights that there were reasons for
slow decision-making. Well, one may only assume that Te Puni Kōkiri did not have its
act together.
3232 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
People listening to this debate should not misunderstand the i ntent of our criticism in
highlighting the issues in this report. We know that out there in the communities there
are a number of Whānau Ora  providers that are doing some very good things. We
understand that they are making the best of what they have in th e challenges of the
current funding environment. But they too would say, if you were visiting their
organisations, that, actually, the whole policy has lacked clarity in its implementation. If
there is anything to highlight in the way in which the Auditor -General has gone about
her task of investigating the effectiveness of Whānau Ora, it would be just that.  She
makes the point that, actually, it is very unclear as to what the objectives are with
Whānau Ora. Yet we see that around about $7.2 million has been put aside for research,
to be able to assess the effectiveness of the implementation of Whānau Ora plans. Well,
where is that research, the collection of ethnicity data that demonstrates that this funding
was to go to all whānau, whoever they are? Te Puni Kōkiri may have collected the data.
However, it has not published it in a way that you can measure outcomes.  The Auditor-
General speaks to those types of issues. Also, there is no demonstration of what the
short-term gains have been in the first 4 years.
The Whānau Ora provider  collectives have had research conducted as well.  We are
informed in the report to expect that research some time soon. If you are going to
continue into the second phase of the Whānau Ora initiative as promoted by the Māori
Party, which is actually about the role of the Whānau Ora  commissioning agencies,
surely the research of the first 4 years would be useful in order to inform that process.
In fact, we had the Prime Minister himself get up in the House and respond to
questions from the Labour leader about what was happening in this space. The Prime
Minister himself pointed to these Whānau Ora commissioning agencies. We have three
of them. We have Te Pou Matakana , we have the Pasifika one, and then we have Te
Pūtahitanga o Te Waipounamu down in the South Island. What is of most interest —and
I challenge other members in the House to stand up —is that there have been numerous
instances of feedback to members on this side of the House that good Whānau Ora
providers have not been contac ted, at all, by these commissioning agencies —not at all.
Yet $68 million - odd dollars has gone as an investment into some of these providers,
and they have not been contacted by the Whānau Ora commissioning agencies. They are
unclear about what the future funding landscape looks like.
This report highlights, I think, some of the real challenges of the effective
implementation of Whānau Ora, a policy that was conceived by the Māori Party and
was part of a coalition deal, but actually one that was not implemented very well. I am
sure that the Minister, in his good conscience, would want to respond to the issues that
have been raised in the report. Indeed, our Māori Affairs Committee considers that we
are the best place to ask questions of this particular report and also seek answers from
the Whānau Ora commissioning agencies about the way in which they intend to roll out
their implementation plans and funding strategies for the second phase of Whānau Ora.
The learnings of this report show us that although innovation occurs in the service
delivery area, it is not consistent throughout the whole country. There is not a
widespread buy -in from the other Government agencies that are key supports to the
successful implementation of Whānau Ora.
I want to highlight something from the report. The A uditor-General said that
“Whānau Ora was not consistently described, which makes it hard for us to describe it
and hard for the agencies to link results to objectives. Some results have not been
adequately reported on …” As a member of Parliament responsib le for the oversight of
good spending of taxpayers’ money, that would concern anybody. It certainly concerns
me, and it certainly concerns the Labour Party.
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3233
This policy, as I say, was the flagship policy of the Māori Party. Who would have
thought that such  a policy, with such high esteem, would have unfair objectives that
could not be measured by those Government departments?

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: That has to be the fault of the Government.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: I think that is the faul t of the Government. That to me
indicates that the Government took a hands -off approach to the implementation of
Whānau Ora, even though some of its Government Ministers were intimately involved
with the implementation, and an arm’s -length approach to mini sterial oversight and
good implementation. We should be concerned.
We should also be cautioned by the recommendation of the Auditor -General that
says that where innovation occurs, let us not stop it. However, let us have a robust
debate about transparency  and accountability for taxpayers’ dollars, which should be
spent in the area they were designed for. Quite simply, there were a number of areas in
which the funds set aside for Whānau Ora did not go to the people who needed them
most. This is a kick in th e guts to providers, which are doing very good work out in the
region. This is kick in the guts to those navigators who are in organisations working
with a number of stakeholders at a community level, trying to get the types of outcomes
for whānau so that they are not going down the wrong path, so that they are able to
build resilience and do things: get employment, get training, lift the aspirations of their
whānau. This is a kick in the guts for those providers, which will fight tooth and nail for
every cent that they get, and continue to argue that working with Government agencies
is so difficult when you have to jump through three hoops and give 50 reports while
going through those three hoops.
The integrated contract environment that the Auditor -General spoke of is a positive
thing. However, there still need to be improvements in that space if the Government is
serious about the new approach that is indicated in Whānau Ora. I note, Mr Speaker,
that you said that there is no ministerial oversight on this  particular report. However, as
a policy that has potential —and if we are to take the inference from what the Auditor -
General has indicated, we should not throw the baby out with the bath water —the new
contracting environment that would help facilitate whā nau-centred outcomes will
require integrated contracts, and it will require innovation in this space and better
coordination of the Government sector. If there is a true intent of the National
Government to support any positive part of this particular init iative, I hazard a guess
that the emphasis should be in this space.
But let us not get away from the fact, Minister, that there are questions that must be
asked of your department. I think that a cynic might say that all along, the grand design
of the Whā nau Ora initiative may well have been to get rid of Te Puni Kōkiri and just
devolve funding straight to iwi. But I am not that cynical. I am sure that the Minister
would want to maintain the judicious oversight of Te Puni Kōkiri and respond to some
of the real challenges here. Why did it take so long for Te Puni Kōkiri to go through
some of these arrangements, these plans, of Whānau Ora collectives and then devolve
out the funding? Why did so many transfers happen over 4 years? Why did Te Puni
Kōkiri not make it a priority to report on the data gathered, to give people assurance that
funding was going to where it needed to be? There was a high emphasis on vulnerable
families in a mid -point change in this particular policy. Why did the Minister not ask
questions?
Why did the Minister not ask questions when there was continual underspending of
funding? I think that is a serious question, because the vulnerabilities over the last 6
years have only increased, not decreased, and here is a perfect pool of funding that
could have supported many, many whānau in need. Why did the Minister not have
proper oversight in this area?
3234 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
It is really important to ensure that as conscientious members of this House we utilise
the Auditor-General’s report as an opportunity to hold  the Government to account, to
hold the Minister to account, to hold his department to account in ways that ensure that
policies are designed to help the most vulnerable, and to change the processes to ensure
that providers are supported and that we can get funds out there to support them.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: A third on admin.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: You know, that is right. It is absolutely unbelievable:
one-third of the funding set aside for Whānau Ora is going on administration. There are
unclear objectives,  which are  unable to be measured and reported on; a landscape of
providers out there who are unsure about what the future holds;  and the setting up of
whānau commissioning agencies where we  are not entirely sure about what their future
accountability structures look like, or what the implementation plans for the next phase
of Whānau Ora will look like. These are all serious questions that must be responded to.
The Auditor-General, I think, has done whānau a very, very great service bec ause
she has supported the need for a different approach, to ensure that whānau who need
good wraparound services have an environment where there is better collaboration so
that they can change their lives. She has actually supported that. She has done us a great
service. She has ensured that we as a Parliament hold the Government to account on the
implementation of a policy.
It is clear that the Minister’s department has been woeful in many areas, and it is
evident that in the second phase of funding —and here is one little question on the
second phase of funding. Can we expect, in Budget 2015, an increase in funding for
Whānau Ora commissioning agencies to implement the second phase? And will the
Minister respond to some of the issues identified in the rep ort prior to transferring
funding to the whānau commissioning agencies? These are valid questions, all as a
result of the Office of the Auditor-General’s report.
I am pleased to be able to have an urgent debate to highlight these issues and assure
those providers out there that Labour is on their side. We know that you are doing good
work, but we must make sure the Government is accountable for a policy that has
actually fallen short of expectations. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: I raise a point of
order, Mr Speaker. Just to check—the bell goes at 10 minutes?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, you have got a 15 -minute contribution. The bell will go when
there are 5 minutes to go.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr
Speaker. Kia ora tātau katoa i tēnei rā. Kia w hai wāhi au ki te tuku i tētahi paku kōrero
ki te kuia, ki te pou o te kōhanga reo kua mate nei inā tata nei. Ko Henrietta tērā. Kai te
tangihia e te motu nā runga i te āhuatanga o tana ngākaunui ki tēnei kaupapa o te
Whānau Ora ka mutu, ki ngā tamariki, k i ngā mokopuna o roto i te kōhanga reo. E kui,
te pou o te kōhanga reo, e moe, e moe, e moe! Ka hoki mai ki a tātau e hui nei i tēnei rā,
e te Whare Pāremata, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora tātau katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Acknowledgments to us all  today. I have an opportunity to
make a brief statement to the eld er matriarch and pillar of the k ōhanga reo movement
who passed just moments ago. That was Henrietta. She is to be mourned by the nation
because of her huge commitment to this policy of Whāna u Ora and, furthermore, to the
children and grandchildren within the kōhanga reo movement. To the matriarch and
pillar of the movement, rest, sleep , and slumber! I come back to us assembled here on
this day, to the House I acknowledge, salute , and greet yo u collectively ; my
appreciation to us all.]
Firstly, can I say that I appreciate the comments made by the Hon Nanaia Mahuta
and, indeed, endorse the comments in respect of the opportunity that this debate has
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3235
given for us to place some issues on the table and, in fact, on the record. It is my role, I
think, to address a number of the concerns, and I wish to do that. I want to do it in a
very considered way, to ensure that all the facts are on the table. I can say that this
opportunity has arisen because of the Auditor -General’s report. I would say this: the
Auditor-General’s report and, indeed, the Productivity Commission’s report told us that
there is huge, huge potential for Whānau Ora and that we should definitely not throw it
out with the bathwater. I wo uld also accept that there are some bits that we have to tidy
up. We need to put it in the context that this kaupapa —this report—was over a 4 -year
period when, in fact, we have moved on. We have moved on to the second phase, so I
want to put it in that context.
One of the questions that is always raised is: what is Whānau Ora? Well, Whānau
Ora is an approach to help families and whānau in need. Just like the people who are
represented by the Rt Hon Winston Peters and by the Hon Hekia Parata, it is looking
after those people who are in need. It restores whānau as masters of their own destinies.
Whānau Ora is not about the Government fixing whānau; it is about whānau looking
after themselves. It is about whānau empowering themselves as a whole to identify what
matters to them, rather than focusing on the individuals in isolation.
There is a statement that says it takes a pā to raise our children, and I agree with that.
This is what the basis of Whānau Ora  is. Whānau Ora requires providers to work
together in the interests of whānau and not just the individual, which is a departure from
strategies used by previous Governments over many years, which have not solved the
issues one iota. So the Government, along with the Māori Party, chose to be bold, to be
innovative, and to come up with a new pathway that might address those issues.
Why was Whānau Ora established? It was established because too many whanau and
families have complex needs, and the Government simply wanted to do something
about it and to make a positive difference—as did we in the Māori Party, the originators
of this kaupapa. Actually, I had better say that we are not the originators of this
kaupapa; it is people like John Rangihau, through the report called Puao-te-ata-tū, who
actually put this ka upapa on the table. I want to acknowledge those who are a part of
that scheme. Whānau Ora means that providers work together with each other to
respond to the whānau needs and use their service contracts to address those needs.
What are the outcomes that Whānau Ora is designed to support? Well, as the
approach is led by whānau, you would understand that outcomes are tailored for its
members. No two families are the same, and therefore from time to time the outcomes
that are measured are clearly going to be  different. Whānau Ora is designed to support
whānau in need. Whānau Ora is intended to restore whānau as masters of their own
destinies.
Whānau Ora is about making people move towards a positive lifestyle —“whānau”
meaning families; “ ora” meaning well -being. Whānau should work towards a stronger
economic base. So it is not just about the doom and gloom, but it is actually about
seeking horizons and looking at future prospects and the potential within whānau. This,
in turn, leads to whānau  being active participants in Aotearoa New Zealand. These
