outcomes were where the original task force report set the scene for how phases one and
two of Whānau Ora would be rolled out.
One criticism in the report was that people did not have a good unders tanding of
Whānau Ora. Well, Whānau Ora, for the record, was radical, it was a new idea, it was
inventive, and it showed that we wanted to look down a new pathway to look at the
potential of families. Back in 1988 Puao-te-ata-tū challenged, in fact, our co untry to
change our approach to supporting families in need instead of concentrating on the
individuals. For decades Governments have counted outputs rather than outcomes, and
3236 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
Whānau Ora is all about being brave enough to measure real change in people’s li ves
over a far longer period.
Whānau Ora has been criticised for being confusing and riddled with inconsistencies.
I think that has been overstated. For far too long we have focused, as I say, on the
individual and what has gone wrong for them. I am unapo logetic about the brave
departure from the status quo. I believe in Whānau Ora, I believe in the results, and I
believe in it because I have seen the results. I have spoken to people who have sat
alongside navigators. In fact, in only one week on the road,  I went out and had Whānau
Ora families sit in front of me, and all of those families, with their children, shed tears
about the impact that not Whānau Ora per se but the individual providers —the
navigators—had had in assisting their families. I am talking  about mothers. I am talking
about gang mothers who have changed their lives. I absolutely believe in this kaupapa.
It is right for this country and it is right for our people.
Who is Whānau Ora for? Well, it is not for the down and out only. As I said, i t is for
everyone. But I will be clear —it is by way of a Māori lens for dealing with these
solutions. Does that mean it is hard for anybody else to see it? No, it is not. Why?
Because at this point in time the statistics I have say that about 35 percent of  families
receiving support from Whānau Ora are from ethnic groups other than Māori and
Pasifika. That tells us it works. It can work for others, but it is definitely through a
different cultural lens, which may be why the Auditor -General suspects that it was hard
to understand. But I take the point. There is no use hiding from it; let us put it out there.
How does it work? Well, Whānau Ora is influenced by what families and whānau
wish to do —not by somebody telling them, but by what they want to do. It pu ts the
mana and the power back in their hands. Sometimes a navigator helps the family to
work it out and guides them as to what might assist them in getting and achieving their
goals. When a whānau visits a social service, the intent is that the provider w orker or
the navigator is able to link up the family with what is required, and I have seen the
benefits of that.
The question was asked around what a whānau plan  is. Well, a whānau plan is the
tool for whānau to say what matters to them. They choose it. A lot of whānau want the
same things. Of course they do—better lives for children, employment, homeownership,
education, health outcomes, and skill development. Those are generic things that most
families want. Some are fortunate to have them.
Developing a whānau plan means that the whole family works together. We are not
just talking about mum, dad, the eldest child, or the four in the house; we are talking
about whānau in the widest sense, because whānau could be the rugby league club
secretary, it could be the parent teacher association, it could be a teacher, it could be the
coach, or it could be all of those. They decide and they define it.
Developing a whānau plan means that everybody works together and that if you have
to find work, everybody pitches in. If you have to give up smoking, everybody assists in
that because if one person in the house is smoking, it affects everybody. That is what it
is all about. A plan usually involves a number of actions. Some actions do not require
Government support, and that is even better. It is far more fiscally neutral and delivers
the results because the family have bought into it.
What are the key elements of Whānau Ora? Well, we have talked about navigators.
Navigators, in my humble opinion, are the key to Whāna u Ora. Why? Because they are
from those communities, they know those communities, they know the people, and they
make the connections. I have seen it for myself. They are the ones who work at the
coalface. They support the family to identify their needs an d achieve their goals. They
are often the link. They join up the family, the whānau, with the services. Or perhaps it
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3237
is information that they might need —identifying early childhood education options for
mum; that could be it. So they are an important ingredient in Whānau Ora.
The other part is commissioning agencies, and these are only a new beast that has
come on the scene. I will not talk about them too much because they are not very
relevant in terms of the report. Suffice to say that they are the seco nd phase of the roll -
out of Whānau Ora. “Beast” is not the best term for that particular element of Whānau
Ora, but I use it in the wider sense, if you do not mind.
Provider collectives —this is the great innovation about Whānau Ora. It actually
brought people together to work for the purposes of the family. It is not just one in one
box, another over there, and another over there. They actually joined hands in the bes t
interests of the families. So Whānau Ora provider collectives are an important key of
this kaupapa. They are accountable for the delivery of services for health, education,
and the social sectors, as well. Whānau Ora supported those collectives to come
together and have a collective impact, not solely focused on their own provider
interests.
Some have asked about the results of Whānau Ora. Well, here it is. We do have the
statistics that the Hon Nanaia Mahuta talked about —9,408 whānau representing 49,625
individuals received whānau -centred services. Of those, 5,499 whānau representing
23,855 individuals worked with navigators. Provider collectives have orientated
themselves towards whānau-centred perspectives to focus not just on the individual.
So what has changed? I have told you that Whānau Ora has had a huge impact on a
huge number of people throughout this country. We must allow it to roll into phase two.
The other questions that were raised are around why it is that Te Puni Kōkiri will be
leading W hānau Ora, and there were,  I suppose, criticisms made by some members
about the involvement of Te Puni Kōkiri. Whānau Ora is based on kaupapa Māori, with
core elements applicable to whānau. That is why Whānau Ora is under the auspices of
Te Puni Kōkiri.
Were there delays in spending that meant funds originally set aside for whānau and
providers did not reach them? Money did not pass hands unless contracts and
expectations were in place. This is prudent management. The expression of interest
process for pro vider collectives was significant, with 300 wanting to be a part of
Whānau Ora. That process and assessment took longer than anticipated. Yes, there were
transfers of resources between financial years. However, I can say this: 99 percent of the
funding intended for whānau and providers reached their hands. The criticism has been
that it did not reach their hands. I am saying to you, on the advice that I have, that 99
percent of that money did reach the hands of those who needed it. The Government
made decisions in July 2013 to move to phase two of Whānau Ora, and all uncommitted
funds were redirected to the Whānau Ora commissioning agencies—that is why.
Another criticism was about why Te Puni Kōkiri spent nearly one -third of the funds
on administration. I have said publicly in the media that Whānau Ora is a new kaupapa.
It was starting up. There were a lot of costs associated with designing Whānau Ora and
the parts of this approach. Going forward, I expect to ensure that all the administration
costs are in l ine with the task at hand. The Office of the Auditor -General counted in its
account the design, development, implementation of phases one and two, evaluation and
action research, and costs for governance groups and regional leadership groups. Te
Puni Kōkir i’s specific administration costs equate to about 20 percent, and it is my
understanding that that is pretty reasonable under normal circumstances within
Government departments.
Will I be investigating the administration and management of Whānau Ora? The
costs in the report referred to are for the last 4 years. They have been accounted for. Te
Puni Kōkiri has received a clean audit report from Audit New Zealand. In each of the
3238 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
last 4 years or so it has received a clean report and all of the money has been accounted
for. Going forward, I have asked the chief executive to ensure her management
decisions and the costs for Whānau Ora are prudent and not over the top.
Whānau Ora has my absolute commitment. Why? Because I have seen the results. I
know what it can do for families, children, mums, dads, uncles, and those in need. There
are so many people in our country who have that need, and the State has failed to
deliver that in the past. Whānau Ora was always going to be a new approach. It was
innovative. It was always going to have some bumps along the way, but there can be no
doubting the evidence that I have had presented to me —and, indeed, that was presented
to the Hon Tariana Turia —that Whānau Ora is right for this country. It does produce
results. In fact, many of the people who receive the benefits of Whānau Ora, with some
of its mistakes, are the people whom many of the people in this House represent.
In that regard, I would hope that I am clear that this Government is committed to
Whānau Ora, as am I, to ensure that the issues that have been raised will be dealt with in
the best possible way. Whānau Ora, kia kaha. And to all of the providers and workers in
Whānau Ora, I say job well done, kia kaha.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Whānau Ora is a new and innovative
approach to working alongside whanau, and it has enormous potential to be successful.
But Whānau Ora is at great risk of death by a thousand cuts due to mishandling by the
Minister for Whānau Ora and Te Puni Kōkiri, and by a lack of commitment from
Government agencies. That is what this Auditor-General’s report shows really clearly.
I want to describe the report in a bit more detail than has been given so far because,
actually, it is very balanced, and I think the Audito r-General has done a great job. But
she shows very clearly that between failing to address issues that have previously been
raised around evaluation and reporting and failing to give clear indications of progress
and success, Te Puni Kōkiri and the Ministe r have failed. Alongside that, a complete
lack of investment or commitment from the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of
Social Development now means that where there is potential for progress and change, it
is being hindered by progressive Government agencies.

items.speaker: Pita Paraone
items.text: Patch protection.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: “Patch protection”, my friend says. The report shows that there
have been some really good outcomes, but it also indicates where those outcomes are at
great risk. I under stand the Minister’s saying that he believes in this programme, but,
with respect, Minister, it does not matter whether you believe in the programme. Your
job is to instil confidence and certainty in the rest of the country that this new and
innovative approach is working and is cost -effective. That is what will ensure that it is
able to continue and build and do better. If you cannot instil that confidence and
certainty, the programme will eventually be cut. We can see that happening. We can see
the progress of that. So right now is the time to be most concerned with doing the best
work for the programme and making sure it has all the best aspects of evaluation,
monitoring, and reporting. It is not a time for sitting back.
We all know that Māori programmes, just like Māori people, have to do significantly
better than others in order to avoid the extra scrutiny, if you like, that we all attract. We
know that that happens. Māori programmes get additional scrutiny; so do Māori people.
We have to do three times  better to get anywhere. So one of the major problems that
this report responds to is a failure to build resilience into the system from the start,
acknowledge that there is extra risk, and, therefore, make sure the programme would be
able to stand up to that risk.
This is not the first report that has criticised Whānau Ora. There was, in 2012, a
serious report showing issues with the funding assessments. We were assured then that
there would be new evaluation and monitoring put into Whānau Ora that would improve
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3239
those systems, but the Auditor -General’s report shows yet again that that has not been
done, and that is a failure of the ministry and Te Puni Kōkiri.
But I will say that the report does talk about favourably about the programme. It is
not just a criticism. The Auditor -General says: “I have no doubt that some
commentators will make light of the successes described in this report and make much
of the criticisms .”—and I think that has been true —“However, an innovative idea
should not be abandoned just because of implementation problems. I earnestly hope that
those involved with the next phase of Whānau Ora are able to take my criticisms on
board and learn from them.”
She also went on to describe a couple of examples where Whānau Ora has worked
effectively, one of which was where a woman who had had mental health issues for 40
years had a Whānau Ora  intervention. A person went to her home every week for more
than a year to assist her to build up her capacity and resilience to operate well within the
whānau. After a bit over a year her family were able to say: “Yes, we trust you with our
kids. We are able to engage with you as a person of our whānau, and we can wrap
around you with some sense of security and certainty.”
I do not know of any other agency  that can consistently provide weekly support to
someone in this situation in their own home. She did not qualify necessarily for major
mental involvement from the health agencies, but Whānau Ora was there to give her and
her whānau the support that they needed.
The report also has an example —a very tragic one in my view —of a Whānau Ora
navigator who was involved with a man who was an insulin -dependent diabetic. He
suffered amputations and he needed more assistance. This navigator worked with this
man’s children to get him prosthetic legs and other aids that he needed, and that meant a
huge amount of advocating, writing letters, working with the ministry and other
agencies, and getting funding for vehicle modifications and bathroom alterations. It
meant helping him to resolve delays in getting his financial entitlements —he was not
getting all that he was due—and it also meant that not only did he get some back -pay in
terms of money he had not been paid but that he was in an improved financial situation.
He was also connected to a rural nurse to help him manage his diabetes.
This whānau needed someone to intervene on their behalf and advocate for them, and
this is what Whānau Ora did. This is what Whānau Ora  does, today, with whānau. But
alongside every story of success is the fact that every time there is a legitimate criticism
of the funding, the management, and the evaluation, the programme is at risk of being
cut. So the Minister has to take these criticisms from the Auditor -General very seriously
and make a very firm commitment to fixing this, because otherwise it will be lost.
The Auditor -General also made significant criticisms of other agencies —the
Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Social Development. One criticism in particular
is the fact that these ministries were not able to describe Whānau Ora, how it works, and
what it does. Actually, I think it is a failing on their part. It is not that difficult to
understand, actually, and they have been working on this now for some years. The fact
that people in the ministries could not describe it is their own failing in terms of not
investing enough in understanding how the programme works.
There was criticism of the agencies for their funding failures and the mismatch of
services. The Auditor -General talks about the fact that the Ministry of Health and the
Ministry of Social Development engaged with Whānau Ora and Te Puni Kōkiri but had
an individualised funding approach. There is a significant mismatch, she says, between
the services that providers must  deliver under their contracts with those ministries
compared with Whānau Ora and Te Puni Kōkiri. She goes on to say that the Ministry of
Health and the Ministry of Social Development have done no work on changing the
3240 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
way they operate—and have no intention to—so that they are working with the Whānau
Ora approach, as opposed to working with an individualised approach.
She describes in this report that providers are very concerned that they may have
been doing this work with this woman with the mental health  issues for 12 months
under a Whānau Ora contract, and that once that ends there is no funding to enable them
to continue to support that whānau in the same way because the Ministry of Health does
not have a contract approach that allows for a whānau appro ach to her needs. When the
Ministry of Health funding and the Ministry of Social Development funding is for
different purposes, when they have different kinds of contracts, and when they are not
engaging with the new approach that is needed and changing th eir own systems so that
they can help to manage the gaps that will always occur when you have one service or
agency involved in the whānau and another coming in behind afterwards, well, of
course there are going to be problems.  Of course there are going to  be failures. Those
failures are not failures of the programme. They are not failures of the approach. They
are not failures of Te Puni Kōkiri or the Minister. They are failures of the Ministry of
Health and the Ministry of Social Development, and their le adership and their
Ministers, in that they have not been properly engaging with Whānau Ora  and
committing to the approach.
So at the end of all that, you end up with a man in similar position, a man who has
not yet engaged with Whānau Ora, and a man who, w hat—never gets his prosthetic
legs, a man who never gets the vehicle or the bathroom modifications? At the end of
that, is the woman with decades of mental health issues never to be trusted by her
family to look after her grandchildren because she cannot g et the intervention she needs
to become safe? Those are the kinds of families in Aotearoa that we in this Chamber
will allow to fall through the cracks because of the failure of the Government, its
agencies, and this Parliament in general to commit to an a pproach that actually works
for the people we are here to serve.
This report is very serious and does need to be taken very seriously. It is a severe
criticism, I think, of Whānau Ora, Te Puni Kōkiri, and the Minister but also other
agencies involved and the Government’s lack of commitment to the concept of Whānau
Ora. Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Whānau Ora was established
from a report that did not cont ain one scrap of empirical fact or evidence. It was based
solely on anecdotal evidence, rumour, and bias. The second thing is that there is nothing
as antiseptic as the statement: “We told you so.”, but New Zealand First did, from the
time we first saw tha t report. What this says, when you look at the answers from the
Government and, in particular, the Prime Minister today, is just how smug and arrogant
this Government has become. It is not prepared to even listen to something as
authoritative as the first investigation of this operation for 4 years by the Auditor -

items.speaker: General. This is what we find
items.text: spending on Whānau Ora  is completely politically
motivated. Four years after its inception, the programme is still a byword for the
squandering of public money.
The sad thing is that there are some great Māori deliverers and providers out there
that had their programmes taken off them and who were sidelined or had to come under
the umbrella of Whānau Ora. What we have got to say today is that we have got no
concern in respect of them —they are doing a fine job. But what we have got to ask
today is who is culpable in this waste and why it is so damaging to the future of Māori
and the taxpayer, as well.
At a time of fiscal restraint, widespread cost -cutting, and hardship for many families,
this so -called programme is deeply offensive to many Māori New Zealanders. It is
offensive to the many Māori who are struggling to pay their bills, find work, and raise
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3241
their children. It is offensive to all taxpayers, who are seeing mon ey that could be spent
on worthwhile purposes being squandered to indulge the Māori Party and its cronies. It
is offensive to the many families in New Zealand facing serious stress, who could make
good use of the extra financial support —$140 million is an incredible amount of
money. Why, it could, for example, easily fund people in this country with very rare
diseases or syndromes, many of whom are Māori, over a period of probably 7 or 8
years.
The latest report by the Auditor -General confirms that there is  absolutely no
evidence that good value for money has come out of the $140 million so far spent on
Whānau Ora. To say that the objectives of  Whānau Ora are vague, amorphous, woolly,
and unmeasurable is an understatement. If there are no clear goals, aims, and objectives,
any spending can be justified. In the history of public expenditure in New Zealand it
will be hard to find any other programme that has so little in the way of justification or
evidence to warrant its continued existence. I know of many bri lliant Māori
programmes around this country and they did not need some dreamtime, esoteric view
of how the world works from the Māori Party.
With the greatest respect, we have spent more time out there. We know what poverty
smells, tastes, and feels like in places like Kawakawa and Kaikohe on the East Coast,
and none of this is designed to help them. What it is designed to help is the bureaucracy,
and I will prove how it does that. Whānau Ora could never withstand any real scrutiny.
First investigation—down it goes. For that reason it has been allowed to obey the usual
standards of open and accountable public administration. As we have repeatedly said,
Whānau Ora is a programme that has never made even the smallest gesture to good
financial practice and acc ountability. It is an embarrassment to Māoridom. In fact,
Whānau Ora has always been nothing more than a grubby and cynical deal between
National and the Māori Party.
All the usual rules for scrutiny and oversight have been abandoned. Those people up
there like Chris Bishop and others talk about accountability: “It’s a tight time. We
haven’t got much in the way of public money to spend.” Consistencies, accountabilities,
sunlight—when it came to this, they turned a blind eye. New Zealanders are right to be
outraged with this waste and squandering of public money. For example, how many
people who benefited from the $40 million in administration costs alone that went to
Whānau Ora were allied with or supported the Māori Party? Even in the contracts
awarded and  the three commissions “appointed” to deliver this kaupapa, how many
people were allied to the Māori Party?
Then the questions were asked today of the Prime Minister: “Prime Minister, how
come a third of all payments made to whānau and provider collective s went to just two
of Te Puni Kōkiri’s 10 regions?”—and guess which two? The ones with Ministers from
the Māori Party. I want to ask Marama Fox about how this works when, for example,
the greatest population of Māori come from the far north, that magnifice nt place
deprived of sound economic and social management. How much money went to them?
How come the two Māori Party Ministers got all the money in terms of percentages?
Just two of the 10 got one -third of all payments. That, Marama Fox, is inexcusable.
Next time you are in Kaitāia or Kaikohe, or in the far north, or in the other regions, or in
the deep south—down there at Ngāi Tahu—explain how this happens, in 2015.

items.speaker: Pita Paraone
items.text: What about her people on the East Coast?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, what about her people on the East Coast.

items.speaker: Pita Paraone
items.text: They missed out.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: They missed out completely. My colleague Pita
Paraone, who is very familiar with the East Coast, of course, knows how they feel down
there. What are we hearing from the local member as to this improper expenditure? Not
3242 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
a mutter, not a murmur, not a syllable, not a sound. How can you possibly face your
people when you go back there, where you are me ant to be their loyal and faithful
servant, knowing that down here you have turned a blind eye?

items.speaker: Here is the next one
items.text: a quarter of all individuals accessing Whānau Ora funding
through the Whānau Integration, Innovation and Engagement Fund in the 2010, 2011 ,
and 2012 years were in just one of Te Puni Kōkiri’s regions. It has got 10 regions, and a
quarter of the funding went to one region. Guess which one? Why, the region of the
former Minister for Whānau Ora herself. And what did the Prime Minister do? This
arrogant and smug man said today that he did nothing—nothing.
We in New Zealand First know the propriety that is required to be an accountable
party. That is why we are the most frugal party in Parliament by miles. We know what it
stands for to be account able, but what do we have here? How does, for example, the
Prime Minister, anybody in the National Government, Marama Fox, or, for that matter,
the member for Whangarei possibly describe this to the Māori people up there —that
$20,000 went from Whānau Ora t o the Mongrel Mob in Dunedin? Did it spend it on
Māori causes and purposes? No. Did it spend it on sick Māori or Māori who needed
education? No. It spent it on, what? Cannabis. How do I know that? Because I raised the
matter in Parliament, and the Minister  denied it and got caught out 3 days later. That is
how I know that. One of the things we do in the New Zealand First Party is we do our
homework—we do our homework. We are not fast on the lip and slow on the hip. No,
we do our homework. We raised that one  then, and that was what you might say was a
dead one as well.

items.speaker: Then we asked
items.text: “How come you gave $80,000 to the Whānau Ora Palmerston North
Māori Women’s Refuge, where it has not got one client?”. No, no, the Māori women
down there who wanted refuge went off to the European women’s refuge. How do you
possibly justify that?
Then, of course, there was the doozy of them all—to use the name of one of the guys
on the backbench of the National Government —$60,000 went to Ōtaki’s Rāhui Rugby
and Sports Club for a  1-day hooley so that it could have whānau connectedness. Now I
know that at Mōtatau and up there in Ōtīria, and, in fact, all around the north and on the
East Coast—

items.speaker: Pita Paraone
items.text: And Whananaki.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: —and, indeed, in Whananaki, I could gain some
serious connectedness with $60,000. And, you know, I have had the temerity of some of
the commentariat who say to me: “But, Mr Peters, they did some good, didn’t they?”.
Well, let me tell you this: with $140 m illion I could do some serious good —yes, I
could—but would it be fair? Would it go to all of M āoridom and, at the end of the day,
would it have this one aspect, which has always been the aspect of unique Māori
service: personal sacrifice? That is something  that is not big over there in the Māori
Party, is it? Or with the National Party —oh no, it is all about egregious self -
advancement.
We in New Zealand First know that with all these programmes there has to be some
sacrifice. There has to be some pain, som e commitment, and some suffering. That is
why we were proud to say from the word go that this programme should be stopped,
and the Auditor -General has now said that everything that New Zealand First has said
was correct.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Can I just start by acknowledging
the considered speech by the front -bench Labour Party spokesman on Whānau Ora. It
was a bit surprising. The Labour Party has been deeply confused by this policy. It
cannot quite decide whether to be for it or against it. It cannot quite decide whether it is
for it or against it, but on the day it made the right decision, which was to critically
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3243
analyse the Auditor-General’s report, support its conclusions, and urge the Government
to implement them, and that is good.
Surprisingly, given the political advantage Mr Peters now has over the Labour Party,
he took the wrong tack. I mean, to have the member for Northland say that he needs
another $60,000 and that that would fix things is, frankly, ridiculous. There is no
shortage of Government money in Northland —no shortage of Government money in
Northland. Now the member, of course, faces the challenge that as he moves on,
apparently, from his career of “egregious self -advancement”, of which he accuses
everyone else, he is now going to have to come to grips with the reality of the continued
ineffectiveness of many traditional Government programmes in Northland —
programmes and services that as often as not undermine what resilience the families in
those lower-income communities in Northland actually have. They have resilience, they
have aspiration, and, too often, the chaotic, crisis-driven interventions of Government in
the lives of those families make them worse, not better—worse, not better.
The reason we are having this debate to day is that the Māori Party, rightly, came to
the view that something different needed to be done. Is there evidence of the need for
something different to be done? Absolutely —absolutely. If you look at the data for
communities around New Zealand, there ar e three factors that, combined, predict pretty
bad outcomes. They are a Child, Youth and Family notification in respect of children in
the household, one parent who has had a custodial sentence —that is more common than
people think; in Rotorua 10 percent of all children have a parent who has had some kind
of corrections-related sentence—and the third factor is spending 75 percent of your life
on a benefit. In Rotorua there are 470 of those families, and I would defy any member
of this House to dispute what the Auditor -General is saying, which is that something
different needs to happen because it is a deeply embedded pattern of persistent
deprivation and social failure.
I saw an example of this the other day in Palmerston North. I saw a video of the male
from a household that had had in 12 months 161 calls to the police station —161 calls.
We know that that is a sign not just of great expense for every one of those calls and the
concern about the welfare of the parents and the children in that household. We k now
that it shows all sorts of other problems, which are long running and intergenerational.
It also denotes a pretty miserable household having an impact on the community that is
very negative.
The interventions that have gone with, in that case, the Whā nau Ora provider, mean
that in the 6 or 8 months since they started there have been no phone calls to the
police—none. That is a dramatic shift. I would not mind betting that if you went and
looked at that family’s interaction with public services for the last 20 years, it would be
regular, it would be crisis-driven, it would be chaotic, it would be very expensive. What
we know is that a lot of it had not worked.
That is why the Government has backed the approach embedded in Whānau Ora.
The Auditor-General’s report draws attention to the nature of the spending. We could go
into that in a bit of detail, but one of the ironies here, of course, is that one reason there
was significant administrative cost was to absolutely ensure that the money could be
tracked so that it could be demonstrated that it was used carefully. For instance, there
was a requirement that a number of Whānau Ora providers did not like, nor the families,
that if the Government gave money to a whānau, it had to be to a legal entity. Yes, it is a
bureaucratic compliance requirement, but I can guarantee that if that was not there, New
Zealand First would be ranting about that today. New Zealand First would be saying
“Why do you just give money to some individual citizen out there? Aren’t all 4  million
of them entitled to the same thing?”. Well, that would have been a fair question.
3244 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
The other issue that has come up is around evaluation. It is interesting to hear New
Zealand First taking the same argument as officials who do not want anything to
change. That argument goes like this: how can you put that programme in place when it
has not been evaluated? Well, the answer is because it did not exist, that is why. If we
followed that argument, we would just stick with the programmes that we know
consistently fail—that we know consistently fail. Part of the money here has actually
been to set up the evaluation to find out whether it has an impact—to find out whether it
has an impact.
In that respect, can I say that Whānua Ora has been subject to more  audits, more
examination, more testing of outcomes, more oversight than any other social
programme. Among the Government’s spending, these numbers over the years add up
to $100 million. Over that period we have spent billions on programmes that have been
unexamined. I would not say they have been unaudited —they have certainly been
audited. They have been subject to high -level oversight and are not subject to anything
like the expectation that they will have an impact, as Whānau Ora is.
The Auditor -General is criticising the outcomes framework. If we knocked on the
head every Government programme that does not have an outcomes framework, we
would have been in surplus 5 years ago. Most Government spending has not had an
outcomes framework, and that is why we  are changing it. A lot of it has no obvious
intent to make an impact. It has got well -intentioned people, it has got providers who
can lobby and get the media and who do really care, it is just that it does not make much
difference.
Whānau Ora is a progr amme—the only one I know of, actually —that from its
inception has been required to make a difference to the lives of people who desperately
need that difference. In some cases it has. In some cases the value for money in year 1
of a programme and year 2 of  something new with quite a different view, cutting across
the way that the Government is traditionally organised, and quite a different aspect on
our families and communities—in some cases that money may not have been applied in
exactly the best way. We a ccept that. The Government accepts the recommendations of
the Auditor-General. We made changes back in 2013 that deal, actually, with a number
of the Auditor-General’s issues, though not all of them, and we will make sure that that
contributes.
I invite e very member of Parliament to look at this, and I welcome today the
considered debate from most parties—except New Zealand First. There is one challenge
for New Zealand First: show us what difference it is going to make in Northland, and
what is the magic n ew recipe? That is what we want to hear from New Zealand First.

items.speaker: All we heard today was
items.text: “Don’t do this.” All we heard today was: “Don’t try to work
with families to help them stand on their own two feet.” Somewhere there is some other
magic recipe that is going to fix Northland. You know what? I wish New Zealand First
knew—because it is a long, hard road, and a lot of solutions have been tried and
failed—as much as it says it does. I just suspect that maybe it does not.

items.speaker: ADRIAN RURAWHE
items.text: Ā, tēnā koe e te Kaiw’akawā
o te Whare nei, otirā, e te W’are tēnā tātou. Tēnā tātou i runga i tēnei kaupapa nunui kei
waenganui i ā tātou iwi katoa puta noa i ngā moutere n ei. Oti noa, e tika ana ki a mi’i ki
a rātou mā, ki te kuia kāta’i anō ka mate. Nō reira, e te whaea haere atu rā.
[And so , my thanks to you , Mr Speaker of this House , but at the same time,
salutations to us of the House, acknowledgments to us in regard to  this massive matter
amongst all of our people throughout these islands. It is appropriate indee d that we
acknowledge those who have passed away, namely the elderly one who has just died.
Therefore, farewell to you the matriarch.]
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3245
Last year during the elec tion campaign whenever I spoke on w’ānau ora, I always
prefaced my comments by making certain that the people I was speaking to knew
exactly which w’ānau ora I was talking about. I always talked about w’ānau ora, the
kaupapa—the concept, the philosophical base that those of us who believe in this
kaupapa operate within. I also spoke about w’ānau ora, the model of practice. That is
the way that providers provide their w’ānau -centred services to the families that they
engage with. Then I talked about the Gove rnment programme, the Government policy
Whānau Ora, and that is what I want to talk about now.
Last year I actually got myself —I do not think I was in trouble, but I managed to
make some statements about the Government policy of Whānau Ora that attracted
comment from the then Minister for Whānau Ora, Tariana Turia, who said that I was
wrong. Today we have a report that actually says that I was right. I was right to
comment on Whānau Ora, the Government policy, because the criticisms that we made
last year have now been reported in the Auditor-General’s report.
I think that every party in this House, and the Government and the Minister in
particular, needs to take responsibility for the issues that have been raised —not to be
talking in this House about the kaupapa or the model of practice, but actually addressing
the issue of the Government policy, which is wrong. That is what the Government needs
to be talking about. It is easy for us to be talking about what is wrong with our families
and bring that to the House as if that is the issue; I can tell the House that that is not the
issue. The issue is the way that the Government is implementing this policy of Whānau
Ora.
In a way, it is a great sadness to me that the Government chose to use the name
“Whānau Ora” for its policy and its programme. It should have left that as a kaupapa, as
a concept, and left it as a model of practice for those providers that deliver the services
to the people. They should own w’ānau ora, not the Government. I do not need, and my
whānau and everyone’s families do not really need, the Government to tell us what
w’ānau ora is. What we need is what the Auditor-General has said in her report.
Last year we in Labour campaigned on a policy of reviewing the Government’s
policy of Whānau Ora, and that is exactly what the Auditor -General has now told the
whole world —that there needs to be a thorough investigation of this Government
policy. That is one of the key points that I want to make to this House because, actually,
what we have heard so far is a lot of justification.
We have heard about everything that is wrong with our families and about how good
the providers are doing, and I agree with that. I agree that our providers out there are
doing an excellent job of delivering services unde r a policy that is quite confused. I can
say that because 4 years ago I was the chair of an iwi health provider in Whanganui that
went through this process, and I am not surprised at the level of administration and the
cost of administration needed to impl ement this policy. The number of hoops that we
had to go through, hurdles we had to go over —change of venues, change of game, and
change of the rules—while this policy started to be implemented meant that it could not
possibly have been anything else but highly costly administratively.
I do not completely blame Te Puni Kōkiri by itself. I think, and I am speaking from
my personal experience, that the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Social
Development were actually, how would I put it —they were not w illing participants in
this process. I got the sense when we met with those ministries that Te Puni Kōkiri was
having to push them forward to make sure that they participated, and I have spoken to a
number of people who have gone through the same experienc e. The cost of
administration was necessary. I think that sometimes Te Puni Kōkiri can be overly risk -
averse and that sometimes it puts too many processes in place. When maybe one
3246 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
process might be sufficient, it will have two or three in place, and this is  what has
happened with Whānau Ora, the Government policy.
The Auditor -General pointed out a number of issues. For example, it has a lot of
potential. I think that is one of the highlights of this report, in a report that does not have
very many highlights. I think that both the kaupapa —the model or practice —and,
indeed, the Government policy have potential if they are done the right way. To me,
quite clearly, this has not been done very well. The implementation of it has not been
good.
Last week I spoke in the annual review debate and I raised the issue of Māori
housing, where in June last year the then Minister announced that a Māori housing fund
would go to Te Pou Matakana, a grassroots organisation, so that it could operate that
funding for Māori housing. After the election, in December last year, that decision  was
overturned, and now it is going back to Te Puni Kōkiri. I wonder whether it is time to
readdress that particular issue in light of the criticisms in the Auditor -General’s report
on Te Puni Kōkiri. Maybe that decision should be revisited and Te Pou Mat akana
should be given a shot at having that funding for Māori housing. While I am on it, what
progress has actually been made in those areas? We have heard nothing about those
policy areas since they were announced.
I think it is really important for memb ers on our side of the House to highlight the
fact that we did have a policy on w’ānau ora. Within the Auditor -General’s report it
says that w’ānau ora actually started in 2002, with a w’ānau ora  policy within the
Ministry of Health, but one of the key things that stood side by side with that policy was
Labour’s funding for outcomes. This is now the basis for the integrated contracts that
each and every one of the Whānau Ora providers has had to go through. This is a really
important point for me to make be cause I think that that is one of the three cornerstones
of the current Government’s Whānau Ora  policy, and that actually started with the
Labour Government. We on this side of the House were talking about having integrated
contracts with organisations that provided an integrated service. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Marama Fox—5 minutes.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: Whānau Ora is an approach to help
families and whānau in need. It is radical. I heard the Hon Annette King question what
is so radical about it. I will tell you what is radical about it. What is radical about it is
that, in fact, Mr Rurawhe was talking about Labour wanting to do something that would
bring an integrated approach to supporting whānau, but it did not actually do anything.
So on one hand Labour wants to criticise Whānau Ora and on the other hand it wants to
claim that it was its idea, which I find quite remarkable.
In fact, this was not our idea. This has nothing to do with Tariana; she did not dream
this up. In fact, she says in her own words that Whānau Ora is from Māori. It is a Māori
concept for Māori people by Māori—for Māori and, ultimately, for all of Aotearoa New
Zealand. This is about value being added to this country based on a kaupapa Māori
perspective. Should we claim it in the Government? Is it wrong to claim kaupapa Māori
ideas? Why? Because they do not wor k? They do work, and 45,000 New Zealanders in
this country have had the benefit of Whānau Ora —yes, up and down the East Coast,
because, yes, there are Whānau Ora  providers on the East Coast, and, yes, in the far
north.
I was invited to the far north to la unch a Whānau Ora initiative that saw Pasifika
whānau and Māori whānau come together. Are we in the Māori Party dealing with
Pasifika needs, not just those of Māori? Yes, we are. That is the Whānau Ora provision
called The Fono, and it has put Whānau Ora p roviders in the far north. Whānau Ora has
benefited people, and everybody has said that. On one hand they talk about how
wonderful these navigators are who go out around the country and support whānau to
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3247
transform their lives and to go from being dependent  on Government services to being
independent and realising their dreams and aspirations. Yes, the catchcry for Whānau
Ora is “Dream it, plan it, live it.” Nobody has criticised that, because that cannot be
criticised.
Whānau Ora navigators are doing good work, but what is the response from the
Opposition when the approach gets criticised? It says “Oh, let’s cut it. Let’s just cut it.
Let’s throw those families back on to the heap, and let’s not give them some provision.”
When the services that are currently out there try to deliver services to whānau—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: We didn’t say cut it; we said cut the spending but don’t cut the
programme.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: You know and I know, Ms Sepuloni. You know —excuse me. Ms
Sepuloni may know, although she may be having trouble grasping this, that when there
is an issue, Child, Youth and Family  rings Whānau Ora navigators. When there is an
issue, Ministry of Social Dev elopment staff ring Whānau Ora  navigators. Why?
Because they have success, and this programme has success.
In fact, I sat in on a Whānau Ora hui with young men who otherwise would have
been tossed on the heap, young men who had been referred for support be cause they
were being thrown out of school. They were sons of gang members and were getting
into trouble. They were on the borderline of being thrown into jail. Instead, what did
they do? They went to Whānau Ora providers, who turned their lives round. I w atched
as 17 -year-old hardened young men softened their hearts enough to ring their fathers
and organise father -son dates. That is what they called it —their words, not my words.
They spent time connecting with their whānau, with their mothers, turning thei r lives
round. They went from having no hope to having a future where they could see
themselves with bright and prosperous aspirational gains they never thought were
available to them before.
Yes, we need to strengthen Whānau Ora. We could take the $300 million that other
services get and put that in Whānau Ora and build the infrastructure, but to say  that the
policy is flawed—the implementation may be flawed, but these things are being worked
on, and that is what we have been doing from the moment we stepped into this building.
Whānau Ora is the way of the future. People all over the world have been asking us
to tell them how this works, because before this time, people only spoke about it. I sat in
a meeting in about 2002 and listened to people talk abou t how we c ould come together
as providers and support whānau. Well, this is it, and it is not about the individual; it is
about whānau. Kia ora.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Marama Fo x from the Māori Party
said that when things go wrong, when there are problems with something, the
Opposition’s first position is to say “Cut it.” At no point have we said “Cut it.”, but
what we are saying is that the responsible thing now is to explore th e findings of the
Auditor-General and to ask the question why. We support the concept of Whānau Ora.
We support the idea of integrated services provision. We support the idea of addressing
the needs of a whole family rather than just an individual, but we have to ask questions
following the release of this report.
The biggest question we have to ask is around spending. One third of the money put
towards Whānau Ora—$42.3 million—went towards administration of the programme.
I want to say that I understand t hat when you start something new, there are going to be
additional administrative costs, but one third of the funding going towards
administration is something that needs to be explored.
The thing is, too, that that $42.3 million —one third of the funding that went towards
Whānau Ora, which has been attributed to administration —is the administrative cost
only at the Te Puni Kōkiri level and at the commissioning agency level. If you look at
3248 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
the providers who would then be commissioned by the commissioning ag encies, there
are going to be further administrative costs there. I do not think that the administrative
costs of those providers will reach one third of the funding that they get. But if they
were to reach that level of funding, you would be spending two thirds of the funding
allocated towards Whānau Ora on administration at the Te Puni Kōkiri level and at the
commissioning agency level, and then at the provider level. Effectively, out of $130
million you would be left with only about $40 million that woul d be going directly to
whānau.
That was never the intention of the programme, from what we believe, with regard to
when the Māori Party first announced it. The idea was that more money would go
directly towards helping whānau. If only $40 million, one thi rd of the funding, is
actually reaching whānau, after you take the administration from Te Puni Kōkiri, the
commissioning agencies, and then the providers, well, effectively, this is how much
money those individuals who were getting help were getting.
We k now there were 43,000 because Te Ururoa Flavell said that about 43,000
individuals were helped by Whānau Ora funding and about 9,000 families. If you add
that up and say that only $40 million made it to the actual ground, then that would be
less than $100 per person who benefited in some way from Whānau Ora. That would be
only $444 per family who benefited from Whānau Ora.
So you can see here that there are real problems with the way in which Whānau Ora
is operating under the National Government, and we need to investigate it further. It is
not just us, on this side of the House, being cynical, but actually it is the respons ible
thing to do, and it is actually what the Auditor-General said needs to be done. It needs to
be explored further. This is not us criticising just for the sake of criticising; this is us
being the watchdog of Parliament, holding the Government to accoun t on its spending
and saying, actually, that this is not responsible, nor is it acceptable —$43 million on
administration just at Te Puni Kōkiri and at the commissioning agency level.
I ran an NGO for 3 years before coming here, a Pacific NGO, and I know h ow hard
our NGO sector works. I know how hard they are working, on the smell of an oily rag. I
know that many of the providers out there have had no funding increases for the last 6
years under this National Government. I also know that it was not all smoo th sailing
when the Whānau Ora funding was rolled out. There were problems that occurred even
within my own Pacific community —competition that came about that was not
necessarily the healthiest. There were issues there with regard to the relationships and
the collaboration that was happening, or not happening, in the sector, so those things
need to be investigated as well.
I do want to also just touch on the fact that the Whānau Ora approach is about
supporting whānau, rather than just individuals. It is about looking at the whole whānau.
It has been problematic, and the report points that out, because that culture or that
kaupapa is not necessarily adopted by the two main ministries that are working
alongside Whānau Ora —being the Ministry of Health and the  Ministry of Social
Development. There are inconsistencies there that also need to be addressed. It is our
responsibility as a Parliament to explore this further.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. The
Hon Hekia Parata—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker.
I am pleased to participate in this debate about Whānau Ora because there has been a lot
of criticism thrown at this initiative, this new approach, because of a fundamental
misunderstanding. This is a revolutionary old concept. Yes, it is new to the Public
Service, and all of the challenges that are attendant upon that are outlined not only in the
Auditor-General’s report but in the numerous reports that have been done since this
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3249
programme first got underway. It is correct, as the Deputy Prime Minister has already
indicated, that this programme has been under more scrutiny than almost any other
programme from its get -go, and it has had to develop a whole range of dimensions that
we do not demand of any other programme. Whānau Ora as a concept is extremely well
understood.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Rubbish! Of course we demand it.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: It is not rubbish. It is not rubbish, and I would challenge
that member to demonstrate to me—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: We demand that the aims and the objectives are clear.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Mehemea kei te mōhio katoa tērā mema ki tēnei kaupapa,
ka mōhio a ia. [ If that member knows everything about this matter, then he will
understand.] So I will tell the House about the other programme that threatens the
Opposition members who are happy to sit on their hands and the parlous situation we
found when we came into Government in terms of Māori, of Pasifika, of families from
poorer homes, which that Government prior to us was happy to sit on.
Here in this G overnment we have been prepared to take some risks. We have been
prepared to work with our coalition partners. We have been prepared to acknowledge
the success of very old and traditional concepts within the Māori cultural context. What
is revolutionary about this is it proceeds from a paradigm where Māori are right, where
all their beliefs, their value systems should be taken into account and imported into a
social services provision where it focuses on the collective entity of the whānau, as the
previous speaker indicated. But the challenge of that is that Public Service departments
have not been accustomed to dealing with those kinds of entities. That has been
challenging and the Office of the Auditor -General has pointed out where some of those
challenges have failed. But does that mean that you toss this out, that you spend the
whole time praying for failure and baying for calamity, as the Opposition consistently
does?
As I said earlier in the House, when we came into Government we found that that
Opposition was happy to consign Māori and Pasifika students to failure. Well, Whānau
Ora is another—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: How much of our university entrance numbers dropped under that
Government?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, it was, and the evidence is unimpeachable, and it does
not matter how loud the member shouts. The evidence is actually unequivocal: Māori
had a 44 percent pass rate at National Certificate of Educational Achievement  level 2;
Pasifika had 51 percent. Under this Gove rnment Māori had a 63 percent pass rate and
Pasifika had 72 percent. Whānau Ora is another initiative that is directed at intractable
problems that that Opposition when it was in Government was not prepared to tackle. It
was happy to sing action songs and waiata, but was that making a material difference to
the whānau? Not at all.
These navigators tackle some really difficult problems. I was in my colleague’s
electorate last week, and I visited Kaiti School. That school has had significant
challenges aroun d attendance, transience, and whānau who struggle with difficulties.
They have had a Whānau Ora navigator in their school for the past 2 years. The
difference it has made is absolutely measurable and palpable. All of the staff whom I
met—the principal, the  teachers—the whānau who came, and the aiga who came
attested to the quality of difference that the whānau navigator has made to their school.
These are people who are struggling practically with how to make a difference for their
whānau.
So, yes, there h ave been criticisms of Whānau Ora. It is still developing. I can say
from some personal experience how hard it is to get a new and controversial, yet risky
3250 Urgent Debates 6 May 2015
and “can make a difference” policy, off the ground. Partnership schools and kura hourua
have attracted the same visceral attacks from the Opposition, as again we seek to push
out the boundaries. We take risks —yes, we take risks. We are unapologetic about that.
We have had some difficulties with one—with one—out of nine schools. These are with
children who really do come from challenging circumstances. We cannot get them to
attend mainstream schools. Those mainstream schools have said those are the failures.
But here is the thing. We are getting raised achievement in all kinds of schools, whether
they are mainstream ones or partnership schools. Kura kaupapa Māori, State -based,
State-integrated—we are getting—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has
expired.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Anne Tolley—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I wish th e Opposition
speakers who have stood in this House today and have criticised and taken the
opportunity to take pot-shots at Whānau Ora had taken the same opportunity to express
their concerns about the low educational results for Māori and Pasifika, the lo w
participation in early childhood education by Māori and Pasifika, the low life
expectancy for Māori and Pasifika, the high benefit dependency by Māori and Pasifika,
the high imprisonment rates for Māori and Pasifika, the high rates of smoking amongst
Māori and Pasifika, the high rates of diabetes and heart disease amongst Māori and
Pasifika, and the high rates of children living in hardship amongst Māori and Pasifika.
The reality is that we inherited a system that, under the previous Labour
Government, continued to throw buckets of money at all of those issues, without any
idea of where that money was going and of what effect that money was having. In all of
the questions that Opposition members have been asking today, all that they have been
interested in  is how much money is being spent on this programme and how many
people are attending those courses. That is not what changes people’s lives. In fairness,
I would have to say that, over the years, successive Governments, both National and
Labour, have stru ggled with how they address the extremely difficult and complex
issues that face too many of our Māori and Pasifika families.
Over the years, the statistics are very clear: we have changed nothing. I applaud the
Māori Party, which was bold enough to come a long and say: “We propose a different
way of addressing these issues.” It may not be perfect. I think the Auditor -General’s
report is actually a really positive report because in it she acknowledges that this is a
new and innovative way of addressing these  complex issues. And, yes, there have been
problems, and she has—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Read the first page.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Yes, I will read the first page. She says: “I have no doubt
that some commentators will make light of the successes described in this report and
make much of the criticisms.” Those three guys sitting there —middle-aged white
Pākehā men who have been in this House for too long —have no idea of the courage it
took the Māori Party to put up this programme and m ake it work. They have no idea.
Phil Goff was part of two Governments that did nothing for Māori and that did nothing
to advance the options and opportunities for those families. They sit there now and they
carp, but the Māori Party had the courage to say:  “We can do this. We need your help.
We need your advice. We need some funding in our communities, and we can work to
make a difference with our families.”
The Auditor-General’s report makes it clear that those families can do it. With the
right support, we can make significant changes. We do need to take learnings from the
Auditor-General’s report, and we will do that. But we will not resile from trying
different ways of reaching out and supporting those vulnerable children, in particular,
6 May 2015 Urgent Debates 3251
and their famili es. I challenge Opposition members to look past their myopic, middle -
class attitudes and reach out to those families too. We could do with their support out
and about in their electorates, and those families could too.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Associate Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): I move, That the House take note of miscellaneous business . I am a
proud New Zealander and I am proud to be part of a Government that is leading a
courageous country and a growing economy. I am also incredibly proud to follow the
speakers on this side of the House, who are out there actually making a difference for
hard-working New Zealanders in all sorts of circumstances, from one end of the country
to the other. We have a Prime Minister who is willing to be courageous and to lead
programmes that might be different from the programmes we have seen from previous
Governments—programmes that are not delivering for New Zealand. This side of the
House is doing things that we believe in, trusting Māori to look at solutions that work
for them in their communities that they are leading.
I want to turn my attention to across the Ditch. I want to talk, as Associate Minister
for Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment, about my experience at one of our
campaign-promised job fairs that was in Melbourne. The very intent of these job fairs is
to attract our Kiwis home. There are 480, 000 of them living in Australia. It was quite
amazing to be part of a conversation with a Māori woman who was in tears. She wants
to come home. She can see the opportunities here in New Zealand, which are so far
greater than what is on offer in Australia. It was really quite moving to realise that we
have Kiwis whom we are attracting home to New Zealand.
To be fair, we are also offering that opportunity to Aussies who want to become
Kiwis. It is interesting that the net migration from Australia, to the year February 2015,
was 2,400. That is the highest level ever since records began in 1978. I think that s ays
pretty clearly how well Prime Minister John Key is leading this country and our
economic recovery. Those are the sorts of things they look at. It was really interesting.
It was about the day that the Kiwi dollar was hitting parity with the Australian d ollar. It
was amazing to get the sense from those Australians that we are no longer regarded as
the poor cousin. We are up there, right alongside them, and actually we are overtaking
them. If you look at our economic performance and if you look at our unem ployment
rate at 5.8 percent as compared with their 6.2 percent, we are heading down and they are
heading up. No longer is Australia the Lucky Country. We have a golden opportunity in
terms of attracting Kiwis home.
I guess one of the challenges when you have a growing economy, an economy
growing as strongly as it is, is that there are a few growing pains. One of those is being
able to fill jobs in industries that we clearly need. These job fairs were very directly
focused on filling jobs in information an d communications technology, manufacturing,
health, construction, trades, engineering, and transport. There are 4,500 job seekers
directly looking at coming here. It was a fantastic opportunity.
As the previous speaker, Minister Parata, said, we are also training young New
Zealanders, Māori and Pasifika students, female and male, at a greater rate than the
previous Government, and probably those students from the past whom the Opposition
in its days in Government left behind. We are actually turning round the results and the
lives and the futures of those very New Zealanders. That is why I get reactions from
tradies in my electorate, like the one I spoke to yesterday, who said “Can you give John
a message for me? Tell him he’s doing a bloody good job, and w e want to keep him
3252 General Debate 6 May 2015
longer.” That is the mood that I get, whether I am talking to groups in Dunedin or
whether I am talking to groups in Northland. Hard -working middle New Zealand, from
one end of the country to the other, knows that John Key, our Prime Min ister, is
delivering for them—delivering in the areas that count.
I want to talk specifically about women’s participation in the workforce, because this
is one of my priorities: making sure that the skills and utilisation of women is fully
realised. This is a Government that is backing New Zealand women to succeed. I am
really pleased to say that the results that came out today in the household labour force
survey show that there are 3,000 fewer women unemployed in the March 2015 quarter.
There are some ve ry specific things that we are doing to engage more women in
employment. Canterbury is a classic example: there is a shortage in the construction
sector. The Ministry for Women has done a very practical, collaborative job with the
sector to get more women into jobs.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Well, what we have now is the
dying months of a shabby, grubby National Government. Oh yes, that last speech by
Louise Upston was  one of the biggest statements of conceit that we have had from a
junior Minister in this Government for a long, long time.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Says the guy who only gets 11 percent.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: There are none so blind as those who will not see, as Mr Jami-
Lee Ross well knows. Ms Upston talked about the job fairs. Well, I tell you what, the
job fairs were wonderful for the Melbourne business community, especially the taxi
drivers because they profited to the tune of nearly $1,3 00 from one Minister alone
ferrying himself around with the Melbourne taxis at the expense of the New Zealand
taxpayer. That was his contribution to the job fair for New Zealand in Melbourne.
What we are observing now —and we can smell it from here —is the rancid smell of
the decay of this Government now starting to rise and now starting to bubble up. Let us
just have a look at it. It is a Government overtaken by arrogance, by contempt, and now
by conceit. Look at the issues: contempt for conflicts of interest in ministerial portfolios,
a failure of economic management of gross proportions —and I am going to come back
to these in a minute —boondoggle and pork barrel in Northland, and they cannot even
get that right. They put it all up there and could not get the mselves elected. There is out
of control spending and abject denial of issues that are screaming out for attention —
house prices in Auckland would be one of them. What we have now is no longer a
Government; we have a dog and pony show. Oh yes, you knew that  was going to come
up. We have got the show -pony leader, who is now more “pony puller” —he is the
ponytail puller from Parnell —and a Government that has lost its way and no longer
knows what to do, as if it ever did.
Let us have a look at this. We expect f rom our Cabinet Ministers  the highest
standards of conduct. We do not expect Ministers to be flippant and cavalier about
conflicts of interest. This Government never gets it right. It thinks “Our people are nice.
They’re good people. How can they possibly do anything wrong?”. That is not the issue
when it comes to conflicts of interest. The issue about conflicts of interest, no matter
who the Minister is —whether it is the Prime Minister or anybody else —is the integrity
of that public office. The public is e ntitled to know that our Ministers—who occupy the
highest and most senior offices in the land —conduct themselves with the utmost
integrity and that when there is a risk, or a potential or real conflict of interest, they step
aside. They should not have to be asked. They should not have to be browbeaten from
office before this happens. I am confident that when the full facts of various situations
concerning this Government over the last few months  emerge, the New Zealand public
will be horrified. They will b e shocked at the increasingly cavalier and contemptuous
6 May 2015 General Debate 3253
approach that this Government is taking to that important part of occupying public
office.
Let us have a look at economic management. This Government will go down in
history as one of the most reckles s that we have ever had. It has ridden the wave —the
complacent wave of high commodity prices —and it has thought “Nothing to do here.
This is all going swimmingly for us. We don’t have to worry about the future, because
we won’t be around long enough to hav e deal with it.” Well, now it is catching up with
the Government. Commodity prices have been falling for well over a year now, and it
knows that the tsunami is about to hit —or the lack of it, actually —which is the $7
billion hole that will emerge in this economy later this year when the farmers cannot get
the returns on their goods and on their work. It will be a $7 billion hole in our economy.
Of course, it will be bigger than that, because there is a multiplier effect as that money
fails to wash through t he economy. Then there will be less work, less income, and less
revenue for many more businesses and for many more working people. That is what is
going to hit New Zealand in the latter part of this year, and this Government could not
care less. That is why the Government members are all looking down now, because they
do not really care about that stuff.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: 3.5 percent growth. 80,000 new jobs. What else do you need to
know?

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: They have ridden the wa ve of the benefits of it, and they do
not care about it. They bury their heads in the sand, like the member opposite —bury
their heads in the sand —because they just do not care. They sit by and say “This is the
sign of success: a rapidly out of control Auck land housing market.” This is their sign of
success. They do not care that innocent Aucklanders —young working families —are
being shut out of the housing market. They never cared about that. They lost the basic
New Zealand egalitarian ethos long ago—they never cared about it, never will. This is a
shabby, grubby Government with no vision that is on its way out.

items.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.role: Minister of Commerce and Con sumer Affairs

items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak. Well, we have had more shock, horror,
overreach, and outrage from Opposition members, who are always jumping up and
down and confecting outrage. That is why I believe that Mr Little is in danger of be ing
overtaken by Len Brown to be the most successful Labour leader in Auckland at the
moment. That is why that party is struggling to engage with New Zealanders and the
concerns that New Zealanders have. That is why this Government is focused on New
Zealand families and what New Zealanders are looking for in terms of jobs, growth, and
access to good education and health care. They have seen that this Government has been
very focused on their needs and their concerns. That is why we continue to have that
high level of support. So if you think that having 74,000 new jobs in this economy that
we did not have this time last year is not important, then I think you are out of touch
with what Aucklanders and New Zealanders really want. That is why we are working
hard to improve our public services in welfare, health, and education.
I want to touch on a couple of the areas in my ministerial responsibility that relate to
how we as a Government can help Kiwi families get ahead. There are a couple of areas.
One is the cost of living. There are two ways that you can improve living standards in
this country. One is economic growth, which is what this Government has a fantastic
track record in —3 percent this year. We are one of the leading growth countries and
economies in the developed world, and we have got projections for further growth over
the next little while. The other way is to make each dollar go further. That is why a
strong, competitive domestic economy is so important. The competition laws, which I
have some re sponsibility for, are fundamental to maintaining that disciplined and
competitive domestic economy.
3254 General Debate 6 May 2015
We have got the cartels legislation, which is halfway through the House and which
we will be progressing very quickly. It is all about sending a clear mess age that we do
not tolerate any of that behaviour. We have also got a review coming up of section 36 of
the competition law, which relates to the misuse of market power. We do not want to
put any barriers in the way of new entrants coming into any industri es in this country,
shaking things up and making it more competitive, so that New Zealanders have more
money in their pockets when they go out and buy their shorts, their shoes, and their
food, in every industry that they deal with. A strong, competitive e conomy and industry
in New Zealand is a fundamental and important thing.
We keep on hearing about house prices. Well, one of the reasons why New
Zealanders have invested in residential housing for so long is that it is very hard for
somebody to steal your  house. The contrary idea over the last 30 or 40 years of putting
your savings into financial markets has been a difficult one. So many New Zealanders
have lost their savings over the years, so the most important thing we can do in financial
markets is bui ld confidence in the system. That is why this Government put through a
huge change in the Financial Markets Conduct Act last year. My focus very much as
Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs is to make sure that we implement that
well over the next cou ple of years. This is so that New Zealanders, when they are
looking at where they are going to put their money, do not have residential real estate as
just one option, but are more likely to invest in financial markets and build on their
KiwiSaver funds, w hich have been so important in building an understanding of those
financial markets.
Also, we are working on a review of the Financial Advisers Act, which is about
giving advice to Kiwis. On the whole, our financial literacy could be improved. We
have put in there a regime for financial advisers for the last 3 years and we want to
make sure that we have got that right, that any conflicts of interest are dealt with
properly, and that the costs and the regulatory burden of giving advice are not so high
that f ewer people get advice. We are focused on that, as we are also focused on the
broader idea of financial literacy.
There is no more important thing you can do for New Zealand families than help
them understand how money works, how interest works, and how to improve financial
literacy within families in their homes in New Zealand. That is why this Government
has more than trebled the amount of money that has been put into budgeting services,
through the Ministry of Social Development, and I think that is a very important step.
We have also been working hard on our consumer laws around the responsible lending
code. Again, we are trying to make sure that people who are offering or lending money
ask basic questions about the ability of the person to pay back lo ans, so that they fully
understand the full extent of those loans.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Tomorrow Auckland Council will vote on the 3 -
year transport budget it will be adopting. Although th e proposal involves a significant
increase in funding in rail, busways, and public transport—all the stuff that Aucklanders
have been asking for—unfortunately, it has to be funded through rates rises because this
National Government is failing Auckland and  not putting the transport budget into the
projects that Aucklanders really need and want.
Last week my colleague Denise Roche, our Auckland issues spokesperson, asked the
Minister of Transport, Simon Bridges, questions about transport funding and investment
in Auckland. I have to set the record straight because, surprisingly, Minister Bridges got
quite a few things wrong. Firstly, he said that the National Government had spent $1.6
billion on rail in Auckland, more than the Green Party had ever spent. I a m not sure
whether the Minister realises that the Green Party has not yet been part of a formal
coalition in a Government, and, therefore, although we could have perhaps dipped into
6 May 2015 General Debate 3255
our parliamentary office budgets to try to fund transport infrastructure i n Auckland, it
would not have paid for much, and it really is the responsibility of the parties in
Government to spend the transport budget.
That $1.6 billion he is referring to was not, of course, the initiative or the idea of this
National Government. It is funding that was entirely committed under the previous
Labour Government. In 2007 , $1.1 billion was committed to Project DART and $500
million to the electrification of Auckland’s rail network, largely thanks to the Green
Party putting pressure on th e Labour Government at the time. So, despite not being in
Government, the Greens were instrumental in getting half a billion dollars of investment
in Auckland rail. Of course, once National came into power , that $500 million turned
into a loan, so rather than actually paying for Auckland’s rail infrastructure, it is forcing
Auckland ratepayers to pay it back, while it does pay for rail upgrades in Wellington. So
this National Government has not committed a single dollar, to my knowledge, to new
passenger rail infrastructure in Auckland since coming to power in 2008.
This is despite phenomenal growth in the rail network. We saw patronage growth of
20 percent in the past year. We are now on track to hit the Government’s arbitrary target
of 20 million rail passengers by 2017, which is 3 years earlier than the Prime Minister’s
threshold for bringing funding for this City Rail Link forward and actually starting it on
time. Of course, that project needed to be started yesterday because it is going to have to
be open by 2017 to meet the needs of Aucklanders. At the rate we are going now , we
will be lucky if it is open by 2021 or 2022, but that is only if National actually sees the
light and commits some funding to this central project.
Mr Bridges also claimed that 99 percent of people commute on the roads. I think he
