reshuffle, mate, I hope you actually land one of those portfolios in Cabinet or even
outside of it. You are doing a good job. I know full well that this is going to be used
later on; I am just saying that I am appreciative of that.
I particularly say that because, as a mayor, I came to this House when the local
government amendment legislation was going through and I, unfortunately, had to sit as
a witness to those submissions put forward by other people who are interested in the
Local Government Act. I was thoroughly disappointed with the way that that committee
attacked members of Local Go vernment New Zealand and other submitters who dared
to criticise the legislation that went through. I am sorry, Nicky, but the behaviour of that
committee and the reports that continue to be discussed around Local Government New
Zealand speak very ill of that committee, in the way it behaved. This Local Government
and Environment Committee is nothing like that. It is a very good committee to work in,
and the work coming out of there reflects that.
It is interesting also to look at the names of the people who have been involved in the
Christchurch Arts Centre over the years. As someone who lived on and off in
Canterbury for 30 years, I see those people’s names here in the legislation going back in
time to 1978—Albert Brownlie, Malcolm Douglass, Peter Dunbar,  Richard Harrington,
Graham Miller, Noel Searell, and Thomas Taylor. Those people have done sterling
work in Canterbury for the Arts Centre over the years and that work is carried on very
ably by Margaret Austin, a person I have great affection for. She is  one of those people
who talked me into standing for Parliament right at the outset and supported me in my
campaign against Ruth “mother of all Budgets” Richardson —a scalp we very, very
nearly got and we did get indirectly when she got fired by Jim Bolger as a result of that
election.
This bill is an easy one to support. It is eminently sensible. The purpose and
objectives of the bill are clearly to set up a better governance structure that makes it
possible for what is going to be a $290 million project i nvolving 23 category I heritage
buildings to be completed on time and with fiscal prudence, and to ensure that the Arts
Centre is managed sustainably going into the future. We can only support that.
I am one of those p eople who spent a few nights in the Dux de Lux, having a quiet
ale here and there. No doubt if I had known him then, I would have probably had a beer
with Matt Doocey as well, as we discussed the ills and the woes of the world, amongst
many students from Canterbury who likewise imbibed a few in those surroundings. The
opportunity to take my children —and now my grandchildren —into the Arts Centre to
enjoy the entertainment, to enjoy the arts, the culture, the vibrancy, and the atmosphere
was something we enjo yed as a young family and I am very confident this legislation
will make it possible for that to continue for generations to come.
3276 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 6 May 2015
There were some issues around —and I am just looking back through my notes
here—the powers of the trust board and the appoint ments, the mechanism by which
people are appointed. Eminently sensible decisions were taken there. Removing the
Minister from any perceived control over who gets appointed I think was a very
sensible move and New Zealand First supports that. Having said th at, I know from
personal experience there have been some very sensible decisions made by some of this
Government’s Ministers in the past, people they have appointed to places, and I thank
them very much for those appointments in the past. I just want to cl ose by saying that it
is a good bill, good work. Thank you very much. It was a pleasure working with the
team on that. New Zealand First will be supporting the bill.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I rise to say just a few words in
support of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. May I begin, first, by
acknowledging the very warm comments from Mr Mark on the other side of the
Chamber. Thank you very much. Part of the collegialit y of the Local Government and
Environment Committee is, of course, due to your ongoing and constructive
contribution to the debate that we have around the table.
We are here tonight to talk about the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. As we
know, it is being set up, essentially, to establish the legal foundations for the trust —
effectively, to enable it to respond to the challenges and the tragedy of the Christchurch
earthquake. We have heard already —far more eloquently than I could ever put into
words—about the challenge that the Canterbury community has had to confront, about
the very special place that the Arts Centre has for the people of Canterbury, and about
how important it is for them that the improvements continue apace and that there is an
enduring legal framework that ensures that what they want from those buildings will
deliver for them and their grandchildren into the future.
During the select committee process, we had a great visit down there, and I
acknowledge here the work of the chair, J en Crawford, and the chief executive officer,
André Lovatt —in particular, André, who helped facilitate that particular tour. We
donned our hard hats and walked around most of the 23 category I heritage buildings,
and we were given a sense of what they were , what they became through the
earthquake, and, more critically, what the vision is for them as they are rebuilt. And I
think to see, first hand, the purpose of this bill expressed not so much in bricks and
mortar but in stone and the fantastic application  of skill puts this particular bill in
context. It certainly did for me. As somebody who is a bit of a historian, I actually
found it really enjoyable. Unfortunately, we could not get into all of the buildings,
obviously—either because of their state of di srepair or because of where they were in
terms of the repair process—but we did walk past the student union building and we got
a sense of why it is still important and needs to be, and has been, captured in this
particular bill.
The Dux de Lux has already  been mentioned tonight. I went there once as a student.
Had I known that I would end up here, I would have paid more attention to the names
that were scrawled on the wall. I probably would have seen halfway up “Megan was
here”, and, possibly, just a little bit lower “and so was Ron”.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Sorry, Mr Chair. Anyway, as I said, it was good to see firsthand.
Moving back to the specific clauses, obviously there are a number here that we want
to reflect on. I think it is right that we have removed clause 8 from the bill. It is
absolutely appropriate that debts accrued by the trust board are adopted by the Crown
should it ever be wound up. It is a sensible commercial amendment. We talked about it
at the time, and I think we have got a sensible outcome there. In terms of the objects,
again, adding new clause 5(2), which requires that all income, benefits, or advantages
6 May 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3277
received by or accruing to the trust board be used to advance the charitable purpose of
the trust, is a belt and braces approach. You could argue that perhaps it was not needed,
but the committee decided that we should put it in for the avoidance of doubt, to make it
absolutely clear about what should happen should that ever occur.
We recommend, of  course, amending clause 6. Again, I think that makes a lot of
sense. It is a sensible amendment to be considered. When we talked about trust
vacancies, there was, throughout the submission process, obviously some debate in
respect of what happens when the re is a vacancy on this new board and in respect of
what the proper role for the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage  should be. There
was some debate and, certainly, some thought put forward by some of the submitters
that we should be careful around the involvement—[Bell rung]

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call Todd Muller.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: There was some debate —[Interruption] I am sorry, do I need to
repeat it? Sorry. There is a particular i ssue here that I would like to hear about from the
Minister in the chair, should she take a call later on. This was an area that we reflected
on: the potential perception of a Minister being involved in influencing any
appointments to the trust board. We m ade some changes  to enable that by deleting
clause 1(d)(iii) of schedule 2, and, ultimately, I think we have landed in the right place.
Now that we are talking about governance, I do want to acknowledge the various
stakeholders who have expressed their sup port for the intent of this bill —in particular,
the University of Canterbury, Christchurch City Council, Heritage New Zealand,
Christchurch Civic Trust, and Papatipu Rūnanga, amongst others. I do acknowledge
their contribution historically and their suppor t for this move from a representative
governance board to a skills -based governance board. But my view is that the task is
only half done because it is now incumbent, I think, on the community to ensure that the
right mix of skills is appointed to govern this trust board into the future.
If I have a challenge for the community, it is, I guess, that it should be global in its
search. Too often in this country, we are very, very keen, in this context, to showcase
our culture and our heritage to the world, and we are often very proud of how others see
our culture, and we are very global in terms of the portrayal of that. But sometimes we
are quite reticent in terms of taking up the opportunities of those who have a global
perspective and are involved in governi ng our heritage. So I put a challenge out there:
let us look beyond just Canterbury for the skill sets to be able to govern and support this
trust board into the future, now that it has moved, and will move, to a skills -based board
as opposed to the representative-based board that is there at the moment.
We had quite a conversation about land. Some of the issues that we discussed in
respect of the titles have already been raised, and why, historically, there has been such
a high number of them. There was, of course, the reference to stone buildings. The chair
of the Local Government and Environment Committee, Scott Simpson, has already put
that question to the Minister, and I think that her perspective will be worth hearing as
well. But, certainly, the recom mendation was pretty clear. There is a tweak in the
wording of clause 4 to clarify that definition. Personally, I think the word “including”,
as I read it, provides the appropriate comfort for those who think that the focus is simply
on the stone buildings  and that that somehow means that the student union building
would not be included in terms of the long -term development of that site. Certainly,
when you go around that site and listen to the people working on it and to the favour in
which the community h olds that student union building, I am pretty sure that that is
going to be part of any ongoing development plan.
Also, having at the annual meeting the requirement to put that conservation plan on
the table and to have it in front of the community and tho se who are interested in,
essentially, the strategy of conservation and what that will look like over time, I think is
3278 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 6 May 2015
a good amendment. It ensures that the community of Canterbury stays plugged into the
vision of this new trust board, and ensures that, ul timately, those buildings and that
incredible cultural asset continue to head in the direction that the community seeks.
Finally, can I acknowledge the Minister for her work. It must be incredibly satisfying
to be part of a process that sees an asset in he r community being protected and
enhanced—as this bill will do. Again, I acknowledge the chairman and those with
whom I have worked on the select committee. I echo Ron Mark in that it was for the
most part very collegial. Thank you, and I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: I am standing to take this call on the
Arts Centre of Christchurch T rust Bill. It is great to be from Christchurch; great to be
from Canterbury. As a young fellow born in the old Calvary Hospital, it strikes me with
some irony that I spent many years as a student investing in the longevity of the Arts
Centre via the Dux de  Lux, and now I get to invest in the longevity of the Arts Centre
through this bill. I managed to wear my new blue suit today, but, like my parliamentary
colleague Megan Woods, I very much wanted to wear my red and black suit —but I am
red and black on the inside.
The Arts Centre is as Christchurch as sitting on the embankment at Lancaster Park,
watching the Christchurch and Canterbury teams through the 1980s Shield challenge
era. The Arts Centre is as Christchurch as sitting in the square watching the Birdman
and watching the Wizard at lunchtime. The Arts Centre is as Christchurch as going up
to Mount Hutt and skiing during the morning and heading down to Sumner and
swimming in the afternoon.
Could I acknowledge the Hon Nicky Wagner for bringing this lo cal bill to the
Committee. You could not find a harder -working Minister and MP than the Hon Nicky
Wagner, and, I suppose for a Canterbury MP myself, she is such a role model with her
work ethic. I also acknowledge Scott Simpson, who is the chair of the Loc al
Government and Environment Committee —a select committee that holds a huge
workload—for his effortless approach in dispensing the work at hand.
The Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill reflects the local, national, and
international heritage significa nce of the Arts Centre. Growing up in Christchurch, I
very much know that Christchurch is deemed the most English city outside England.
The Arts Centre is the heart of that, along with the Hagley Park, our beautiful botanic
gardens, the Avon River, which w eaves its way through the city, with the willow trees,
and, of course, the great Christchurch Cathedral. But most of all, I suppose, it is our
archaic one -way system through the city, and the great English street names, like
Hereford Street, Manchester Str eet, and Lichfield Street. The bill is a key part of
protecting and preserving the Arts Centre of Christchurch for the future. As many will
know, Christchurch experienced severe earthquakes, and the Arts Centre was impacted
on by the first earthquake in September 2010, and subsequently in February 2011.
Since we are in Committee, I would just like to take some time and talk to the
clauses. Clause 8 was removed —this one would have transferred trust property to the
Crown on an interim basis in the event that  the trust was to be wound up. Omitting this
clause avoids debts accrued by the trust board being adopted by the Crown. Also, new
clause 5(2) was added, requiring that all income, benefits, or advantages received or
accrued to the trust be used to advance the charitable purposes of the trust. We do know
that this Arts Centre has considerable potential for income and revenue streams. Before
the earthquakes and the subsequent closure of the Arts Centre, there were up to 1.5
6 May 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3279
million tourists turning up at the Arts Centre every year. They went along to see the
Court Theatre. They went along to see the many markets, as well as the art studios. I
myself can remember going along to the range of cuisine and food carts there as well,
and, of course, to the Dux de Lux , which we have heard a lot about tonight. There is
also the amending of clause 9 to state that the Charitable Trusts Act 1957 applies to the
trust and the trust board.
I think we need to remind ourselves here of the scale and the size of this work.
Currently this restoration project is the largest in the world, at a scale of around $280
million to $300 million.

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: It is $280 million to $300 million. This is currently the world’s
largest restoration project, and we do know that the Christchurch Arts Centre is also the
largest cluster of heritage buildings in New Zealand. What we need to do is think about
this gem within the story of the earthquake recovery. There are a lot of views put
forward, but if we do not take stock of the good stories of the Christchurch recovery we
are going to miss these great stories.
The Local Government and Environment Committee did go down and convene the
committee in Christchurch, where we heard the very succinct and eloquent submissions
of the chief executive officer, André Lovatt, and the trust chair as well. It was great to
get a tour of the Christchurch Arts Centre from them. My colleague Todd Muller has
talked about it tonight. Their energy and enthusiasm and thei r passion are what is
driving this forward, as well as the support of Christchurch, Canterbury, New Zealand,
and also the rest of the world. What I mean by that is that they took us into the
stonemason room, and around that room they have flags from all ar ound the world.
Each flag represents a different type of nationality of stonemason. Many of these people
have contacted the Arts Centre off their own bat because they want to be part of this
restoration project. It is currently the largest project of its kind in the world. It is great to
see this workforce coming from around the whole world to instil this specialist skill of
stonemasonry. Christchurch’s Art Centre will be rebuilt. We are very much looking
forward to that gem of the Christchurch recovery.
We also amended clause 6 and in schedule 2 added a new clause 12 to enable the
trust board to amend its constitution. I would ask the Minister whether we could maybe
hear a bit more about what Jen Crawford, the trust chair, and André Lovatt, the chief
executive officer, spoke about. It is a shift from representation to a skills -based
governance model. They explained that what they would be doing is moving to a skills -
based governance model where individuals will be appointed by an appointments
committee so that the trust board has a strong set of skills to address the issues that will
come up through this restoration project, but it will also ensure that this board will have
the right skills and experience to take the Arts Centre forward over the next 10, 20,  30,
and 40 years. So I would hope that the Minister will be able to respond to that —to
ensure that the implementation of this new governance system will achieve the outcome
that they hope for. Thank you.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call Simon O’Connor.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): I would be biased if I said that was the
right call. I am very pleased to stand and take a call on this, the Arts Centre of
Christchurch Trust Bill. I am very conscious —and I probably must apologise to
Minister Wagner and others —that I am an Aucklander. I do apologise, but I actually
think that the arts is something that moves well beyond just Canterbury and
Christchurch. It is something for the whole country.
3280 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 6 May 2015
I want to a cknowledge the work that is already being done and add to some of the
questions that my colleagues have been putting to the Minister tonight. I want to signal
to the Hon Nicky Wagner that there are a few thoughts I want to raise. As an initial
context, I remember the Arts Centre well from trips down to Christchurch in the past. I
remember it for two reasons: not only for the art and for the drawing together of people
and the expression they bring but also for the architecture. When I returned after the
Canterbury earthquakes, that was something I felt quite profoundly and quite sadly. But
really what it comes back to is the people. I think, inherently, what is happening here is
drawing the people back together. That is not only in the bill but in the governa nce
structures and so forth. If I was to push that a little bit further in some ways, picking up
on what the Greens spoke about earlier —I think it was the member Eugenie Sage —
actually, this has been quite a collegial discussion and environment in which to progress
things forward.
The arts are important. Anyone who knows me knows I am a great supporter of the
arts—everything from the Royal New Zealand Ballet to the opera, to the Auckland
Philharmonia Orchestra, and the like, and also the other forms of the arts and expression
that we have—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: The NZSO?
SIMON O’CONNOR: Oh, sorry, I have been remiss. I have shown my Auckland
bias. I have been instantly reminded by the Hon Christopher Finlayso n of the New
Zealand Symphony Orchestra, of course. I say that as context because, of course, what
the Arts Centre does is touch on a whole different range.
Some people might be questioning, as we look at this bill tonight in the Committee
of the whole Ho use, why we are bothering with something such as the arts. I cannot
help but be drawn to what Churchill once said —granted, in the context of the war and
the devastation there. He was asked by someone: “Why are we actually putting all this
money into the ar ts? Why are we putting it into the arts when there are much more
important things?”—in this case, the war. Churchill said: “Well, what are we fighting
for?”.
I think that is a really important context when we come to Canterbury and to this
particular area. What we are after is a really important expression. If I may share one
quick expression. When I lived in Fiji for 2 years, around a vocational—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: I raise a poin t of order, Mr Chairperson. I am just seeking your
advice. I know that we decided to take this bill as one part, but now we are about to hear
about his Fiji trip. He has talked about the Auckland orchestra in the context of
Christchurch. I just think it is  going a little bit broad at the moment, and I would like
you to—

SIMON O’CONNOR: If I may, actually —the context, the element, of Fiji, despite

SIMON O’CONNOR: Vanaka vaka levu, au kila —anyway, we will leave it there.
Let us not continue, or we might get into trouble.
6 May 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3281
The key part about the Arts Centre here is tha t it is a new opportunity to take what
has been an existing trust and to build on the strength of it, but to bring about new
opportunities. We have heard from many members about the great work that Jen
Crawford, as the chair, has been doing, as well as And ré Lovatt as the chief executive
officer. What we are seeing in this bill is an attempt to change the structure to move it
towards something that is more skills -based. We have heard that from other members. I
think that in a time of crisis, if you will, it  is really important often to move from the
representative, which respects the sort of normality of the situation, to bring it back into
the context of crisis. This means you need skilled people from the community to help
drive this forward. We have heard it from the Local Government and Environment
Committee, and when you read through the report, you can see that a lot of
consideration has been given to this: how do we do it better?
For those of us who have worked in community groups, on community boards,  with
sports groups, and otherwise, we always know that there is an ebb and flow. We are not
expecting the crises of Christchurch, but there are ebbs and flows when there are times
where you move from normality into the need for skills -based leadership. It  is really
good to see that in place here. I think , though, I would appreciate some of the insights
from the Minister on why she sees th is to be comprehensively skills based and why
there is no need, or not a specific need, for some representation, or mayb e the two will
blend in there. The other is, and it is one of the first things that was drawn to my
attention, around clause 8. The select committee was very cle ar on  the need for the
Crown to be removed in terms of transferring the trust property to the Crown. I think
this is quite a fundamental question. The Crown is trying to step back. I think there is a
paradox in that.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I just want to reflect
on some questions that have come up during the debate. First of all, I want to reflect on
Scott Simpson’s question. Scott Simpson was concerned about the reference to the stone
buildings of the Arts Centre. As we have heard signific antly tonight, the stone buildings
are a cluster of 23 magnificent stone buildings. They are all neo -Gothic buildings, just
like the provincial chambers, just like the Christchurch Cathedral, just like the
Canterbury Museum, just like some of the buildings  in Christ’s College. They are
wonderfully detailed, they are very special, and they were built over a period of about
50 years from about the late 1880s forward. It is particularly important that the stone
buildings are emphasised in this bill. It reflect s the wording of the original trust deed
and represents the importance of these stone buildings to those people who set up the
trust. It also, of course, represents the heritage significance. The Local Government and
Environment Committee supported the vie w of the trust board on this point, but it did
propose an amendment. It was an amendment to the definition of “The Arts Centre”, so
that it did include other buildings on that site. I think that is the right thing to do.
In reference to Todd Muller’s reque st, in terms of the removal of the Minister for
Arts, Culture and Heritage —I think that was a wise thing to do. It did remove any
possible idea—any misperception—that the Minister wanted to influence the board, and
showed that the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board would be truly independent.
In relation to Matt Doocey’s comments on the English names of Christchurch streets,
they are indeed reflecting the English provinces and we do have the Arts Centre on
Worcester Street. He may be interested to know  that the way the names were picked is
that they were names of dioceses of the Church of England, and that is how we get
Madras, Barbados, and Montreal Streets—so not just English streets.
Finally, to Simon O’Connor —in terms of the purpose of the bill, of course it is to
provide quality governance for the future. I think the present trust board was well aware
3282 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 6 May 2015
of the need for a comprehensive, skills-based board, and I think that will futureproof the
board going forward.
All in all, I thank the Committee mem bers for their comments and debate tonight.
This is a good bill and I support it.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAM S
items.text: I rise to take a short call on
the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill. I recall when we were discussing
this bill a week or two ago, in its second reading, that there was some concern expressed
by the members of  the Local Government and Environment Committee . The only
submitter who presented, of course, was the Christchurch City Council, and there was
some concern that the officials were not , perhaps,  paying due deference to the issues
that actually brought this bill before Parliament. The issues are really that there had
been some errors in previous rating decisions and deliberations by the Christchurch City
Council, which meant that ratepayers could, in fact, charge the city council on the
technicalities, because the council had not put the appropriate motions at the time that
the rates were being set. This happened over a period of a few years —I think, from
memory, in excess of 10 years—and what this piece of legislation seeks to do is validate
those rates retro spectively. I know that we are not comfortable about retrospective
legislation, but in this case this legislation provides the opportunity for the Christchurch
City Council to, I guess, ensure that in future ratepayers will not take any action against
it.
It is not an insignificant piece of legislation, because there are various parts of the
rating mechanism that need to be addressed , and several years that need to be covered ,
as well. So it does look at various aspects of rating and it does also look at various areas
within the Christchurch City Council realm, such as Governors Bay and Church Bay. It
looks at various mechanisms, such as ensuring that the water loan rates on those two
bays, for example, are taken care of.
I am comfortable that this piece o f legislation will, in fact, provide the opportunity
for the Christchurch City Council to ensure that its processes are now complete and now
compliant, and I am sure that the Christchurch City Council has taken due note of the
fact that it got itself into a bit of a difficult situation by not providing the right
mechanisms at the time that the rates bills were to be delivered. On that  note, there is
really not much more to say on the matter, so I thank you for the opportunity, Mr Chair,
and I commend the bill to the Committee.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I too rise to speak on
the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill at the Committee of the  whole
House stage. If anyone has been following this debate over the last few weeks, they will
6 May 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3283
understand that nobody likes to talk about retrospective or validation legislation. There
have been a few bills in this Parliament over the last couple of years  that have fallen
into these categories, and Parliament has struggled. We prefer things to be correct; we
do not like to have to go back and clean them up afterwards. However, it is
acknowledged in this case that a validation bill is the most practical, th e most cost -
effective, and the best way to address these historic rating irregularities of the
Christchurch City Council.
The bill seeks to validate rates irregularities going back to 2003 -04, right through to
2012-13. It all began after the Local Governm ent (Rating) Act 2002 was passed. The
council deliberately sought to simplify its resolution for setting rates and paying
penalties for unpaid rates. I think that was a positive desire. I think we are all aware of
the need for plain language in local gover nment legislation. These new simplified
resolutions were used successfully until the rules were found in 2012 to be technically
inadequate. Now, the council at that time was able to correct the 2013 -14 rates
demands, but at that stage the rating resolutions had been out of order for 10 years.
When the error in the rates setting was discovered by the Department of Internal
Affairs in 2013, the council treated it really seriously. It was shocked that defective
resolutions had been accepted by the department for 10 years without any concerns, and
that the council’s auditors had never commented on them. So the council commissioned
a legal review, councillors were briefed, and as soon as possible the information was
collected and analysed. It held the council meetings open to the public and the minut es
were available, so it was a very open process. As I have already said, at that stage the
council was able to correct its 2013 -14 rates resolution, and it has now changed the
process so that every year compliance is verified by legal and audit requiremen ts. The
council is apologetic. It takes full responsibility for the errors prior to 2013. Its desire to
further this bill demonstrates the seriousness of the situation. There is a major legal risk
for the council if the errors are not validated.
The counc il has always been very open with the public about the errors and open
about the steps that it has taken to rectify them, and, actually, the public have been
largely accepting of the situation. No approaches were made to the council during the
notification period of the bill and no submissions were made by the public to the select
committee. But let me make it clear that in terms of the irregularities of the rates
resolutions, all the required rating information —the rating years, the dates for the rates
instalments, the penalties, the calculations, the dates for the payments—was available to
the public. It just was not stated in the rates resolutions. Let me also make it clear that
no ratepayers have been disadvantaged by this resolution. In fact, nobody not iced the
error for over a decade.
So it was an error, yes, and of course we need our local councils to be accurate with
information and to write resolutions correctly, but it was a victimless crime. I note that
once notified the council took immediate action to rectify the situation, but I also note
that over the decade in question the personnel in the council had mostly changed, so the
new council staff have had to take on the responsibility of fixing the past resolutions
and of preparing this bill. I thank them for that. I particularly thank—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. Seeking your advice
again, it has just been pointed out to us that the Minister, during this Committee stage, is
giving her first reading speech word for word. Is that appropriate?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, that is not a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: May I just complete my discourse. I would like to thank
the council staff —the staff who have been new to the council in the last 10 years —
particularly Jane Parfitt, who was the acting chief executive officer at the time. It is not
nice to have to take responsibility for other people’s errors and clean up after them ,
3284 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 6 May 2015
especially on top of all the other work that the Christchurch City Council is doing in
terms of rebuilding our city.
So I support this bill. It is the easiest, the most cost efficient, and the practical way to
correct past irregularities and to ensure t hat the Christchurch City Council’s resolutions
now comply. Thank you.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: The Green Party is supporting the Christchurch City
Council (Rates Validation) Bill. I do not think it is a v ictimless crime, though, in terms
of what the city council has done. It means that we are here having to deal with
rectifying its errors. My call will be a brief one, but it is just that it is interesting that the
Minister Nicky Wagner, in terms of sponsor ing the bill as the local member, talked
about the council being very open about the errors that it had made and very open about
the way in which it was going to rectify those errors. That contrasts markedly with the
lack of transparency of the Government and the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority in terms of the spending of hundreds of millions of dollars on the anchor
projects, where there is very little information that is provided, despite large amounts of
public money being used, and where Offici al Information Act requests are delayed and
are heavily redacted when they are finally answered.
Part of the thing that this bill will do is actually enable the city council to recover
outstanding rates and penalties. They amount to about $684,000, which is a significant
amount, given the city council’s budget shortfall. That shortfall, of course, is in part due
to the anchor projects being foisted upon the council by the Government. We support
this bill. The member in the chair has very ably gone through the reasons for it and the
way in which the council has tackled those errors, but one of the things that I have been
puzzled by is that, in a mere 3½ years in this House, I have spoken on three rates
validations bills. The former Minister of Local Governme nt the Hon Dr Nick Smith did
a lot of tub -thumping, criticising local government, when at the time he really should
have been ensuring that there were much better guides being produced by the
Department of Internal Affairs to assist councils in how they pa ss their rates resolutions
to avoid getting into the situation that the Christchurch City Council has. I am pleased
the department is now, somewhat belatedly, working with Local Government New
Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers to improve  council practice in
setting these rates resolutions, and ensuring that the resolutions are clear and actually
follow the provisions of the Local Government (Rating) Act.
This is an uncontroversial bill, we will be supporting it, and I think that we have
canvassed all the reasons for that in earlier speeches. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I will not trouble the House for too
long with this call. It is a very short bill; I think i t warrants a very short speech. I would
like to echo the words of the previous speaker, Eugenie Sage, and say that the Labour
Party is supporting this bill, but we do share the concerns that far too often we are in
this House doing validation bills. We ack nowledge that the work has been done by the
present council to rectify the problems that have been found in terms of a resolution
around levying of the rates. It is not something that we want to do. We urge this House,
this Parliament, to do far more in te rms of ensuring that we do not get into this situation
again. It is my pleasure for Labour to support this bill.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a pleasure, as chairman of the
Local Government and Environment Committee, to take a call on this bill as it
progresses through the House through its Committee stage. I want to acknowledge the
local member, the Hon Nicky Wagner, who has ably supported and sponsored this bill,
under difficult circumstances in a way. I do not think that any local member takes any
pleasure at all in bringing to the House a piece of validating legislation. In the second
reading we heard from a number of people, myself included, who were, I think,
6 May 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3285
unhappy about the prospect of us having to consider it. This is quite a succinct, short,
and pithy bill that actually fixes irregularities that relate to payment dates for rates and
the authority to impose penalties on unpaid rates that occurred through a mistake, a lbeit
an honest mistake, made by the Christchurch City Council.
This is a local bill. The irregularities, as the sponsoring member indicated, actually
were victimless in terms of nobody having suffered financial loss or cost. But the
council has really ju st dodged a bullet because if, in fact, any ratepayer had decided to
bring legal action against the council during any one of those 10 years before the error
was discovered, there would have been significant potential for financial loss, not only
to the co uncil but to the wider ratepaying group. The Christchurch City Council failed
to state in its rates resolution that the rates were payable by instalments and not only
that but what the payment dates for those instalments might be and what penalties, if
there were to be any, might or might not be added. So it failed to state some very basic
things. I hasten to add that these errors occurred some 10 years or more ago —several
chief executive officers ago —and the opportunity, I guess, to seek retribution from t he
people who were responsible for ensuring that the errors did not occur has long since
passed.
However, notwithstanding that, it is my view that the council should perhaps have
been a little more contrite in terms of its submission to the select committ ee. We went
and heard the submission. There was only one submission; this was it. It was just a mere
two pages from the council. It was the only submission that was received. I have to say
on behalf of the committee that we were singularly underwhelmed by the presentation
received from the council staff and councillor who presented to the select committee in
Christchurch on the day that we had the hearing.
Sections in the bill are actually quite short. Clause 5 validates the payment dates for
the rates in a way that did not occur during the rates motion. Clause 6 validates any
penalties that may have been added to those rates through the error and omission that
took place some 10 years ago. Clause 7 declares that all money received by the council
in payment of the rates and any penalties paid in respect of those rates during the period
in which the error was unidentified will in fact be validated and that there will be no
potential for recovery from ratepayers who may have felt that those rates had been —as
they were—collected constitutionally, in terms of legality, illegally by the Christchurch
City Council.
Clause 9 goes on to validate the specified rates. These comprise the council’s
uniform annual general charge and seven targeted rates where irregulariti es have been
identified in terms of section 23 of the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002. These
resolutions were made so that the purpose of this bill is to validate those resolutions, so
that the status would be that the previous resolutions would then be  validated from
2004-05 through to the financial year 2012-13.
So I think that it is fair to say that in terms of the impact of this error that occurred in
Christchurch City, the council is very lucky to have got away as lightly as it did. This
was during  a period of time when the chief executive officers were being paid most
generously by the ratepayers. They were negligent in their role in ensuring that the
correct motions were passed, that the correct financial motions were made available to
the elected councillors. I for one felt very unhappy that the council actually showed no
contrition at all for that. I acknowledge that the current councillors and current council
staff were not personally responsible, but not withstanding that, there were very
significant errors. If the errors had occurred in other jurisdictions where members of the
public and ratepayers had been perhaps testing of this situation, then there would have
been very significant financial cost to the council and ratepayers. The legal cost  alone
would have been enormous.
3286 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 6 May 2015
This piece of legislation affirms that all money received by the council in payment of
the rates, and any penalties paid in respect of those rates, to be and to always have been
lawfully paid and received by the council. S o what that means is that there will no
longer be an opportunity for any disgruntled or offended ratepayer to bring a
retrospective piece of litigation against the council in a way that may have allowed the
council to become further financially compromised  if such a piece of litigation had
taken place.
Although the funding impact statement for each year of the errors included all the
information that was required —so on the actual rates bill the correct information was
there—notwithstanding that, the formal  proper motions had not been passed by the
elected councillors, the people who are elected by the good citizens of Christchurch to
ensure that local government legislation is enacted and passed according to law. That
did not occur, and those people were po tentially very vulnerable. So this piece of
validating legislation ensures that the errors and omissions made by staff and
councillors long gone are, in fact, put right.
As other speakers have said, this House does not like to consider these sorts of
validating pieces of legislation. Regrettably, we are all too often put in a position where
errors of this sort at a local government level do occur, and it is up to a local member,
who has no real opportunity to put right the error, to come to the House, seek  the time
of the House, seek the goodwill of a select committee, and then put it to the House —
where time and effort is occupied at not inconsiderable cost to the taxpayer —to ensure
that things are put right on behalf of the innocent ratepayers of Christchurch.
I hasten to add that this is not a small territorial authority. Christchurch City Council
represents one of the largest council operations in the country. The level of expectation
that rests upon it is surely at the high end of the spectrum in terms of compliance, in
terms of fulfilling its role as local body legislator, and in terms of protecting the rights
and interests of the ratepayers. So I am not in any way going to discount the roles and
obligations of smaller jurisdictions, of smaller councils , but I think that sometimes they
may not have the same access to legal counsel and the same access to professional
advice and information that the very large councils do.
Christchurch City Council is a very significant enterprise. It is an enterprise tha t is of
large size and volume and that pays its senior staff extraordinarily well in order to get
things right. On this occasion, over a period of not 1 year, not 2 years, not 3 years, not 4
years, but, in fact, a whole decade, these errors were not spotte d. These errors were not
spotted by the highly paid professional staff of the council and then the councillors were
not made aware of it. Perhaps worse, to add insult to injury, nor was the error spotted by
the auditors who were also charged with ensuring that these kinds of errors do not slip
through the cracks.
This is an unfortunate piece of legislation. It is a piece of legislation that I would
prefer, as chair of the select committee, we did not have to bring to the House.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I am very conscious of the fact that we do need to
progress quickly so we can get another bill drawn out of the ballot, so I will not take up
too much of your time up here, like some people appear to be trying to do . I do

good speakers—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Get on with it, Ron.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Jonathan, Jonathan —have a holiday, mate. It is coming soon; do not
worry. Anyway, so this is what I mean —the collegial atmosphere was in existence, and
then someone arrives in the Chamber. But never mind; we will move through.
I do apologise if I am actually going to repeat some of the things that have been said,
but I do have to get them on the record for New Zealand First, so bear with me, please. I
6 May 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3287
have got to applaud Scott Simpson again. That speech hit the nail right on the  head. I,
unfortunately, was not able to be at the Local Government and Environment Committee
hearings in Christchurch that day, but the one comment that came back consistently —
and the member Scott Simpson has put it on the table here today —was about the
attitude and the behaviour of the Christchurch City Council officials. There are some
good members on that committee from the Government side. They have all expressed
their dismay and their concern at the behaviour. I would like someone on the
Christchurch City Council to read the Hansard, to replay these speeches from this
evening, and to take a message, because this message comes from the whole of the
select committee.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: No, it doesn’t.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Well, that messag e about the behaviour of Christchurch City
Council—well, OK, Labour is distancing itself from that; New Zealand First is not.
New Zealand First is not. New Zealand First does not like passing retrospective
legislation to tidy up muck -ups, mess-ups, stuff-ups from people who get highly paid —
well paid—to not make such mistakes. We do not actually like having to support this
piece of legislation, but we will because it is the quickest, cleanest, and most sensible
way of tidying up an inexcusable situation that  has arisen and been allowed to occur
over 10 years.
I am going to take the opportunity to mention some of the things that I raised during
the select committee hearing. I have heard a lot of rhetoric from certain people
promoting super-cities and telling me such things as that they bring a greater capacity to
employ people with high skill sets that small councils cannot. Let us be clear about this.
Carterton District Council is the third -smallest council in New Zealand. It has never
made a stuff -up like th is. It cannot afford to pay people the exorbitant rates that that
former chief executive officer of Christchurch City Council, who became infamous all
over New Zealand, got. In fact, I think he got fired or dumped from Hamilton, went
down to Christchurch, inflicted his misery down there, and got paid an absolute fortune
for doing so, and yet oversaw this debacle as one of a couple of chief executive officers
who oversaw it.
The process and the procedures that most competent, well -run councils have is that
they have a run sheet sitting there to guide the mayor and to guide the council through
the motions that have to be put, and the run sheet is accurate. The run sheet is not
inaccurate and does not lead the councillors or the mayors into such a debacle. The
person who, at the end of the day, is ultimately responsible for making sure that that run
sheet is accurate and that those resolutions that are moved are legally binding and
accurate and in compliance with the law is the chief executive officer. End of story.
It is absolutely appalling that we end up dealing with an issue where the uniform
annual general charges were not correctly passed and seven targeted rates were
inappropriately described in resolution, and that we ended up here. For the council to
then turn up at the select committee and behave in such a way that was less than contrite
I find absolutely astonishing. And that comes from me, someone who lived in
Christchurch for 30-odd years and spent a hell of a lot of time working with people like
Vicki Buck, Garry Moore, and a whole bunch of Labour councillors whom I got to
know very, very well through my time being a Labour Party member down there.
So this annoys us in New Zealand First. It annoys us that we are wasting the time of
the House and th e time of the select committee and the taxpayers’ dollars tidying up a
mess that should never have occurred, and it annoys us that the council should have
been less than contrite and, in fact, came across as somewhat flippant and arrogant
about the whole t hing. It annoys me as a former mayor of a small rural council that I
continually hear about how wonderful super -cities are. Let us be clear: Christchurch
3288 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 6 May 2015
City Council is a super -city. It is the first super -city. I actually also find it quite ironic
that the Minister who is having to bring this legislation to the House as a member and
actually advance it through was also herself a member of Environment Canterbury as
well.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEP ULONI

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I am pleased to rise and take a call on the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill , sponsored by t he Hon Nicky
Wagner, MP for Christchurch Central. The Local Government (Rating) Act provides an
avenue for councils to amend incorrectly set rates. In the case of Christchurch, it was to
correct irregularities that occurred in the resolutions setting the C hristchurch City
Council’s rates for the financial years 2003 -04 to 2012 -13. In particular, as we have
already heard from my speech on the previous reading, Christchurch City Council had
been in breach of the Local Government (Rating) Act for some 10 years —some 10
years. It seemed that the council may have felt that its oversight of resolutions required
would eventually right itself, but it did not. Perhaps with the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes
the resolutions error was the furthest thing from its immediate at tention. But the
problem, as suggested, just moved over for the urgency of the earthquakes. Were the
council bureaucrats aware pre -earthquake of the rates resolution issue? Did they know
that, if left, the Government may intervene? And did the councillors know about the
situation? Or was this a genuine oversight? Was it arrogance? What was it? We in this
House will never really know. For all our posturing and finger pointing here today, we
must conclude that we will never know what happened there, even incl uding those
auditors. And who kept an eye on those auditors? We will not know.
What we do know, though, is that we are here today. This National -led Government
is righting the wrongs of the past. We are doing that. Some of this stuff happened back
in the time of the previous Government. It was unaware of it. The window for the time
of the Christchurch City Council rates resolution has passed. We need to move on. We
have been here before, though, have we not? The Government has passed retrospective
legislation pertaining to rates validation. Let us look at the first time we passed
retrospective legislation on rates validation. The member Damien O’Connor sponsored
the Tasman District Council (Validation and Recovery of Certain Rates) Bill  during the
