items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: I take great pleasure in rising to make a brie f
contribution in the Committee stage of the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation)
Bill. I have a couple of comments to make, but I do actually have a question for the
Minister in the chair, Nicky Wagner, which I hope at some point she may be able t o
address. My specific point that I want to make actually references comments that have
been made in this debate already by the honourable member Major Ron Mark from the
New Zealand First Party. In response to some of the things Ron Mark said, I have to sa y
that I share his view that the Local Government and Environment Committee works
together very well and in a collegial way under the able and eminent chairmanship of
the honourable member Scott Simpson, the member for Coromandel.
Although none of us want to have to deal with such an issue, this has been a bill that
we have worked our way through in a calm, considered, and consistent manner,
listening to the views of the only submitter on this bill, which was the Christchurch City
Council. We have come up with a pragmatic solution to the issues that were faced due
to the incorrect charging of rates over a period of years. I would like to refer to the
preamble to the bill, recitals (2)(a) through to (2)(i)(ii), which refer specifically to the
period over which rates were incorrectly charged.
This is an issue that has come up before in the course of discussion around this bill,
but one of the key elements that distinguishes this bill from many of the others we see is
that it contains a large degree of retrosp ectivity—that is, it has a retroactive effect. We
have previously discussed the pros and cons of such a state of affairs. In fact, I believe
that last time I referred to the great British legal theoretician A V Dicey, who was an
Oxford Vinerian Professor o f English Law and debated the different benefits and
consequences of having retrospective clauses in legislation. This, however, I think
would fit Dicey’s definition of a curative provision in this bill, because it sets right a
wrong. It is not entirely a victimless crime, which I think is a term used by the Green
Party member Eugenie Sage. In fact, the Minister herself might have used that term. It
3290 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 6 May 2015
is not entirely victimless as there are some affected parties, but it certainly is not by
righting this techn ical failure made by council staff and advisers and councils
themselves in the resolutions they passed over a very long period of time —in righting
this wrong—it is restoring the state of affairs that should have existed had everything
been properly done. T here are no real victims to this change that is being proposed in
this piece of legislation.
I want to single out in particular the sponsoring member as it is a local bill, a bill
local to Christchurch, but also it is a bill brought forward by the local m ember, the Hon
Nicky Wagner. I think she is an excellent, very hard -working, very assiduous member
who has brought us a simple, clear, and concise but very well -formed piece of
legislation, which does exactly what needs to be done.
The question, I suppose , I have for the sponsoring member in the chair goes to the
specific detail around what we are actually retrospectively validating. The question that
I have is about the uniform annual general charge —if the member has any information
on this—that is being retrospectively validated. What kind of proportion is that amount
compared with the seven other targeted rates that are being retrospectively validated? It
is certainly something we went through in the select committee, but I am still not
entirely clear ab out the scale of retrospective validation of the uniform annual general
charge as compared and contrasted with the seven other targeted rates, which I think
encompass issues such as water and drainage board rates. If there was an opportunity to
hear from the sponsoring member on that I would certainly welcome that.
The other question that we had in the select committee that we asked the council —
which was the only submitter on this bill—when we were going through line by line and
analysing each clause of this bill. It did not exactly have the tone, I think, of response, in
my perception, that the honourable Ron Mark detected in that I did not quite see
arrogance, but I certainly saw a slight dismissiveness in the reaction in terms of taking
accountability an d responsibility for these mistakes that were made in the past, as
referenced in the preamble to this piece of legislation. The question I have is around
whether this can happen again and whether the validating legislation was absolutely
necessary, given t he council has corrected this in its own internal processes to make
sure that in its own case, anyway, in its locality, we are not going to see such an issue
arise again in the future.
What we heard from the council did contain elements of dismissiveness and elements
of, perhaps, pushing the blame on to staff who were no longer in their offices within the
city council today. I acknowledge that this has been an ongoing problem for many,
many years, in fact going back to 2003, throughout the periods of tenur e of two
different Governments of the Realm of New Zealand, and certainly different councillors
and council officials have cycled through that organisation over that time period. I was
somewhat taken aback that there was not an entire degree of acceptance that the fault
was with the council for not having followed what are clear provisions in the basic
legislation that councils are required to enforce and to carry out under section 119 of the
Local Government (Rating) Act.
Although it is pleasing to see that this is being remedied, I think there were a number
of members on the committee —including, clearly, Mr Mark from his comments, but I
think others, particularly on this side of the House —who were not entirely pleased to
see a council not taking full responsibility for its past conduct.
Although it is absolutely imperative that we do pass this legislation to correct the
situation that exists and to make sure that those $600,000 or so worth of retrospectively
unpaid rates that currently cannot be legally c ollected because they were not correctly
levied in the first place —to make sure that those $600,000 worth can be collected —I
would be very interested to hear from the Minister in the chair, the sponsoring member
6 May 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3291
of this bill, whether there was any informat ion that she might be able to provide the
Committee around the breakdown of the annual uniform general charge versus the
seven other targeted rates, just so we can get an idea of their relative scale.
Other than that small question, I think this is an exc ellent, well -drafted piece of
legislation. Although it is retrospective it does not have any of the monstrous effects of
retrospective legislation such as the Habeas Corpus Suspension Act 1794, which, I
think, is held up by many as the gravest example of a n evil piece of retrospective
legislation. For that reason I take enormous pleasure in commending the bill to the
Committee and hope to hear contributions from others on the other side of the Chamber,
who so seldom allow a bandwagon to pass them without ju mping on board. Rather than
having a curtailed debate, rather than having democracy crushed in this Chamber by an
Opposition who wants to silence debate on an issue that I think we all agree on, let us
hear a meaningful, useful, and decent contribution fro m Opposition members. Mr Mark
did a very good job and I just wish the Labour members could do the same.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I would just like  to
respond to the questions in terms of the uniform annual general charge. It was correctly
stated that there were seven ratings that were irregularly passed —this is on top of the
general rating irregularity. Two of them were concerned with the Church Bay  sewer
loan rate and the Church Bay water loan rate, and it was in terms of the fact that they
were a fixed amount per rating unit.
The same thing was also to do with the Governors Bay sewer loan rate and the
Governors Bay water loan rate. On top of that they failed to state that there was liability
for a restricted water targeted rate and that that was calculated on the level of service
through the restricted water supply system. On top of that there were two rates to do
with waste minimisation and the fa ct that they are fixed amounts per rating unit. I think
that is probably the key issue here.
Finally, there was a water fire service connection rate. Again, that was calculated on
a number of connections, as provided for by the city council’s rating impac t statements.
Getting to the uniform annual general charge, the key issue here was that they failed to
say that it was calculated on the number of separately used or inhabited parts of the
rating unit. That was the key issue. These ones here were not the a mounts of the rates; it
was the fact of how they were to be charged. Thank you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: I move, That the question be
now put.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be now put.
Ayes 58
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 12.
Noes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I rise just to spend a few moments
actually talking on the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill. I find what we
have watched as we have gone through this d ebate absolutely extraordinary. We have
had a conversation earlier where everyone contributed to the debate and now we are on
to something that is actually perhaps just a little bit more uncomfortable for the
members of the Opposition, particularly those f rom Canterbury. They do not want to
participate in the debate. They walk out. They say that they do not like local bills. Well,
local bills deserve the respect of actually being debated. When councils have delivered
3292 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 6 May 2015
us something that we have to do retrospe ctively, it deserves our attention. It deserves us
identifying areas that need to be improved, so we do not do this again. The flippant
disregard from half of that lot over there, who have disappeared, saying that they do not
want to continue the debate is, I think, a disgrace.
Specifically, I would like to talk about some of the components and particularly the
clauses in this short and focused but important bill. In particular, I would like to talk
about the changes that are included around naming the due  dates and the penalties,
validating the annual general charge, and , particularly, the seven other targeted rates —
the Church Bay sewer loan rate, the Church Bay water loan rate, the Governors Bay
sewer loan rate, the Governors Bay water loan rate, the restricted water targeted rate, the
waste minimisation rate, the water fire service connection rate, and the uniform annual
general charge, which were included specifically in clause 4 of the bill. It was raised as
a particular question earlier.
We have had quite a lot of debate today particularly around the process. We heard
the Minister answer one question in particular in her immediate comments, when
introducing tonight’s conversation, around how the process has improved , particularly
with the Christchurch  City Council in terms of how it manages its processes internally
to ensure that it is at best practice in respect of notifying and setting rates and the
process around that.
I just want to echo the importance of this bill sending a message not only to
Christchurch but also to other councils around the country, around the Government’s
expectation that best practice is followed at all times. We heard from the member Mr
Mark, in a very considered and impassioned contribution earlier to this debate, around
the provision of run sheets and the importance, specifically, of councils following those.
His experience was that this is relatively easy to do, and he was surprised that in this
case this city council missed that. Yes, of course there is Audit New Zealand,  which can
provide a double-check in terms of further confidence. But, quite frankly, this should be
picked up in an internal process check that the chief executive officer should oversee,
and there should be their own internal controls to make sure that this does not happen.
We should not be put in the position, quite frankly, of having to do this revalidation
bill. The  council should have had the internal controls in there from day one,
particularly when you reflect that this was a changing approach. Thi s was a council that
was trying to simplify a process. When you try to simplify a process you change from
the status quo. You would assume, therefore,  that there was some focus put on the fact
that the council was changing what it had done, compared with what it used to do, and
would say: “L et us ensure that we have got our ducks lined up and we are doing this
correctly in terms of the due process expected of us. ” It did not happen , i t should
happen, and our expectation is that we would not have to be put into this position again.
I do acknowledge the speed with which the Christchurch City Council reacted when
this was brought to its attention in the last couple of years. But as has been raised
tonight, I was left wanting in respect of the attitude at the s ubmission process by the
Christchurch City Council. Maybe I am being a bit harsh, but process improvement can
take an organisation only so far. Attitude and culture are important, too. I think that in
the context of this bill, and particularly for the Christchurch City Council, this is a point
just to reflect on. Yes, you can turn up to a submission process and talk relatively
obliquely to the process changes that you have brought in to ensure that it will not
happen again. The Christchurch City Council off icers can talk to a process
improvement, but it is very important that those same officers reflect on the importance
of culture in their organisation, to be able to ensure that they do not allow this sort of
thing to happen again. We never got the sense of  that. We never got the sense that,
actually, the Christchurch City Council saw this as an appalling indictment on its own
6 May 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3293
collective approach to managing issues like this. It was seen as : “Well, you know,
sometimes these things happen and sometimes the Go vernment, or Parliament, needs to
fix them up for us. ” It has been raised earlier, and I just want to reinforce that it is
something that we were not impressed with.
In closing, I want to acknowledge the Minister in the chair, the Hon Nicky Wagner.
She has brought forward two really important local bills and has managed them through
with élan and compassion and focus for her community. Of course, I will echo the
support that our chairman, Mr Scott Simpson, has received. He is a great chair, and it is
a ple asure to be part of a normally collegial Local Government and Environment
Committee, although perhaps there have been cracks tonight. I look forward to seeing
this bill pass. Thank you.
Preamble, Parts 1 and 2, schedule, and clauses 1 and 2 agreed to.
Bill to be reported without amendment presently.
House resumed.
The Chairperson reported the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill without
amendment, and the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill without
amendment.
Report adopted.
SOCIAL SECURITY (CLOTHING ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS AND
UNSUPPORTED CHILDREN) AMENDMENT BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: I move, That the Social Security
(Clothing Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill be now
read a third time . Many of us in this House think that we are very important. Many of
us in this House, particularly on a day such as this, talk about our members’ bills, about
getting “my” bill through, and about having the House’s support for “my” bill. This bill
certainly carries my name, but this is not my bill.
I want to go through some dates that are very important, because they have led to this
place and this time, and to a night where once again these children got caught by
politics. Once again these children got caught in the game that some people play inside
this House with legislation. We go back originally to 1999 and to a woman by the name
of Di Vivian, who a year before had become a grandparent raising grandchildren and
realised how little there was by way of support for kin caring —how children uplifted in
exactly the same circumstances and placed with strangers were given  support by the
State, by their country, by their Government, by their society, but when placed with
those who had a blood relationship to them, they received none. It is Di Vivian whose
name should be on the top of this bill. It is Di Vivian who should be  standing here and
being acknowledged when finally this bill goes through this House.
Di Vivian started in 1999, and in May 2001 the Evening Post reported:
“Grandparents are ready to march through the streets if the Government continues to
ignore their con cerns, says the national co -ordinator of Grandparents Raising
Grandchildren, Diane Vivian.” That was back in 2001. In September 2005 Helen Clark
promised that the approximately 700 grandparents and carers who received
superannuation would get the same paym ents as any foster parent. In December of that
year the then social development Minister, David Benson -Pope, made a public
statement that the longstanding anomaly between relatives and non -kin foster parents
would be addressed in the 2006 Budget. That Budget came and it went, and this promise
3294 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 6 May 2015
was not delivered. In June 2008 the then social development Minister, Ruth Dyson,
announced a decision to give $24.6 million over 4 years to the more than 7,500
caregivers, including many grandparents, who were, at tha t time, parenting more than
10,300 children who could not be looked after by their parents. However, it was not
quite what it was made to look like in that press release. Because although, certainly,
there was some equality being promised, firstly, it was delayed until an implementation
date of 1 April 2009, and, secondly, it did not include the add -on payments such as the
clothing allowance—hence this bill.
But we go on. So in 2009 it was placed inside the Budget for 1 April 2009, and it was
to be deliver ed on. We all know, however, that an election happened in 2008, and so
there came a change of Government. The big fear at that time for the Grandparents

items.speaker: Raising Grandchildren Trust and kin carers was
items.text: “We’re going to get caught again.”
They were caught ins ide a political environment not of their making. These are merely
children who need clothes.
But now I want to actually acknowledge the previous Minister for Social
Development, Paula Bennett, because Paula Bennett, and the National Government,
delivered on that Budget promise in 2009. They promised parity with non -caregivers
around the unsupported child’s benefit, and they delivered it. It was also that Minister,
and a National Government, who provided 500 respite care places a year for
grandchildren and a week -long holiday health camp programme. That was incredibly
well received by the grandparents and the communities that actually look after these
children, many of whom have physical, emotional, and intellectual disabilities. The
respite that that provid ed was greatly welcomed. In June 2012 this Minister, Paula
Bennett, also announced a tailored version of a Toolbox parenting group that was to be
provided free for grandparents raising grandchildren.
I am sure that there are people out there, if they have managed to stay up this late and
sit through the last lots of debate while waiting for this bill, who will be wondering why
I am actually paying this sort of respect to the Hon Paula Bennett because I sit on this
side of the House. I am doing so because i t is not my bill. I am doing so because she
deserves it. She took the promises made by a previous Government and she made sure
they were implemented. She went further—

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: No, give it a minute, give it a minute; we will get to that. But
let us be clear about who delivered what, and let us be honest, and let us give credit
where credit is due. This should not be about politics; this should be about the children.
I take on board that comments should not come from either side, to be frank. This is not
about politics; this about these children.
There was a ministerial task force in late 2013, and I know that the Hon Paula
Bennett put her neck out inside her Cabinet and inside her caucus when s he announced
$10 million every year for 4 years to deliver around the school and year start -up
payment, the establishment grant for when children first come into the home, and also
for the Extraordinary Care Fund. So I acknowledge her, and I do so with no problem
whatsoever, because the facts are the facts and they should be known.
This started with Di Vivian. Without her we would not be here, but it was Ministers
who took it up. I wanted to acknowledge, and I did acknowledge, that Ruth Dyson put it
in the Budget, and at that time it did not cover the clothing allowance —neither did what
was delivered by the Hon Paula Bennett. It is not a criticism of either party; it is the fact
of the reality of history.
What we have now is the recognition that I need to apologise to the caregivers and
the kin carers now, because although I believe that there has been a will on the part of
the Hon Paula Bennett, and I believe there is obviously a will inside this House, to
6 May 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3295
deliver for these children, I have had to put in a  delayed implementation date. There are
many reasons for that, and all of them are political. All of them are political, all of them
are financial, and none of them have anything to do with those children.
So I apologise, and I apologise with a but. I hate doing that, but I apologise because I
felt that it was more important to get this equity etched into legislation so that it cannot
be removed. It is much harder to remove equity out of legislation than it is to put it in.
So although I apologise that the  implementation date is not where you want it to be
because I could not advocate well enough to get it there, I acknowledge the history of
where we have come to at this point. I acknowledge the need. I acknowledge it, and I
commit right now that whether I am in this House or out of this House I will watch the
2018 Budget and I will do whatever I can do, wherever I am —and you ask anybody
who is on a select committee with me how I can advocate —to make sure that every
party that said that it supported this bil l maintains this promise, whoever is writing that
Budget in 2018. Kia ora.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is a privilege and an honour to take a call on this
third reading of the Social Security (Clothing Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported
Children) Amendment Bill. I just want to acknowledge Tracey Martin, who is the
sponsor of the bill, a member’s bill. The words that she has shared, with passion and
with desire and with commitment, are reflective of Mrs Martin and her desire to see that
this bill is championed not only in the select committee but also through legislation, so
that it does achieve the intended result, which is to have clothing parity.
If we were to simplify the bill —and it is not a lar ge bill but it is a bill that makes
amendments that are actually very important —the amendments are not large; they are
small but they are effective. I suppose it is reflective of the children Mrs Martin is
talking about. There are often children who are un seen and unheard, and they are
vulnerable, and yet although they are small, they are actually very important. So I
think—and we acknowledge—that the bill is important.
Although Mrs Martin talked about politics, politics is also about leadership, and I
think that is what is important here. It is the leadership that is shown to be able to take
up that response. At the same time too it is the sort of leadership that politics has, and I
want to state this on the record for those who are listening out there, bec ause it actually
reflects on both sides of the House. Whoever is governing at that point in time is
weighing up a number of different options. So you have got kin carers, you have got
unsupported children and orphans —vulnerable children —and on the other ha nd you
have got education and you have got health. There are lots of demands where you have
to balance the aspect of where you put your resources to best reflect the needs in regard
to where they are at.
So I want to take up the points that Mrs Martin has  put around that. Actually, the
Hon Paula Bennett did take up the concern and champion the cause to ensure that $10
million was set aside to ensure that the kin carers and also grandparents raising
grandchildren were actually represented. One of the things  that both Mrs Martin and I
did work on, and she made it very clear, was the ministerial reference group. That was
chaired by Katherine Rich, and also Diane Vivian was there, who was a bundle of
energy and joy. But at the same time too she was constantly a dvocating, and I think if
there is one person I know who is such a strong advocate it is Diane Vivian. And I too
want to acknowledge Diane Vivian for her role in the Grandparents Raising
Grandchildren Trust. She actually conducted a survey, and in regard t o the results of
that survey she wanted to say that her points were evidence -based. I think that was
really important because that was also what she put on the table as well.
I want to acknowledge Linda Surtees from Fostering Kids, who, again, was also a
very strong advocate, and when we were talking about clothing parity for foster carers
3296 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 6 May 2015
and kin carers, she too understood the importance of ensuring that was there as well.
Also, the famous Katie Murray from all the way up in the far north, who reminded us
very clearly that there are a number of Māori children who were actually in this
situation and who were vulnerable. In fact, they made up the largest proportion of
children who are in care. Of the 12,000 who are in care, at least a third if not more of
those children were Māori and were actually part of Māori whānau and family as well. I
think that her advocacy along with the others was absolutely important to this.
Along with the reference group, though —I want to make mention of this —Mrs
Martin made it rea lly clear that all of the things that we were doing, the Extraordinary
Care Fund and so forth, were not around the clothing parity. She made sure that the bill
would find a passage so that it actually had a way of addressing those areas of concern
as well.
I too want to commend Mrs Martin, and I want to talk just briefly about some of the
points that we have been sharing here. One of the ones is around kin carers. We know
that there are 12,000 children who are in care. I think the thing is that the issues t hat
have been the cause of that also need to be of concern. These are vulnerable children,
whether it be because of the death of parents, either both or one, or whether it be
through the breakdown in the family. It could also be through abuse and neglect. Often
we heard the stories of when there was a knock on the door and there were these
children who were bundled up and taken over to the care of grandparents, who often
then had to readjust their own lives to be able to accommodate the care of these
children. We believed that it was really important that we needed to address this as well.
So in acknowledging kin carers, and this bill has brought them to the forefront, we can
now acknowledge that not only are there foster carers but there are kin carers, and  we
acknowledge the role that they play.
I also want to talk about the Toolbox parenting groups that Mrs Martin has been
talking about because I think that is quite critical. So along with the Grandparents
Raising Children Trust and Parenting Place, one of  the things that Diane Vivian talked
about was the fact that often carers are in their twilight years. Here are grandparents
heading towards retirement, and all of a sudden they are faced with having to raise
children again. So they then have to readjust t heir lives, so the work that has been done
through the Government and through the Ministry of Social Development is to be able
to partner with The Parenting Place to set up Toolbox parenting groups that allow them
to have what they call a refresher course,  really. I know that a number of grandparents
have appreciated that as well.
The other area that I think has been important, which is relating to the bill and is in
support of the bill, is in regard to the Extraordinary Care Fund. I do remember that in
one of our reference group meetings it was actually Katie Murray who brought up this
point. She said that when we have these children in our care there comes a time when
you want to lift them out of the challenges that they face. They are often emotionally,
physically, and psychologically traumatised. So how do you then find a pathway for
them to be able to reach their full potential? That is what she talked about. She then
said: “What if there was an opportunity to have a fund that allowed them to do extra
things that would support the development of these children’s potential?”. That is
actually what has happened out of that. One of the recommendations was the
Extraordinary Care Fund.
I am happy to report to the House that 300 children and young people have b enefited
from this. In fact, the fund now gives grants of up to $2,000 per child, and in this round
of funding we have distributed 360,000 of those. The areas that the fund goes towards
are extra tutoring for kids who are struggling in school, for instance , or orthodontic
work not funded by the Ministry of Health. It covers costs to attend national and
6 May 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3297
regional sports tournaments. In fact, Katie talked about that, and that for the children
she was caring for, and other carers whom she knew of, there was a c hance that they
could actually then maybe represent a regional sports team. This was a great chance to
be able to give them confidence. It was an opportunity to be able to build on their
potential, and then, hopefully, out of their confidence and their pot ential, it would bring
them out of the trauma that they were currently facing and experiencing, and actually
give them a sense of hope to be able to develop their full potential as well, and we think
that is important.
One of the things the fund has also g one towards is music lessons where the child
can progress ahead of their peers as well. Only 36 of those applicants were unsuccessful
in the inaugural funding round, and so we think that has provided extra support to these
children. Again, the key areas th at have come out of the words of the grandparents
raising grandchildren and the kin carers is this: they want their children to thrive, they
want them to achieve, and they want them to belong, and that is really important as
well.
One of the other areas of  support that goes with this bill is around the dedicated
person at Work and Income. This actually is important, because although we have got
the bill that is in place, one of the complexities and challenges that have come out of the
ministerial reference group’s conversations was often them going to explain their
situation to Work and Income. Grandparents were unsure, because it was often their
own children, obviously, and how would they explain some of the challenges that they
faced—that there was a break down in the family, or abuse and neglect? So what has
actually happened is that the Government has ensured that Work and Income has
assigned a manager at the national office to work with the grandparents raising
grandchildren, and field officers, to ensure  that there is sensitivity and understanding,
but also that the pathway to receiving the support is one that is a lot more seamless, and
that the grandparents will receive the support that they need as well.
I just conclude my remarks —and I do take on boar d what Mrs Martin has said,
which is that there is a commitment that has to be made —a promise has been indicated
in this bill. Yes, we know that the start date for this bill has been delayed to 2018. I
think that is a good omen, obviously, for the 2017 ele ction for the National
Government, which will continue to keep its promises —not only to Mrs Martin,
because, as she said, this bill is not about her; actually, this is about the children, it is
about the grandchildren, and it is about the kin carers.
So I conclude my remarks by acknowledging you, Tracey Martin, for your advocacy
and your championing, and also acknowledging Diane Vivian, a champion for
grandparents raising grandchildren; Linda Surtees, for Fostering Kids; Katie Murray up
in the far north; an d also all of the other grandparents raising grandchildren and kin
carers who are out there. We desire and hope that all the support that has been given,
even through this bill, will be of much support. Finally, as I said, these children will not
only reac h their full potential but they will thrive, they will achieve, and they will
belong. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am going to be very brief, because on this side of
the House we are still optimistic that if the Government does indeed support this bill it
will see it passed tonight.
I want to restrict my comments to, really, only three things. First, my thanks to
Tracey Martin, because even though, as she has so humb ly and eloquently put it, she
does not consider this bill to be hers, every bill needs a champion, and she has been an
excellent champion. So I thank her for her work. We have got to acknowledge people
like Di Vivian and the Grandparents Raising Grandchild ren Trust for their work and
their advocacy. Yes, this has had a long history —no one is denying that—but we owe it
3298 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 6 May 2015
to them to move swiftly on something as important as this. Finally, I acknowledge the
small, lost opportunities that we have had. We have not  quite achieved parity with this
bill. If we were achieving parity, we would extend to those who are receiving the
unsupported child’s benefit all of the special allowances that a foster carer receives.
There are more allowances than just a clothing allowa nce. We will continue to
campaign for all of those additional benefits to be received until absolute parity is
reached.
Finally, it is not Tracey Martin’s fault that this is not coming in until 2018. She
absolutely did her best. There have been many reaso ns given on that side of the House
as to why it has been delayed; I do not think any of them stack up. In 2018 that
Government might not even be in office. So at least we can give this guarantee: it is our
intention that we will be in office, and we absolu tely guarantee this bill will be
implemented as soon as we reach office. That is the guarantee that we give. The reason
why I am still so disappointed that we are waiting that long is because all of us received
these letters and these images from children asking for us to put this through
immediately. I will leave my final words to the note I received that said: “I am nearly 5
years old. Please do not make me wait till 2018 for the clothing allowance. Grandma
and grandad are on a pension.” I do not even thi nk they should have to wait longer than
tonight.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: It gives me a great honour to rise and
speak to this third reading of the Social Security (Clothing Allow ances for Orphans and
Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill. To start with a quote from Victor Hugo,
“Nothing is more powerful than an idea whose time has come.” I think the time for
Tracey Martin’s idea has come. I think it is time for her bill to be passed into legislation.
I acknowledge Tracey Martin. I am yet to have a member’s bill pulled out of the ballot
myself, so I congratulate her on following this bill right through the legislative process.
I also want to take some time to acknowledge Tracey Mart in for sharing some of her
personal stories with us at previous readings to give this bill a context and a
background. It is very much something to remind ourselves that in a country like New
Zealand, it is our personal stories and our experiences that bin d us together and move
this proud nation forward.
While we are talking about the care of children, I just want to acknowledge that
yesterday was the International Day of the Midwife. New Zealand has a world -leading
midwifery system, and I think we need to  take time to acknowledge yesterday’s
International Day of the Midwife. I know that from personal experience. Obviously I
did not use the service for myself, but my wife did last year. It is a fantastic service,
especially for new parents who obviously do not have an instruction book and are
learning as they go. To engage with your midwife at the start of the pregnancy and to
have her support the whole way through, from birth to aftercare, is an amazing support.
I worked for a number of years for the British National Health Service, and I know for a
fact that it does not have the level of care in midwifery and the same system of the
continuity of care of one midwife through. So I just acknowledge midwives in New
Zealand.
This bill is about supporting childr en’s development. We know that children’s
development is important. If a child does not develop rightly or correctly or go through
the right transition of developmental stages, this can cause problems and poor outcomes
during their teenage years and later on in their lives. We know that for children,
especially from the ages of 0 to 3 years, their brains are being hard -wired at this stage
and there is a great amount of neurological development. In fact, I went to a breakfast in
the Grand Hall here a few wee ks ago, hosted by the Brainwave Trust, which promotes
understanding, research, and evidence around neurological development with young
6 May 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3299
people. It is a very important stage of their lives, and it is an amazing commitment that
kin carers make to step in and support young children at this stage to ensure that they
get the best start in life, and to ensure that they reach their full potential.
Of course, not all kin carers will be supporting young children. Some will be
stepping in at the age of a young adult. We know from our own experiences —I am sure
that everyone in this House will know —that it is an important developmental stage
being a youn g adult and moving into adulthood, and there are a lot of issues going on
around the time of pubescence to do with identity, and making that transition towards
supporting yourself. We do know that young people need good role models and they
need good suppo rt systems round them. That is why this bill is right about supporting
kin carers who step in to keep young people on the right track to making them
productive citizens in New Zealand.
I used to work in the Tavistock Clinic in London. It is where the atta chment theory
was developed by Bowlby. We know that young people who have a strong attachment
to people in their lives, whether it be their biological parents or kin carers, will go on to
lead very productive lives. So it is about supporting this. It actua lly reminds me very
much of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. We know that young people have physiological
needs around food, water, shelter, and air, and you can describe clothing as a
physiological need for a young person. We know that young people need safet y from
violence and abuse. But it is also about love and belonging. I think that this is what this
bill represents about supporting carers who take the decision to step in and provide love
and belonging to young people who are not biologically their children.
I think it is right that the Government takes steps to support these carers in any way it
can. I do not think it is right that foster carers currently get this allowance but
unsupported carers do not. It is great that this bill will give them parity. We know, with
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, that those young people who progress up that triangle go
on to have self -esteem, confidence, and to make the right decisions in life. Of course,
the top is around the self -actualising of reaching their full potent ial. We know that we
hope and aim for every young person in this country to go on and reach their full
potential, to be productive, and to drive New Zealand forward.
This member’s bill will give orphans and unsupported children a clothing allowance
parity with foster children. Currently, orphans and unsupported children, including
some who are looked after by their grandparents, miss out on a clothing allowance that
is available to foster children. The bill seeks more parity between the financial
entitlements for orphans and unsupported children and the financial entitlements for
foster carers.
The purpose of this bill is to increase financial support for kin carers who are looking
after children, such as grandparents raising grandchildren. The Social Servi ces
Committee has suggested inserting a new section into the Social Security Act 1964 to
add a clothing allowance for caregivers who receive an orphans benefit. This addition
will ensure children are treated equally regardless of their circumstances and wh o their
caregiver is.
We know that there are up to 12,000 New Zealand children being cared for by wider
family members. That is 12,000 —that is a considerable group of young people in New
Zealand. This might be because of the death of a parent or a breakdo wn in a family
arrangement. I know for myself, dealing with constituents in my area, that I am
supporting examples of this relationship. One couple, who were actually friends of the
biological parents, decided to step in and look after two young kids. Ther e was another
example where grandparents decided to step in and look after a very young child.
I know from my own experience —I am learning very quickly as a new parent —the
commitment, the patience, and the resources that you need to be an effective parent . I
3300 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 6 May 2015
can only imagine what it is like to step in to this arrangement with kin carers and to
continue to provide those things. I think that needs to be applauded, and that it is right
that we are ensuring parity for the clothing allowance between foster care rs and carers
of orphans and unsupported children.
This is part of a bigger picture —the White Paper for Vulnerable Children —
committing an extra $10 million to provide further support for kin carers. The $10
million, which is a capped fund, has the agreeme nt of the Minister for Social
Development that they will work with Tracey Martin to look at providing further
financial assistance to kin carers in a better, more targeted way. There is a ministerial
reference group that has been formed, which includes rep resentatives from the
Grandparents Raising Grandchildren Trust, which is currently working through options
on how this extra funding will be applied. This member’s bill will give orphans and
unsupported children clothing allowance parity, and I commend it to the House. Thank
you.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: It is with a slight sense of frustration that I am going to get
only a minute to speak on this bill and that it is not going to pass tonight because we
have had very  long, rambling speeches from Government members on bills that have
unanimous support in this House. So often those speeches were not on topic and that
has resulted in us being unable to pass this bill, which is fundamentally about
supporting orphans and u nsupported children in this country. That, to me, is a pretty
embarrassing reality for this House. Even though, again —another embarrassing
reality—that support would not kick in until 2018 because, again, of the miserliness and
penny-pinching of this Gover nment, which is prepared to spend several million dollars
on a flag referendum that nobody wants. It is spending more money on that than it
would have cost to give equality to these children with a clothing allowance, which was
initially intended by the member.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

WEDNESDAY, 6 MAY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
POINTS OF ORDER 
Tabling of Documents—Description of Documents 
Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader —Labour): I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. Yesterday you set out a very clear set of requirements for tab ling documents: 
the source, the date, and a brief description. Yesterday the Minister of Health tabled a 
document, with the approval of this House, that does not have the source identified and 
has a different date from that claimed by the Minister in the H ouse. I am going to ask 
you to look at this because we want consistent application of your requirements for the 
tabling of documents. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I will look at the matter. 
ORAL QUESTIONS  
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economy—Employment 
1. CHRIS BISHOP (Nation al) to the Minister of Finance : What reports has he 
received on the outlook for the New Zealand economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance): More positive reports on the outlook 
for the New Zealand economy. Treasury released its Monthly Economic Indicators  
report for April. It says that economic growth looks set to continue over the first half of 
2015, supported by business and consumer confidence and elevated levels of investment 
and hiring intentions, despite recent easing of those measures. The cost of living has 
fallen in each of the last two quarters for the first time since 1999, and inflation 
expectations and the expectation of businesses to increase their prices remain subdued. 
With no sign of emerging inflation or interest rate pressure, which might normally be 
expected when an economy is growing at 3 percent, the economy is exhibiting capacity 
for further sustainable growth. 
Chris Bishop: What are some of the current challenges and opportunities for New 
Zealand businesses and households? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : One of the challenges is, of course, the reality of lower 
commodity prices. This includes the fall in dairy prices, which has continued in April. 
Dairy prices are now back at levels last seen in December 2014. However, it is worth 
putting this in an international context. Between mid -2011 and December 2014, New 
Zealand terms of trade have actua lly increased by 3 percent. In the same period, the 
Australian terms of trade fell by 23 percent, due to a large fall in the iron ore price. So, 
although dairy prices are down, overall our terms of trade are roughly flat, and that 
compares favourably with Australia, where the terms of trade have fallen by 23 percent. 
Grant Robertson : In light of those answers, how does the Minister reconcile his 
trumpeted 3 percent growth figure with the fact that in Northland unemployment is 9.9 
percent, in Manawatū and Wanganui it is over 7 percent, and in Gisborne and Hawke’s 
Bay it is over 7 percent, and that wage rises over the last period have been the lowest 
that they have been in 2 years —where is the benefit in growth in the economy for 
working New Zealanders? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : At any given time the growth rate is an average across the 
country. The member, I presume, is not suggesting that someone is making up the 
growth numbers. They come from Statistics New Zealand, which has stat utory 
3216 Oral Questions  6 May 2015 
 
independence. If the member wants to use anecdotes, unemployment in the South Island 
is under 4 percent. I have to say, coming from the South Island, we would welcome 
people from Wanganui, Gisborne, and Auckland turning up to fill the empty jobs in t he 
South Island. One of the surprising things about this cycle is how sticky unemployment 
appears to be in some areas where, clearly, there are not as many jobs as there are in the 
South Island. 
Chris Bishop: What reports has he received sho wing how growth in the economy is 
helping to deliver more jobs and higher wages for New Zealanders? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Labour market statistics released today show that 16,000 
more people were employed in the March quarter, meaning that in  the year to March 
74,000 jobs were added to the economy. Labour force participation is now at an all-time 
high of 69.6 percent and New Zealand has the fourth -highest employment rate in the 
OECD—that is, the fourth-highest proportion of the working -age population actually in 
work. Average wages increased by 2 percent over the same period, well ahead of 
inflation of 0.1 percent. 
Chris Bishop: What were the main drivers of employment growth over the last year? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Employment growth has been reasonably broad -based. 
Construction added 23,000 additional jobs. Retail, accommodation, and food services 
added 14,000 jobs, and we know that Labour’s “manufacturing crisis” continues, 
because the manufacturing sector added 1 6,000 jobs in the last year. Members in the 
House may recall that in 2011 the Budget forecast 170,000 additional jobs by about 
now, and the economy is over 20,000 ahead of that forecast. 
Dr David Clark : I seek leave to table a document pre pared by the Parliamentary 
Library, dated yesterday or today, which— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Dr David Clark: Yesterday, I am pretty sure. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The member is making a point of order. I wish to hear it. So 
it is dated today, we have established. 
Dr David Clark: Either yesterday or today. It came into my in-box overnight. 
Mr SPEAKER : All right. Just quickly describe the document and I will decide 
whether to put the leave. 
Dr David Clark : The document is clear that a third of the economic growth is 
attributable to the— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I do not need any more. The point of tabling that document 
is to make a political point. It is not to inform members.  
Dr David Clark: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.  
Mr SPEAKER: Is the member attempting to relitigate a decision I have just made? 
Because that will require the member to be leaving the Chamber immediately.  
Dr David Clark: It is a point of clarification. 
Mr SPEAKER: I am not interested in a point of clarification. If it is a fresh point 
of—[Interruption] Order! The level of complaints I had because of the noise coming 
from this sector yesterday means that I intend to do something about it. I have ruled that 
I am not interested in putting that piece of information to the House. It does not require 
a point of clarification. My mind is absolutely clear. If the member has a fresh poin t of 
order I will hear it, but I am not going to have arguments continuing on that particular 
point of order. If the member wants to leave the Chamber, he is certainly welcome to do 
so. 
Hon Annette King: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER : Order! This is a point of order. It had better be a fresh point of 
order. 
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3217 
 
Hon Annette King : Do you intend to rule on the length of answers we are getting 
from the Minister— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The member will also resume her seat. I will judge, as I have 
said on many occasions, the length of answers. But when there are constant interjections 
coming from my left -hand side to the Minister who is answering the question, clearly 
that gives the opportunity for the Minister to then be responding to those interjections. 
Whānau Ora—Auditor-General’s Report 
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
have confidence in his Ministers’ implementation of the Whānau Ora programme in 
light of the Auditor -General’s report finding $42 million of its $138 million budget in 
its first 4 years was spent on administration? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Andrew Little: After the $42 million spent on administration and the untold millions 
eaten up by service providers, how much Whānau Ora money is actually reaching 
families in need? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I do not have the exact number, but I can quote the Auditor -
General’s report where she talks about the success Whānau Ora has had for the many 
families that they spoke to. 
Andrew Little : Wh y, when 2 years ago the Government announced Whānau Ora 
was being overhauled because it was wasteful and ineffective, has nothing changed? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Quite to the contrary, actually. I acknowledge that there were 
some early teething  issues. When you try something new against a very complex and 
complicated environment, and an environment that actually had not been delivering for 
those families, I accept that there were some teething issues. But there are now joint 
agencies, and what has happened is there are now three commissioning agencies. I think 
the new structure that is in place is seeing a greater provision of services for those 
families with those complex needs. 
Andrew Little : When did senior Ministers on the Cro wn-iwi Whānau Ora 
Partnership Group advise him that there were issues of wasteful spending in Whānau 
Ora? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I simply do not have those dates, but I do know that over time 
there have been reviews. As I said, the system was n ew and it was trying to tackle these 
needs for complex families. I think it is actually building into a programme that has 
been very successful for those families. In fact, if you go and have a look at the Ministry 
of Health, for example, it has done a rev iew of Whānau Ora general practices and 
compared them with mainstream general practices, and it has gone on to say that 
Whānau Ora performs as well or better. This is a new way of doing things —putting 
families at the heart of solving those issues, with a n avigator, with these commissioning 
agencies, and I do think it is building into a programme that is delivering results. 
Andrew Little : Why has it taken the Auditor -General’s office and an expensive 
audit report by her to identify the wastef ul spending and the $42 million spent on 
administration, when he had Ministers such as Bill English and Steven Joyce sitting on 
the Crown -iwi Whānau Ora Partnership Group who were there to advise him on the 
progress of the implementation of Whānau Ora? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I do not think the member accurately categorises things. What 
has happened is there were some one -off costs and there has been a new way of doing 
things. I think that came with those costs and with some early teething issues. But the 
changes that took pl ace took place because of the review work done by a variety of 
Ministers, including the work done by Te Puni Kōkiri and by Tariana Turia, when she 
was in Parliament. It actually led to these commissioning agencies, and I think they 
3218 Oral Questions  6 May 2015 
 
have done a much better job of tightening up the system and delivering the results we 
want. 
Andrew Little : Having spent $137 million of taxpayers’ money on Whānau Ora, 
does he agree with the Auditor -General that “It was not easy to describe what it is or 
what it has achieved.”; if so, what consequences will his Ministers face? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Firstly, as I said, the Auditor -General’s report does not cover, 
for the most part, the phase where now you have got the commissioning agencies. So 
that is the first point I would make. Secondly, what I would say is that this is an area 
where we have always spent a lot of money —successive Governments have, and 
actually they have failed to deliver results. One of the reasons is that these families have 
very, very complicated needs. So when you look at Whānau Ora, which nowadays has 
commissioning agents, within that it has the providers that go out there and it has 
navigators—the people who actually sit alongside the families and help them navigate a 
range of different agencies and support measures. Actually, I think that is the right way 
of tackling a very complicated and difficult area. 
Andrew Little: Does he accept that had he bothered to get value for money out of 
Whānau Ora and other Government programmes he would now be in a position to keep 
his promise to post a surplus in the Budget? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, quite the opposite, actually. This Government, over the 
course of the last 6 ½ years, has challenged the siloed approach that was in place under 
the previous Government. Actually, what it has delivered are far better results. That is 
why the Government is actually quite happy to have Better Public Services targets, why 
it actually measures those targets, and why, from everyt hing from health to education to 
welfare, we are delivering better results for New Zealanders. We are doing things a 
different way and, frankly, it is a more integrated and better way. 
State and Social Housing—Sale of Housing Stock 
3. TODD MULLER (Natio nal—Bay of Plenty)  to the Minister for Social 
Housing: What recent announcements have been made about the next steps of the 
Government’s Social Housing Reform Programme? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Housing) : Bill English and I today 
announced that Tauranga and Invercargill have been selected as the first regions for the 
proposed transfer of Housing New Zealand houses into community ownership. This is 
another important step in creating a more effective and efficient social housing sector, 
and is a fantastic opportunity for community housing providers in these areas to deliver 
housing services locally.  No decisions have been made on the number of houses that 
will be transferred into community ownership. 
Todd Muller: Why have these areas been selected? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT: Tauranga and Invercargill have been chosen because they 
have active community housing providers, as well as stable demand for social housing. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: And docile MPs. 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : And I might add to that member that they have also got 
fantastic members of Parliament in both places who actually understand their 
communities and are able to do that. Actually, what is really important is there are very 
good local people who understand local needs and are able to deliver services locally. 
We want to back that, and that is part of this programme. 
Todd Muller: What does this announcement mean for tenants? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : I think it is really important that tenants understand that 
they will continue to be housed for the duration of their needs, that their rent will not go 
up if houses are transferred, and that their eligibility for income -related rent will not 
change unless their own circumstances do. These are tenants in these regions with long 
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3219 
 
and medium-term needs, which gives community providers the opportunity to integrate 
housing with other services that they might provide, like mental health and disability 
support and alcohol and drug counselling. The whole Social Housing Reform 
Programme is about helping more l ow-income and vulnerable New Zealanders receive 
the support that they need. 
Budget 2015—Return to Surplus 
4. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by all his statements in relation to the Budget? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, in the context they were given. I 
particularly stand by my statement that Budget 2015 will be delivered in the context of a 
strong and growing economy and improving Government finances. 
Andrew Little: Having failed to keep his promise to get the books into surplus this 
year, will he guarantee New Zealanders that he will not be breaking any other promises? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I think New Zealanders are smart enough to work out that this 
is a Government that has picked up a hell of a mess from the previous Labour 
Government. It was a disaster that it inherited —a pil e of unfunded programmes and, 
frankly, economic leadership that would be welcomed in Greece but actually is not 
welcomed in New Zealand—and it has tidied the shop up. 
Andrew Little: In light of his backdown on getting to surplus this year, when will he 
be honest with New Zealanders and give a real date on when he will finally post a 
surplus? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : It is important to understand that the data that will be in the 
Budget, like the data that is in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update and all the 
others, is put together by Treasury based on the best estimates it has. As I said to the 
House yesterday, interestingly enough, the revenue number for the Crown over the next 
4 years is $15 billion lower than it would  have been, because of low inflation. It 
happens to be great for businesses and for consumers— 
Hon Member: Take some responsibility. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, actually, I will take responsibility for the fact that the 
economy is growing, we have got the fifth -highest employment rate in the OECD, and 
New Zealanders are flocking back to New Zealand having left in droves under the 
previous Labour Government. 
Andrew Little: Can he confirm that he also has not kept his pr omise to lift exports 
from 30 percent of GDP to 40 percent —in fact, exports have fallen back to just 29 
percent of GDP? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am truly ambitious for New Zealand and for myself , but I 
never realised that Andrew Little was so a mbitious for me, because that is our 2025 
target. He is clearly expecting me to win quite a few elections between now and then. 
Andrew Little : In light of the consistent slide in prices in recent global dairy 
auctions, when can New Zealanders expect him to finally keep his export promise? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I thought we traversed this in the House yesterday, but the 
Government is not responsible for dairy prices. I know that the Opposition might want 
to blame us for them; it certainly did not want to give us any credit for them when they 
were going up, but it does seem to want to criticise us when they are going down. But, 
actually, here is a pretty simple test. We want to grow our exports. Let us sign up to the 
Trans-Pacific Partnership. We are in. Are you in? 
Andrew Little : Having failed to keep his promises, when will he stop making 
excuses, front up, and admit he has let New Zealanders down yet again? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : We are not making excu ses; we are actually presenting the 
Government’s books. Actually, if the member wants to look at any indicators from 
3220 Oral Questions  6 May 2015 
 
consumer confidence, business confidence, right indicators, wrong indicators, the 
election result, the exchange rate movements—all of those things are indicators that it is 
not me who is telling New Zealanders that the country is going well; it is actually New 
Zealanders who are indicating to pollsters and others that the country is going well. 
Hon Member: Give them some credit. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, so give those New Zealanders credit; they know what 
they are talking about. 
Human Rights, Saudi Arabia—Trade Agreements 
5. JAMES SHAW (Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by his statement 
in relation to trade with Saudi Arabia that an “… FTA gives us yet another reason for 
those relationships to grow and be closer together …”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prim e Minister) : My statement actually referred to the 
potential free-trade agreement with the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the 
Gulf, which covers six Gulf States. I stand by my statement: a free-trade agreement with 
that group gives another reas on for relationships to grow and be closer together and 
more focused for our businesses. 
James Shaw: Why is he giving preferential treatment to a regime that has beheaded 
72 people this year—three of whom were beheaded the day he flew out? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I do not think you can say we are giving preferential 
treatment. What we are doing is trading with Saudi Arabia and with other countries that 
make up the Gulf cooperation council. That is not actually new. The member probabl y 
knows that our trade with the Gulf States is our fifth largest. In fact, we sell more 
exports to the Gulf States than we do to the United Kingdom. Actually, we have been 
doing trade for a long period of time. Eighteen senior business leaders came with me  
because they actually see this as a market of opportunity. In the last question I just had 
the Leader of the Opposition telling me he wanted us to do more in terms of exports. 
Well, that is what we were doing last week: leading a trade delegation to grow our 
exports. 
James Shaw: Has he raised human rights with the Saudi regime, and will he make 
any preferential trade agreement conditional on human rights being improved and 
beheadings being stopped? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : In terms o f the latter part of the question, no; in terms of the 
former part of the question, yes. In fact, we had quite an extensive discussion with King 
Salman, and we did raise human rights. And, actually, I might make the point that not 
only did we raise it and have a reasonably extensive discussion  but we did more than 
President Obama did, who did not actually raise human rights when he went to Saudi 
Arabia. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! [ Interruption] Order! Supplementary question, James 
Shaw—[Interruption] Order! I am on my feet. I have called for order again, to allow Mr 
Shaw to ask a supplementary question; the barrage continued. I will next be asking 
somebody to leave the Chamber, to demonstrate that we have got to have a level of 
decorum while questions are being asked. 
James Shaw: Given that he has raised beheadings and human rights abuses with the 
Saudi regime, what evidence does he have that the Saudi regime is improving its human 
rights and stopping beheadings as a result of our trade agreement with them? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I do not have with me the details of their record in this area 
over time. But what I would say, though, is that there are two ways of approaching these 
things, are there not? One is, ultimately, one of isolation, and one is engagement. And if 
the member is suggesting that we should put Saudi Arabia into the camp of isolation, 
then that is a legitimate argument you can make. But I would say that we also do not 
6 May 2015 Oral Questions  3221 
 
agree with the death penalty in c ountries like the United States, and is he really arguing 
that because Texas executes people we should actually have an isolationist policy when 
it comes to the United States? My experience as Prime Minister is that when you have 
good trading relationships , when you get to know people better, you can have more 
fruitful discussions. And, actually, over time, I think you genuinely see change. I am not 
saying Saudi Arabia has a record that we want in human rights, but the evidence that 
people on the ground, at  least, suggested to me, is that over the last few decades it has 
improved a bit. 
James Shaw: So does he stand by his statement to this House “I will not … stand by 
… when people out there are being beheaded”, or does that apply only to non -trading 
partners? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I absolutely stand by that statement. And there is a difference 
between a country that has its own constitution, its own laws, and decides to follow 
those laws, and the actions of a terrorist group. I might not agree, and I do not agree, 
with the death penalty, but, as I said to the member, it is not solely unique to Saudi 
Arabia. It is also true in the United States and other countries. It happens to be true, as 
we know from last week, in Indonesia. In  the end, actually, there is quite a lot of 
difference between a country and a terrorist group like the Islamic State of Iraq and the 
Levant (ISIL). 
James Shaw : Does he think it makes any difference to the people who are being 
beheaded whether they are being beheaded by the Saudi regime or by ISIL? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I think the member is actually better than a sort of somewhat 
flippant question. When people die it is a terrible thing, and I do not agree with 
beheadings. But I am just saying that people live in that country and those are the rules 
and laws of that country, just like we have rules and laws over here that people might 
not agree with. 
James Shaw: How bad would human rights abuses have to be in another country for 
New Zealand not to give preferential trade treatment to that country? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I do not think we are giving preferential treatment. What we 
are trying to do is negotiate a free -trade agreement, which allows access on a  more 
beneficial footing to both parties —and this happens to be the Gulf States, Saudi being 
one of those six partners. If the member’s argument is that we should not actually 
negotiate free-trade agreements with countries that have human rights records th at we 
do not agree with, then you could apply that to quite a number of countries —and they 
are countries that the previous Government also signed free-trade agreements with. 
Whānau Ora—Auditor-General’s Report 
6. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does 
he stand by his statement in regards to Whānau Ora, “They have to be ambitious 
themselves—it’s a higher trust model and it has the potential to deliver better results not 
only for families, but also for taxpayers who are not currently getting the value for 
money they should be.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Does he agree with the Auditor -General in regard to 
Whānau Ora that, using her words, “It was not easy to describe what it is or what it has 
achieved.”, or that “We could not get a consistent explanation of the aims of the 
initiatives in Whānau Ora”, or that “the situation has been unclear and confusing”; and 
what, if anything, has he done about it? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: In terms of the latter part of the question, quite a bit, actually. 
There has been a tightening up  of the system with the commissioning agents and 
various other reviews that have taken place. In terms of the former part of the question, 
3222 Oral Questions  6 May 2015 
 
as I say, improvements have been made, but it is a new way of doing things in a highly 
complex area. The member happe ns to be the MP for Northland. He probably knows 
that in Northland there are some very complicated cases with families that need help 
across a range of agencies. I am sure that when he is in his electorate office on 
Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays , and Fridays, when he is not in 
Parliament, seeing those constituents, he will have many of them coming to him talking 
about those complicated needs. I look forward to seeing those constituents seeing him— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The answer is too long.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Talking about Northland, how come a third of all payments 
made to Whānau Ora provider collectives went to just two of Te Puni Kōkiri’s 10 
regions, and those two regions also happened , by sheer coincidence , to be where two 
former Māori Party Ministers come from; and what did he do as Prime Minister to stop 
this blatantly preferential treatment? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I reject the member’s proposition. Section 5 of the report  has 
where all the money was spent and the different agencies that got them. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I asked him a very 
serious question, and I am waiting for an answer. It is no use saying to me that section 5 
has got where the money was spent. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The Prime Minister rose to his feet and disputed the figures 
that the member had given in his question. That is an answer. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: If he wants to dispute that fact, which is easy to analyse— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Just ask the question. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I am asking the question—all right? 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The member will resume his seat. Now he will stand and 
withdraw that remark immediately or leave the Chamber. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Which remark, Mr Speaker? 
Mr SPEAKER: Stand and withdraw, without embellishment. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Well, I withdraw the remark if it was offending you, but I 
had two remarks there. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Just withdraw the remark, otherwise I will be— 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I withdraw. 
Mr SPEAKER: Now the member, when I ask him to take a supplementary question,

would find a passage so that it actually had a way of addressing those areas of concern 
as well. 
I too want to commend Mrs Martin, and I want to talk just briefly about some of the 
points that we have been sharing here. One of the ones is around kin carers. We know 
that there are 12,000 children who are in care. I think the thing is that the issues t hat 
have been the cause of that also need to be of concern. These are vulnerable children, 
whether it be because of the death of parents, either both or one, or whether it be 
through the breakdown in the family. It could also be through abuse and neglect. Often 
we heard the stories of when there was a knock on the door and there were these 
children who were bundled up and taken over to the care of grandparents, who often 
then had to readjust their own lives to be able to accommodate the care of these 
children. We believed that it was really important that we needed to address this as well. 
So in acknowledging kin carers, and this bill has brought them to the forefront, we can 
now acknowledge that not only are there foster carers but there are kin carers, and  we 
acknowledge the role that they play. 
I also want to talk about the Toolbox parenting groups that Mrs Martin has been 
talking about because I think that is quite critical. So along with the Grandparents 
Raising Children Trust and Parenting Place, one of  the things that Diane Vivian talked 
about was the fact that often carers are in their twilight years. Here are grandparents 
heading towards retirement, and all of a sudden they are faced with having to raise 
children again. So they then have to readjust t heir lives, so the work that has been done 
through the Government and through the Ministry of Social Development is to be able 
to partner with The Parenting Place to set up Toolbox parenting groups that allow them 
to have what they call a refresher course,  really. I know that a number of grandparents 
have appreciated that as well. 
The other area that I think has been important, which is relating to the bill and is in 
support of the bill, is in regard to the Extraordinary Care Fund. I do remember that in 
one of our reference group meetings it was actually Katie Murray who brought up this 
point. She said that when we have these children in our care there comes a time when 
you want to lift them out of the challenges that they face. They are often emotionally, 
physically, and psychologically traumatised. So how do you then find a pathway for 
them to be able to reach their full potential? That is what she talked about. She then 
said: “What if there was an opportunity to have a fund that allowed them to do extra 
things that would support the development of these children’s potential?”. That is 
actually what has happened out of that. One of the recommendations was the 
Extraordinary Care Fund. 
I am happy to report to the House that 300 children and young people have b enefited 
from this. In fact, the fund now gives grants of up to $2,000 per child, and in this round 
of funding we have distributed 360,000 of those. The areas that the fund goes towards 
are extra tutoring for kids who are struggling in school, for instance , or orthodontic 
work not funded by the Ministry of Health. It covers costs to attend national and 
6 May 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3297 
 
regional sports tournaments. In fact, Katie talked about that, and that for the children 
she was caring for, and other carers whom she knew of, there was a c hance that they 
could actually then maybe represent a regional sports team. This was a great chance to 
be able to give them confidence. It was an opportunity to be able to build on their 
potential, and then, hopefully, out of their confidence and their pot ential, it would bring 
them out of the trauma that they were currently facing and experiencing, and actually 
give them a sense of hope to be able to develop their full potential as well, and we think 
that is important. 
One of the things the fund has also g one towards is music lessons where the child 
can progress ahead of their peers as well. Only 36 of those applicants were unsuccessful 
in the inaugural funding round, and so we think that has provided extra support to these 
children. Again, the key areas th at have come out of the words of the grandparents 
raising grandchildren and the kin carers is this: they want their children to thrive, they 
want them to achieve, and they want them to belong, and that is really important as 
well. 
One of the other areas of  support that goes with this bill is around the dedicated 
person at Work and Income. This actually is important, because although we have got 
the bill that is in place, one of the complexities and challenges that have come out of the 
ministerial reference group’s conversations was often them going to explain their 
situation to Work and Income. Grandparents were unsure, because it was often their 
own children, obviously, and how would they explain some of the challenges that they 
faced—that there was a break down in the family, or abuse and neglect? So what has 
actually happened is that the Government has ensured that Work and Income has 
assigned a manager at the national office to work with the grandparents raising 
grandchildren, and field officers, to ensure  that there is sensitivity and understanding, 
but also that the pathway to receiving the support is one that is a lot more seamless, and 
that the grandparents will receive the support that they need as well. 
I just conclude my remarks —and I do take on boar d what Mrs Martin has said, 
which is that there is a commitment that has to be made —a promise has been indicated 
in this bill. Yes, we know that the start date for this bill has been delayed to 2018. I 
think that is a good omen, obviously, for the 2017 ele ction for the National 
Government, which will continue to keep its promises —not only to Mrs Martin, 
because, as she said, this bill is not about her; actually, this is about the children, it is 
about the grandchildren, and it is about the kin carers. 
So I conclude my remarks by acknowledging you, Tracey Martin, for your advocacy 
and your championing, and also acknowledging Diane Vivian, a champion for 
grandparents raising grandchildren; Linda Surtees, for Fostering Kids; Katie Murray up 
in the far north; an d also all of the other grandparents raising grandchildren and kin 
carers who are out there. We desire and hope that all the support that has been given, 
even through this bill, will be of much support. Finally, as I said, these children will not 
only reac h their full potential but they will thrive, they will achieve, and they will 
belong. I commend this bill to the House.
