MATT DOOCEY (National—Waimakariri): It gives me a great honour to rise and 
speak to this third reading of the Social Security (Clothing Allow ances for Orphans and 
Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill. To start with a quote from Victor Hugo, 
“Nothing is more powerful than an idea whose time has come.” I think the time for 
Tracey Martin’s idea has come. I think it is time for her bill to be passed into legislation. 
I acknowledge Tracey Martin. I am yet to have a member’s bill pulled out of the ballot 
myself, so I congratulate her on following this bill right through the legislative process.  
I also want to take some time to acknowledge Tracey Mart in for sharing some of her 
personal stories with us at previous readings to give this bill a context and a 
background. It is very much something to remind ourselves that in a country like New 
Zealand, it is our personal stories and our experiences that bin d us together and move 
this proud nation forward.  
While we are talking about the care of children, I just want to acknowledge that 
yesterday was the International Day of the Midwife. New Zealand has a world -leading 
midwifery system, and I think we need to  take time to acknowledge yesterday’s 
International Day of the Midwife. I know that from personal experience. Obviously I 
did not use the service for myself, but my wife did last year. It is a fantastic service, 
especially for new parents who obviously do not have an instruction book and are 
learning as they go. To engage with your midwife at the start of the pregnancy and to 
have her support the whole way through, from birth to aftercare, is an amazing support. 
I worked for a number of years for the British National Health Service, and I know for a 
fact that it does not have the level of care in midwifery and the same system of the 
continuity of care of one midwife through. So I just acknowledge midwives in New 
Zealand.  
This bill is about supporting childr en’s development. We know that children’s 
development is important. If a child does not develop rightly or correctly or go through 
the right transition of developmental stages, this can cause problems and poor outcomes 
during their teenage years and later on in their lives. We know that for children, 
especially from the ages of 0 to 3 years, their brains are being hard -wired at this stage 
and there is a great amount of neurological development. In fact, I went to a breakfast in 
the Grand Hall here a few wee ks ago, hosted by the Brainwave Trust, which promotes 
understanding, research, and evidence around neurological development with young 
6 May 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3299 
 
people. It is a very important stage of their lives, and it is an amazing commitment that 
kin carers make to step in and support young children at this stage to ensure that they 
get the best start in life, and to ensure that they reach their full potential.  
Of course, not all kin carers will be supporting young children. Some will be 
stepping in at the age of a young adult. We know from our own experiences —I am sure 
that everyone in this House will know —that it is an important developmental stage 
being a youn g adult and moving into adulthood, and there are a lot of issues going on 
around the time of pubescence to do with identity, and making that transition towards 
supporting yourself. We do know that young people need good role models and they 
need good suppo rt systems round them. That is why this bill is right about supporting 
kin carers who step in to keep young people on the right track to making them 
productive citizens in New Zealand.  
I used to work in the Tavistock Clinic in London. It is where the atta chment theory 
was developed by Bowlby. We know that young people who have a strong attachment 
to people in their lives, whether it be their biological parents or kin carers, will go on to 
lead very productive lives. So it is about supporting this. It actua lly reminds me very 
much of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. We know that young people have physiological 
needs around food, water, shelter, and air, and you can describe clothing as a 
physiological need for a young person. We know that young people need safet y from 
violence and abuse. But it is also about love and belonging. I think that this is what this 
bill represents about supporting carers who take the decision to step in and provide love 
and belonging to young people who are not biologically their children.  
I think it is right that the Government takes steps to support these carers in any way it 
can. I do not think it is right that foster carers currently get this allowance but 
unsupported carers do not. It is great that this bill will give them parity. We know, with 
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, that those young people who progress up that triangle go 
on to have self -esteem, confidence, and to make the right decisions in life. Of course, 
the top is around the self -actualising of reaching their full potent ial. We know that we 
hope and aim for every young person in this country to go on and reach their full 
potential, to be productive, and to drive New Zealand forward.  
This member’s bill will give orphans and unsupported children a clothing allowance 
parity with foster children. Currently, orphans and unsupported children, including 
some who are looked after by their grandparents, miss out on a clothing allowance that 
is available to foster children. The bill seeks more parity between the financial 
entitlements for orphans and unsupported children and the financial entitlements for 
foster carers. 
The purpose of this bill is to increase financial support for kin carers who are looking 
after children, such as grandparents raising grandchildren. The Social Servi ces 
Committee has suggested inserting a new section into the Social Security Act 1964 to 
add a clothing allowance for caregivers who receive an orphans benefit. This addition 
will ensure children are treated equally regardless of their circumstances and wh o their 
caregiver is.  
We know that there are up to 12,000 New Zealand children being cared for by wider 
family members. That is 12,000 —that is a considerable group of young people in New 
Zealand. This might be because of the death of a parent or a breakdo wn in a family 
arrangement. I know for myself, dealing with constituents in my area, that I am 
supporting examples of this relationship. One couple, who were actually friends of the 
biological parents, decided to step in and look after two young kids. Ther e was another 
example where grandparents decided to step in and look after a very young child.  
I know from my own experience —I am learning very quickly as a new parent —the 
commitment, the patience, and the resources that you need to be an effective parent . I

can only imagine what it is like to step in to this arrangement with kin carers and to 
continue to provide those things. I think that needs to be applauded, and that it is right 
that we are ensuring parity for the clothing allowance between foster care rs and carers 
of orphans and unsupported children.  
This is part of a bigger picture —the White Paper for Vulnerable Children —
committing an extra $10 million to provide further support for kin carers. The $10 
million, which is a capped fund, has the agreeme nt of the Minister for Social 
Development that they will work with Tracey Martin to look at providing further 
financial assistance to kin carers in a better, more targeted way. There is a ministerial 
reference group that has been formed, which includes rep resentatives from the 
Grandparents Raising Grandchildren Trust, which is currently working through options 
on how this extra funding will be applied. This member’s bill will give orphans and 
unsupported children clothing allowance parity, and I commend it to the House. Thank 
you.
